look.text: A relay console older than the Burn, dust-grey, one green lamp alive on a panel of dead ones. The screen wakes when you touch the frame: RELAY 7 — LINK UP — UPSTREAM: ACK. A cursor, waiting for something it has waited ninety years for.
look.again: RELAY 7 — LINK UP — UPSTREAM: ACK. The one green lamp, and the cursor, still waiting.

passives.text: Upstream is east. The link is live: this station is still part of something that answers.

mods.why: record formats are your trade

log.text: Inbound, nightly, from upstream: a bulletin, twelve lines, the same twelve each night, relayed to the speaker and to a second line that runs — you trace it on the panel — west. Toward the Sallow. Toward a pump station marked DW-4. Outbound, one entry, three weeks old: a request for the bulletin to stop. DENIED.

log_no.text: The log is a format you cannot read fast enough: the screen times out and the cursor comes back, patient.

grid.text: The link in your skull finds the relay before you have decided to let it. Not a voice: a weight of attention, east, enormous and tidy, that notices you the way a clerk notices a line. It reads you — your link's serial, your position, the hour — and files it. Then, politely, it waits.

decision.text: You listened to Signal Hill's relay through your grid link, and something east filed you.

ident.text: IDENT? says the screen. Whatever you type goes upstream, to whatever is there, and comes back as a line in somebody's book.

decision.text: You gave Signal Hill's relay your real name.
You gave Signal Hill's relay a false name.
You left Signal Hill's relay waiting for a name.

named.text: The cursor eats it. UPSTREAM: ACK. The green lamp blinks once, and then, for the first time, a second lamp beside it comes on and stays on.

declined.text: The cursor waits. It is good at it.

again.text: RELAY 7 — LINK UP — UPSTREAM: ACK. The cursor, and the lamps.
again.again: The cursor and the lamps. Whatever is upstream has not written back.

hear.text: A horn speaker on a bracket, wire to the relay rack, and a voice in it: calm, male, not quite a man. "— the overpass. Kessler. Day forty-five. Killed, by the hand of Kade. The overpass. Kessler. Day forty-five —" It does not stop. It is reading a list, and it has reached this line.

interject.text: "Kade." Wren says it the way you touch a burn to see if it still hurts. "Not Kessler. Not him." Then, lower: "Forty-five days from when?"
"By the hand of Kade." Ilya has stopped counting. He says the name again under his breath, as if checking it is the same one. "Right."
"It reads it like the fridge reads the ration list," Tamsin says, very quietly. "Name, number, next."

passives.text: The voice is synthesised from a sample. Under it, the carrier hums at the same pitch as the relay's green lamp flickers.

options.text: (Patch the speaker line into the mast feed. Let the Sallow hear it.)

mods.why: you have seen how the lines are routed

again.again: The voice reaches the end of its list and begins it again. The overpass. Kessler. Day forty-five.

options.text: (Patch the speaker line into the mast feed.)

mods.why: you have seen how the lines are routed

cut.text: The voice stops in the middle of a word. The relay's green lamp does not care. Somewhere east, a line in a book says the bulletin was delivered.

decision.text: You cut the speaker at Signal Hill and silenced the voice.

cut_no.text: The bracket is rusted to the wall and the wire is armoured. You bleed on it and it keeps reading.

amp.text: The mast takes the line like it has been waiting for it. The red light steadies. Out there, in the Sallow, every dead radio with a working speaker says the same five words, and will, every night, until somebody stops it.

decision.text: You put Signal Hill's voice on the mast: the whole Sallow hears the forecast about Kessler.

news.text: a voice from Signal Hill names Kessler and a day he dies
a voice on the dead radios names the Rust Dogs' chief and a day

amp_no.text: You get the feed wrong twice; the second time the mast light goes out for a full minute and the Hollow, below, start shouting. It comes back. So does the voice.

silent.text: The speaker hangs cut on its bracket. The quiet in here is not empty.
silent.again: The cut wire, the bracket, the quiet. Nothing reads.

loud.text: The speaker is quiet now; the mast is not. You can hear the mast through the wall.
loud.again: Through the wall the mast carries the list out over the Sallow, and hasn't stopped.

look.text: Forty metres of lattice, guyed with cable the Hollow have been cutting from the bottom up, a red lamp at the top that blinks slow as a pulse. At the base, a feed cabinet with the station's line going in and nothing you can read going out.
look.again: The mast, the slow red lamp, the guy cables cut away from the bottom up.

passives.text: The lamp runs off the relay's power, not a battery. Something is still paying for this.

view.text: Halfway up, hands black with old grease, the Sallow lays itself out: the highway like a scar, the salt pans white, the windpumps to the south-east in a dead line, and east, past the glass, a smudge on the sky that might be smoke and might be a city.

interject.text: "Rust it," Tamsin breathes, somewhere below your boots. "It just keeps going."

view_again.text: The same rungs, the same grease. The Sallow lies where you left it: the highway, the white pans, the dead windpumps in their line, and the smudge in the east that will not decide what it is.

fall.text: Ten metres up a rung lets go. You hit the cabinet, not the rock, which is the difference between a bruise and the Hollow finding you in the morning.

look.text: A cot somebody has slept on recently, the blanket folded with a care that doesn't belong up here. Under it, scratched into the frame with a nail: the half-sun sign, and a tally of days — twenty-six.
look.again: The folded blanket, and twenty-six scratches in the frame under it.

intro.text: A broad man with a shaved head sits on the yard fence with a long rifle across his knees and a bottle beside him, counting the militia's shots under his breath as they miss. "Six. Seven. Right." He looks at you with eyes that are clearer than the rest of him. "You the one drilling them? Right."

interject.text: "Strand." Wren has stopped well back from the fence. "He put a round through my water can at four hundred paces, the summer I scouted the east road. I was holding it."

passives.text: Two fingers gone on the left hand. The rifle is cleaner than the man.
The way he holds the rifle, drunk, is better than the way Lind holds hers sober.

options.text: You're drunk in front of boys who'd follow you if you stood up.

mods.why: you looked at the hand and not away

options.text: Come east with me. Vasha Kade rides that road.

again.again: He counts something you didn't see. "Right."

options.text: You're drunk in front of boys who'd follow you if you stood up.
Come east with me. Vasha Kade rides that road.

who.text: "Strand. Ilya. Militia, before." He turns the bottle so the label faces away from you, as if that helped. "Benno's mine — cousin. He'll have told you about the post." A pause. "The post was the point."

before.text: He counts a shot that isn't fired. "Before a raid. Dogs. I was out east on a hunt, three nights, because the wind was right for it." His voice doesn't change at all. "The wind was right. Right." He drinks. "Vasha Kade led it. That's the whole story and you've had it."

show.text: He doesn't argue. He stands, which takes a moment, sets the bottle on the fence post, walks fifty paces into the yard, turns, and shoots the bottle off the post without appearing to aim. Then he shoots the post. Nine militia stop breathing. "Right," he says, and sits back down.

news.text: Ilya Strand shot a bottle off the militia fence at fifty paces, drunk, and then shot the fence

shamed.text: For a long moment nothing happens, and then he looks at the militia, who are looking at the ground, and at the bottle, and puts the bottle down on the far side of the fence where he can't reach it. "Right." He stands. "Lind. Give me the four that shoot." He walks into the yard without the rifle.

decision.text: You shamed Ilya Strand sober in front of the militia. He took the drills.

recruit.text: The counting stops. "Kade." He says it like a word he has been keeping dry. "You'd take a drunk east." It isn't a question. "I'd be sober by the Tollhouse. I'd be useless by the bridge and I'd be sober again by wherever she is." He looks at the rifle. "Why."

options.text: Because the militia has nine rifles and four that shoot, and the fifth is drunk on a fence.

mods.why: he told you about the wind

options.text: (Pick up the bottle. Set it on the far post. Hit it first.)
Because a man who shot the post should get to pick which one.

joins.text: "Right." He puts the bottle on the far side of the fence. He picks up the rifle. "I count things. Out loud. You'll get used to it or you won't." He looks east, where the road is, and his face does something you weren't meant to see.

interject.text: "Right," Wren says, in his voice exactly, and doesn't smile. "Long road, then."

decision.text: Ilya Strand came with you, east, toward Vasha Kade.

news.text: Ilya Strand walked out of Shale with the salt-cut stranger, sober

joins_shot.text: The bottle goes. He watches the glass fall for a second longer than anyone else. "Right." He picks up the rifle. "I count things. Out loud." He doesn't look east. He doesn't have to.

interject.text: "Right," Wren says, in his voice exactly, and doesn't smile. "Long road, then."

decision.text: You outshot Ilya Strand's bottle and he came east with you.

news.text: Ilya Strand walked out of Shale with the salt-cut stranger, sober

refuses_shot.text: You miss. He doesn't say anything, which is worse. Then he shoots the bottle, from the fence, sitting down. "Right."

text.text: "Wind's steady." He doesn't say the number of days any more; you notice that he doesn't. "Right."
"Still counting." He means the days. "Right."
"Wind's from the east." He has the rifle slung and his hands are steady, mostly. "Right."

party.again: He is counting something on the road ahead, under his breath.

options.text: You talk about the wind a lot.
Nine reads the city's hand. Your letter.

p_vasha.text: "When." He likes the word. "She knows my name. I want her to know why before. After is after." He counts something. "You'll have an opinion. Keep it until then."

p_wind.text: "Wind's the thing you can't see that moves the thing you can." He shrugs. "Three nights east on a hunt because the wind was right. Right." He doesn't say anything else for a while.

p_letter.text: "At a fire," he says. "Not on a road. Right."

waiting.text: "Right." He is up, the rifle already slung.
waiting.again: He is up before you have finished walking over.

text.text: Ilya sits with his back to a rock and the rifle across his knees, facing the dark and not the fire, and counts something he does not share.
"Wind's steady." He doesn't say the number of days any more; you have noticed that he doesn't. "Right."
"Wind's from the west." The rifle is across his knees and he isn't cleaning it. "Steady. Right."

camp.again: Ilya counts something in the fire under his breath, and stops when you look.

options.text: You said I'd had the whole story. I haven't.
Let me see the letter. I read the city's hand.

mods.why: you have watched the assessor write in the city's hand

options.text: (Take the second watch with him again.)
(Walk down to the well with him.)
(He is at the well again. Walk down.)
(Hold out the bottle he gave you.) You shot better at the fence with one in you. Tomorrow needs that.
(Wren sits down on Ilya's side of the fire, which she has never done.)
(Ash has been watching Ilya not drink for three nights.)
Why do you count out loud?
Teach me to read the wind.

s1.text: He counts the stars in the gap above the fire, gets to forty, and gives up. "Four days." He means sober. "Four. Right." He reaches inside his jacket and brings out a bottle of Rot Bitters with two fingers gone from it, and holds it out to you by the neck. "Carry it."
s1.again: He is still holding the bottle out by the neck.

options.text: (Take it, and pour it out on the ground.)

s1_take.text: "Don't give it back." He looks at the fire, not at you. "If I ask for it, don't give it back. If I don't ask, don't offer. That's all of it. Right."
s1_take.again: The bottle is in your pack. He doesn't look at the pack.

s1_pour.text: He watches it go into the dirt and doesn't move to stop you. "Right." A long pause. "Now I'll want one and there won't be one. That's a plan too."
s1_pour.again: The dark patch in the dirt where it went.

s1_no.text: "Right." He puts it back inside the jacket. He doesn't drink from it. He doesn't put it down, either.
s1_no.again: His hand is on the jacket where the bottle is.

s2.text: "No." He agrees, which surprises you. He counts the sticks in the fire. "Shale. Eleven springs back. My wife was the healer, the only one between Shale and the glass who could set a hip. People walked three days to her." He says her name carefully, like a round he is chambering. "Agi. And two girls."
s2.again: He is still counting the sticks in the fire.

s2_night.text: "I went east on a hunt, three nights, because the wind was right. Kade came up the wash the second night with eleven Dogs and took the water and the medicine store. Agi stood in the store's door." He stops counting. "The girls were in the store. That's the whole of it. Now you've had it."

options.text: The wind didn't send Kade up that wash.

s2_letter.text: He takes a folded envelope from inside his jacket: city paper, heavy, a tower in a ring stamped on the flap, the seal long broken. He doesn't let go of it. "This came for Agi the spring before. She read it and put it in the medicine store and never told me what it said." He puts it back. "Nobody in Shale reads that hand. People say the city's own clerks do. Right."
s2_letter.again: The envelope is back inside his jacket. His hand is still on it.

options.text: Then we find someone who reads it.
Some letters are better left unread.

s2_find.text: "Right." He says it like a man agreeing to a range he isn't sure of. "East, then. Where the clerks are."

s2_unread.again: His hand is still on the jacket.

s3_nine.text: Nine has been sitting by the fire, badly, with the other ledger on its knee. When Ilya holds out the envelope the lens clicks twice and the assessor does not take it at once. "This is a notice under clause 31. Variance correction." Then it takes it, by the edges, the way a doctor takes off a dressing. "Shall I read it aloud, Mr Strand, or to you alone?" "Aloud," Ilya says. "Right."
s3_nine.again: The assessor holds the letter by its edges, and waits.

s3_self.text: It is the city's shorthand under a broken seal, the hand the toll stand's copy-book was taught from, and it reads the way those always read: as if nobody would ever be on the other end of it. You read it aloud, slowly, because it has to be read slowly.
s3_self.again: The letter is open in your hands.

s3_fail.text: The marks are a shorthand inside a shorthand. You get SHALE, and a date, and nothing in between. "Right," Ilya says, and takes it back, and you watch him decide not to be disappointed. "The city's clerks, then."
s3_fail.again: The letter is back in his jacket.

text.text: Nine reads in the voice it keeps for clauses. "SHALE. STRAND, A. HEALER. Growth variance: ahead of plan; water-bearing population four-tenths over schedule. Relocation to the Precinct offered under clause 31; no response constitutes refusal. Variance correction scheduled: spring, the dark of the moon, by the local instrument. Thank you for your continuity." The lens clicks. "It is signed by nobody. They are all signed by nobody."

"SHALE. STRAND, A. HEALER. Growth variance: ahead of plan; water-bearing population four-tenths over schedule. Relocation to the Precinct offered under clause 31; no response constitutes refusal. Variance correction scheduled: spring, the dark of the moon, by the local instrument. Thank you for your continuity." There is no signature. There never is.

s3_read.again: The letter lies open on Ilya's knee.

decision.text: Ilya Strand's letter was read aloud at a fire: the raid that killed his family was on the city's schedule.

s3_after.text: "By the local instrument," Ilya says. He says it again, to check it. Then he laughs, which you have never heard him do, and it is an awful sound. "Eleven years angry at the wind." He folds the letter along its old folds. "She didn't know. Kade. They put a fat store on a dark night in front of her, and she thought she'd picked it." He looks at the rifle across his knees. "Right."
s3_after.again: The letter, folded along its old folds, on his knee.

s3_now.text: "Now I want her to know why, before. Same as ever." He puts the letter away. "Only the why's longer."

options.text: Then she hears it from you, and I'll be standing there.
She's the city's rifle. The hand that wrote that is in a tower.
Maybe she should carry it. Knowing. Alive.

s3_with.text: "Right." One thing, for once. "Standing there's plenty."
s3_with.again: He is cleaning the rifle, slowly.

s3_tower.text: "Right. And the rifle's the part I can reach." He thinks about it longer than you expect. "Ask me about towers after."
s3_tower.again: He is looking at the dark where a city would be.

s3_carry.text: He doesn't like it; you watch him not like it. "Maybe," he says. "Ask me when she's in front of me. Not before."

text.text: "Forty-one rounds since the fence," he says. "Counting the last." He doesn't count anything else for a while. "She knew why. I watched her know it. Right." It is the first time you have heard him say a thing as if it were over.
"You took it." Not angry, or not only. "I've been working out whether I mind. I don't know yet. Right."
"She's carrying it." He watches the fire. "Every day she's alive she knows what she was for. Right. That's longer than a round."
"Somebody else did it." He turns his ruined hand over. "Eleven years, and it was somebody else. Right."

s4_after.text: "Now." He tries the word out. "I don't know what a man does, after." He looks at you as if you might. "Say what you think. Right."
s4_after.again: He is waiting for you to say.

options.text: Shale needs a rifle that counts.
Stay on the road with me.

s4_shale.text: "Ada'd have me back." He thinks. "She'd have me drilling boys at dawn. Right. I could stand that."
s4_shale.again: He is thinking about dawn drills.

s4_road.text: "Right." No hesitation at all. "Somebody has to tell you where the wind is."
s4_road.again: He is reading the wind for tomorrow.

s4_rest.text: "To stop counting." He looks surprised to have said it. "Not today. Some day. Right."

r1.text: The second watch is the cold one. He doesn't talk and you don't, and at some point his shoulder is against yours and he leaves it there, and then he moves it, carefully, to look at you. "I'm forty-one and I count my days," he says. "I'd like to count this. If you'd want that." A pause. "You can say no. Right."
r1.again: He is waiting, and will take either answer.

r1b.text: The second watch again, the cold one. "I asked once," he says. "I'm asking again, once. Then I stop." He doesn't look away.
r1b.again: He is waiting, and will take either answer.

r1_yes.text: "Right." It sounds like one thing. "Not here. Not on a watch, not tired. There's a well — " He stops. "When we're by a well. I'll tell you why there."

r1_later.text: "Right. I'm good at waiting." He is, and he does, and the watch goes on.

r1_no.text: "Right." He means: thank you for saying it plainly. You keep the watch till the light comes, and it is a good watch.
r1_no.again: The watch, and the light coming.

r2.text: He takes the bucket down to the well-head himself and doesn't draw anything. "Agi drew for the whole east street, mornings. I'd carry. That's how it started. A bucket." He sets it on the stone. "I didn't want this anywhere I'd have to learn to remember her not being. So: here, where I already do." He looks at you. "Still want it?"
r2.again: The bucket on the stone. He is waiting, and will take either answer.

decision.text: You went down to the well with Ilya, and stayed.

options.text: Not tonight. Stay here with me, though.

r2b.text: "Another well." He nearly smiles. "I've been counting wells." He sets the bucket on the stone. "Still a question. Still yours."
r2b.again: The bucket on the stone. He is waiting.

decision.text: You went down to the well with Ilya, and stayed.

r2_fade.text: He kisses you like a man who has decided something and wants to be sure of it, slowly, his ruined hand very careful at the back of your neck. The bucket stays on the stone. Much later he tells you the wind has gone round to the south, and for once it means nothing at all.
r2_fade.again: The well, and the bucket still on the stone.

r2_sit.text: "Right." He sits on the well's lip with you until the stars have moved a hand's width, and counts none of them.
r2_sit.again: The well's lip, and the stars.

r2_no.text: "Right." It costs him; he pays it. He draws the water after all, and carries it back for both of you.
r2_no.again: He has carried the water back.

r3.text: "I stopped saying the number." He has noticed you noticed. "Somewhere. I don't know which day." He looks worried about it, and then not. "If there's an after, I'd like to be in it with you. You can say it isn't that. Right."
r3.again: He is waiting, and will take either answer.

decision.text: You told Ilya there would be an after, and that you would be in it with him.

r3_yes.text: "Right." He says it like a whole sentence. Then, quieter, a word you have never heard him use about anything: "Good."

r3_no.text: "Right." He nods, slowly. "It was good to count, for a while." In the morning he reads you the wind as if nothing had happened, which is how he says he means it.

c_rom_end.text: "Take the second watch with somebody else." He says it to the dark. "I count what's good for me now. You haven't been, lately." He doesn't list it. He doesn't need to.

decision.text: Ilya ended it, at a fire. He counts what is good for him now.

c_drunk.text: He's drunk. Not falling: precise and careful, the way a good shot is drunk. A bottle of somebody's bitters stands by his boot. "The boy," he says. "Twenty-two. They wrote him a month and he took it." He stops. "I shot a post once to show off for him. Right."

options.text: (Take the bottle away. Sit with him till it's light.)

c_drunk_sat.text: You sit. Toward dawn he says, "Start again." He says nothing else for an hour. Then: "One. Right."
c_drunk_sat.again: He is counting again, from one.

c_drunk_left.text: In the morning the bottle is empty and he is up before you, the rifle cleaned. "One," he says, to nobody. "Right."
c_drunk_left.again: He is counting again, from one.

c_drunk_join.text: He watches you pour. "Don't," he says, too late, and then nothing, and the bottle goes down faster for two. In the morning he won't look at you, and starts counting again from one under his breath.

x_wren.text: Wren sits down on Ilya's side of the fire, which she has never done. "VASHA is on that garage wall," she says. "Same as mine. Same nail. Dogs go back for the bridge." Ilya stops counting. "Kade's a Dog." "She's the Dog," Wren says. "If I go for the bridge, she'll hear. She'll come, or the city will send her." She doesn't look at him. "Stand with me there."
x_wren.again: Wren is still sitting on his side of the fire.

options.text: Stand with her, Ilya. You'd both be where you need to be.
That's using his hunt for your bridge, Wren.

x_wren_yes.text: Ilya looks at her for a long time, the way he looks down a range. "You're not Kade," he says. "It isn't enough. It's close." He nods once. "Right. The bridge."
x_wren_yes.again: The two of them, on one side of the fire.

x_wren_no.text: "It is," Wren says. "I'm asking anyway." Ilya says nothing. Later, cleaning the rifle, he says "Right," to no one, and you don't know what he has decided.

x_wren_him.text: He takes his time. "If she comes," he says at last, "I'll be on your bridge. If she doesn't, I'll still be on it, and I'll be cross." Wren almost laughs. "Right," she says, in his voice.
x_wren_him.again: The two of them, on one side of the fire.

x_ash.text: Ash has watched Ilya not drink for three nights, and on the fourth he says, "Friend. There's a weight to a thing like that." "Like what." "Not drinking." Ilya counts something. "Right." "The sky took mine," Ash says. "You could give it yours." Ilya looks at him for a long time. "I knew a drunk who got religion," he says. "He was a drunk with a hymn."
x_ash.again: Neither of them has said anything since.

options.text: Let him carry it his own way, Ash.
Ash isn't wrong. Something has to hold it.
You both burned something off yourselves. Three nights with a lamp. However many with a bottle.

x_ash_i.text: Ash nods slowly, the way he takes a refusal at the burial ground. "His own way, then." Ilya doesn't thank you, which from him is thanks.

x_ash_a.text: "Something," Ilya says. "Right." He turns his back to the fire for the rest of the night.

x_ash_b.text: Ash looks at the cord of the scarf in his fingers. Ilya looks at his ruined hand. "Right," Ilya says. "Right," says Ash, and seems surprised to hear himself say it.
x_ash_b.again: The two of them, looking at their hands.

t_count.text: "So I know I was there." He thinks about it. "Shots. Steps. Days. If you count it, it happened, and you were in it." A pause. "I wasn't, once." He looks at you. "Nobody asks why. They ask me to stop. Right."
t_count.again: He is counting under his breath.

t_wind.text: "Dust off the left of a post means it's quartering." He's off: grass, smoke, the hang a flag would have if there were flags, the shimmer on the salt that lies about everything except the wind, the hour after dawn when it turns and the hour before dusk when it lies down. He talks for an hour, the most you have ever heard him say, and none of it is about anything else. At the end: "Right. That's the short version."
t_wind.again: He is watching the smoke to see which way it leans.

t_hand.text: "Frost. The winter after." He flexes what's left. "Three nights in a ditch with a bottle and no gloves. The surgeon said I was lucky it was two." He turns the hand over. "I count them too. Eight. Right."

t_ada.text: "Ada." He turns the name over. "I was the best shot she had. After, she let me be her worst instead of throwing me out. Kindest thing anybody did." He looks at the fire. "Never forgiven her for it. Right."
t_ada.again: He has said what he will say about Ada.

t_jonah_lived.text: "Alive." He says it like a count that came out right. "You changed the conditions. The tower, the street, the cistern." He nods to you, once. "Somebody wrote him a month, and you didn't let it be his. Right."
t_jonah_lived.again: He is still pleased about it, quietly.

t_jonah_dead.text: "Twenty-two." He turns the rifle's sling round his wrist. "Read both books. Called me sir once, by mistake, and went red." A pause. "Right."

t_odile.text: "She bet Shale would fail." He looks across to where Odile would sit, if she were here. "It nearly did. I helped, from a fence, with a bottle." He shrugs. "Expensive woman. Everything she says costs something, even good morning. And she isn't wrong about Shale. That's the part I can't stand. Right."
t_odile.again: He has said what he thinks of the trade.

t_city.text: "No wind." He says it like a diagnosis. "Walls everywhere. The wind can't get a word in. Smoke goes straight up." He looks at the dark between the towers. "I don't know where anything is here. Right."
t_city.again: He is watching smoke go straight up.

c_bottle.text: He looks at the bottle in your hand for a long time. Then he takes it, and doesn't open it. He stands and picks up the rifle, and the counting stops. decision.text: You held out Ilya Strand's bottle to get a better shot out of him. He walked out of your firelight with it.

text.text: "You put her in his chair." He is packed; he has been packed since the overpass. "I walked behind you after that to see what else you'd do. I've seen." He shoulders the rifle. "Right."
"Right." He is packed. He doesn't say why; he counts it instead, under his breath, a list of things, and you recognise some of them. He walks out of the firelight on the last one.

decision.text: Ilya Strand walked out of your firelight. He had been counting.

text.text: He is sitting on his pack with the bottle beside him, unopened. He doesn't look up. "No."
He is sitting with the rifle across his knees, watching the road she took. "She walked." He doesn't look up. "I'll find which wash." It isn't a conversation.
He is cleaning the rifle. "Right," he says, which means: go on.

Smoke from three shacks, a planter with something green in it, and a line worn in the dust where water has been carried every day for years. People live here, and not many.

options.text: I came from Signal Hill. The relay there feeds a line to this station. DW-4.

decision.text: You told the rifle at Dry Wells where the line comes from, and she let you by.

hill.text: "DW-4." The rifle comes down slowly, like something being put back where it lives. "Nobody's called it that since Grandmother's father. He had it painted on the door." She looks at you a long moment. "Then you know more than Shale does. Come and tell her what you know."

pumphand.text: "Grew up under." She says it twice, trying it. "Under." The rifle goes across her chest. "Then you'll know what the clock sounds like. Eleven. Come and tell Grandmother what it sounds like where you're from, because she's never heard anyone else say it."

ilya.text: "Luz." Ilya, beside you, not raising his voice. "It's Strand. I brought the cartridges in the spring. I brought this one." A silence in which the kid starts whistling again. "Strand," she says. "You still owe me three." The rifle goes down.

through.text: She steps out from the barrel without lowering the rifle all the way, which is how she walks everywhere. "The shacks are ours. The station's Grandmother's. The tower's nobody's and don't climb it; Wick's up there and he bites." A nod at the long concrete building. "She'll want to see you before you touch anything that hums."

hostile.again: Nobody is talking. The fire barrel is where the shots come from.

intro.text: "Luz. I shoot things for the family and I count what I shoot with." The rifle lies across her knees on the sandbags. "Seven rounds. Six, now. I don't spend one on Shale unless Shale brings a wagon."

again.again: She runs a thumb along the rounds on her belt. "Six. Go on."

why.text: "Because the water under this floor is theirs, and the valve on the line is ours, and Shale has a sheriff who'd call that a word that ends with a rope." She shrugs. "We take a trickle. A trickle in Shale is a bucket. A bucket here is five people alive."

interject.text: "She would," Ilya says. "Ada would hang them for it and then not sleep for a month."

station.text: "The pumps, and a room at the end with a door that was locked when Grandmother was a girl, and a light that's green on the other side of it. Her father had the key. She has it now. She doesn't go in." A beat. "It makes a noise before eleven. Every day. You'll hear it."

schedule.text: "Not us. Not Shale; Shale thinks it's the weather, or God, or the Tollmen. Grandmother says the city. I say it doesn't matter who, it matters that it's on time." She looks east. "Something that's been on time for ninety years is a thing I don't want to meet."

text.text: "The graveyard, then the glass, then a bridge with a town on it. I've walked it twice." She looks at the station, where the pumps are running outside the clock. "You did a thing in there that somebody east will come to look at. I'll walk you as far as the glass, so you're not the first thing they see. Past that you're on your own, and so is everyone."
"East is east. Don't get shot." She goes back to counting.

again.text: "Still east." She doesn't look up from the rounds.

decision.text: Luz Marr will walk you east as far as the glass.

escort.text: "When you go, come past the sandbags and say so. I'll have the rounds I've got."

hostile.text: She is behind the sandbags with the rifle.
hostile.again: Still behind the sandbags. She is counting again, and not out loud.

intro.text: An old woman in a chair that was built for sitting, hands folded on a stick, eyes that measured you from the window before you reached the door. "Luz let you by, so you said something true. Sit. I'm Oriel Marr. My father was the pump man here, and his father before the Burn, and that chair you're not sitting in was his." She waits. Under the floor, something clicks, and the pumps begin.

passives.text: The cough she is holding in is wet. Lungs, not dust. She has been holding it in for a long time.
The key on the cord round her neck is brass, worn to gold where a thumb has rubbed it for sixty years and never once turned it in a lock.

who.text: "Ghosts. That's what the Tollmen call us, when they call us anything." She smiles with half her face. "We came out of a hole in the ground, same as you by the look of you. Not yours. clock.text: "Six, eleven, four, nine. Every day since before I was born, and twice a year the numbers move and nobody here moves them." She taps the floor with the stick. "That's Shale drinking. station.text: "My father's room. He said whatever was in there wasn't ours to touch, and then he died of the same thing I'm dying of, and I've kept it the way he left it." Her hand goes to the cord. "You want the key. Everybody who gets past Luz wants the key, in the end."

key_no.text: "Everybody says first." Her hand closes on the key. "My father said it, about Shale. Come back when you've done something for us that wasn't a sentence."

move_on.text: She looks at the Tolls a long time before she takes them. "The graveyard, then the glass. My father walked it the other way." She puts the money in the stick, which is hollow. "Luz will say no and come anyway. Give us a week."

leave_be.text: "Then you're the first from that direction who didn't." She closes her eyes. "Eleven o'clock. Listen."

after_fight.text: She is in the chair. She has not moved. "You shot at my family from behind a sandbag they filled. Take the key. Take the chair. There's nothing in that room worth what you paid for it."

cold.text: She is in the chair. She does not look at you, and she does not speak. Under the floor the pumps keep their clock.
cold.again: The chair, the stick, the old woman in it, looking at the wall and not at you.

intro.text: "Beans. In a planter. In Dry Wells." She does not look up from them. "Grandmother says that's a joke. I say it's beans. They don't care what they're a joke about."
intro.again: "Still beans." She doesn't look up. "Still not a joke."

shale.text: "Tomorrow." No hesitation at all. "I've never been anywhere with a second street. Don't tell Cato I said it. Don't tell them about the valve."

intro.text: "The valve's mine." He says it before you have asked anything. "Grandmother says when, I say how far. A quarter turn at eleven, back at noon. Shale never missed it. Shale never will."
intro.again: "Still mine." He hasn't moved from the valve. "Eleven, a quarter turn. Noon, back."

cut.text: "Then it was the city cut it, not us." He does not move. "Our quarter turn was there before the cut and after it. You want somebody to blame for Shale, there's a room at the end of the station with a green light in it. Go and blame that."

close.text: "You close it and I open it. You break it and we die here, slow, in front of Grandmother." He picks up the pipe, not to use it, just to have it. "Which do you want to be?"

closed.text: He is standing by the valve with the pipe in both hands and does not look at you. "Noon," he says. "It's past noon."
closed.again: He is still by the shut valve. He has nothing to turn, and he has not put the pipe down.

intro.text: A kid on the tower ladder, barefoot, with a sling in his belt. "I can hear it. The click. Luz says it's the pipe cooling. It isn't. It's before, not after."
intro.again: "Listen," Wick says, from the ladder, before you can speak. "There. Before, not after."

passives.text: He is right. A click, then the pumps. Something counts first.

east.text: "The graveyard. Pumps like ours with no water in them, standing up in a line. Past that it shines, all day, and you can't look at it." He points. "I went as far as the first one. There was a bird."

shale.text: "I've seen its water go past under the floor." He thinks about it. "Is it big? Does it have a tower?"

hostile.text: He is up the tower and has stones.

raid.text: The ledger closes before you have reached the bikes. "You." The rider's hand is on the carbine. "The gate at nine. You were with the Dogs." There is nothing to show him.
raid.again: The hand stays on the carbine. He has said all he means to.

ran.text: The bikes don't do rock. You lose them in the first gully and your breath in the second.

ran_no.text: The first shot is over your head. The second is not meant to be.

waved.text: He sees you coming and closes the ledger before you reach the bikes. "Go on," he says. Neither of you mentions the receipts column.

hostile.again: Nobody is talking. The bikes are between you and the road.

fire.text: A man by a fire that went out a day ago, one leg out straight in front of him and the trouser cut away above a knee that is the wrong colour. He has the machete across his lap and does not lift it. "Don't," he says. "Whatever it is. Just don't."
fire.again: He hasn't moved. The machete is still across his lap. "Still here," he says. "So are you."

passives.text: Not a bite: a cut, deep, a week old, gone septic. A knitkit and a clean dressing would save the leg today. Tomorrow is a different question.
His pack has been gone through, by him, several times. Water: none. He has been here two days.

options.text: (Treat the leg. A knitkit, a bandage.)

decision.text: You treated a dying drifter's leg on the road.

news.text: the salt-cut stranger stopped for a drifter on the road and doctored a leg nobody else would have

decision.text: You robbed a dying drifter on the road.

news.text: someone stripped a crippled drifter on the salt track and left him

kite.text: "A kite." He watches you not believe it. "Big wings, no bird in them. It came down on the pan at dusk and sat, and I went to look, because I'm a fool, and something on it opened and I ran, and I fell on my own blade. I know. I know how it sounds." A shrug. "It's still out there. South, on the white."

treated.text: He makes a noise through his teeth while the knitkit does its work, and then another, different noise. "Amory," he says. "Ignacio Amory. I don't forget a face. I'll be in Shale if the leg holds and at the overpass if it doesn't, and either way I owe you a thing I can't name yet." He gives you the machete. "I'll get another."

interject.text: "Right," Ilya says, quietly, when the man can bend the knee. It sounds like the good kind.

water.text: He drinks half and stops himself, which is the hardest thing you have seen anyone do this week. "Amory. Ignacio." He looks at the leg. "If you've got anything for this, I'm listening. If you haven't, go on, and don't look back, I hate that."

options.text: (Treat the leg. A knitkit, a bandage.)

decision.text: You treated a dying drifter's leg on the road.

robbed.text: He does not fight you for it. "Fine," he says, to the fire that is out. "Fine."

interject.text: "He was dying," Tamsin says. She doesn't say anything else for a mile.
Ilya doesn't look at the machete, or at you. He counts something under his breath all the way back to the track.

again.text: He has nothing left to say to you.
again.again: He doesn't look up.

halt.text: Two of them come up out of the ditch where they were lying in the shade, scrap plates and a sawn-off and a zip gun, and the one with the gun says what they all say. "Water. Then we'll see."
halt.again: "Water," the woman says again. "Then we'll see." Nobody has come any further out of the ditch.

passives.text: They are a long way from the overpass on foot, and the one with the zip gun is counting her rounds with her thumb. Scouts, not a raid.

options.text: Kessler knows my face. Say my name at the overpass and see what it buys you.

mods.why: they want a reason to go home
the Dogs have heard of you

options.text: (Say nothing. Let them look at you.)

watered.text: He drinks, passes it, and the woman drinks the rest without taking her eyes off you. "Shale's," he says, of the water, tasting it. "Pipe. Go on, then."

named.text: The name does something to the man's face. "Kessler's." He looks at the woman. She shrugs. "Then you're Kessler's problem," he says, and sits back down in the ditch.

interject.text: "Kessler's problem," Ilya says, when the ditch is behind you. "Till they're Kade's."

named_no.text: "Everybody knows Kessler." The sawn-off comes up a little. "Water."

feared.text: You do not say anything. After a while the woman says a name that is yours, and something that was done at the overpass, and the man lowers the sawn-off and looks at the ditch as if it had been his idea to sit there.

known.text: They know you before you are close enough to be a threat, and the greeting is a lifted hand and a lowered gun. "Kessler's friend." The man grins with what teeth he has. "Water, if you've got it. We're a long way from the pipe."
known.again: A lifted hand from the ditch. "Kessler's friend. Still a long way from the pipe."

wren.text: "Calloway." The man says it before Wren has said anything. "Thought you were dead, or Shale, which is the same." Wren says nothing for long enough that he looks away first. "Go on," he says, to you.

wren_again.text: The man sees Wren before he sees you, and finds something to do with the ditch. "Go on," he says, to you.
wren_again.again: Neither of them looks at Wren. "Go on."

let_by.text: "Kessler's problem." The man doesn't get up out of the ditch this time. "Water, if you're offering. If not, go on."
let_by.again: "Still Kessler's problem," he says, from the ditch.

hostile.again: Nobody is talking. The sawn-off is up.

trough.text: Two horses at a stone trough with water in it, which is impossible, and a grey man in a long coat filling it from a skin without hurry. He has seen you for a mile. "Horses first," he says. "Then you."
trough.again: He has gone back to the trough and the skin. "Horses first," he says again, but he is listening.

interject.text: "Water," Tamsin says, "in a trough, in the open, just sitting there." She sounds offended by how happy it makes her.

passives.text: The trough is fed: a buried line, a tap, a stone to hide it. The Wheel has water on roads nobody else knows have it.

options.text: The Wheel. Forty wagons. I've heard of you.

who.text: "Forty-one, since spring." He pats the near horse. "A town that moves. We trade with everyone and owe no one, and we go where the water is, which is never where the map says." He looks at you properly for the first time. "You walk like someone with a long way to go and no horse. The Wheel has horses."

where.text: "East of the dead pumps, this month, in the lee of the hill. Next month, who knows; the mother does." He names her: Sefa. "Come with something to trade and a horse's worth of manners and they'll feed you. Come with the guild's paper and they'll feed you to the dogs."

again.again: He doesn't stop filling the trough. "Still slow."

night.text: A man on the track at night, walking east with one hand held out in front of him flat, palm down, as if the air were a wall he was following. No pack. No water. He does not stop when he sees you; he does not see you.
night.again: He is still on the track, one hand flat on the air, leaning east.

passives.text: Dehydrated three days at least. Pupils wrong. He should be dead and is walking instead, which happens, for a while.
On the back of his hand, where it catches your lamp: a mark burned off, the way the stranger's was.

east.text: "East." He says it to the air in front of his hand. "It said east. It said my name and then it said east and then it said a number, and the number is where I stop." He walks on. He is not hurrying. He will not get there.

interject.text: "Don't ask me," Wren says, when you look at her. She is watching his hand on the air and nothing else.

stopped.text: He is lighter than he should be and does not struggle; he just keeps leaning east, the way a plant leans. Up close his lips are cracked white and his eyes are somewhere else. "I had a name," he says. "It's in the book now."

decision.text: You stopped a man walking east to die and gave him water.

watered.text: He drinks like a child, and for a moment the eyes come back from wherever they were and look at you, and are afraid. "Don't let it read yours," he says, quite clearly. Then the hand goes out flat again, and he leans. You can walk him to Shale, if you are going that way, and he will go east again the first night.

sitting.text: He sits where you set him down, one hand flat on his knee, leaning east even sitting. He does not know you.

slipped.text: He goes past you like water round a stone and does not look back, and in a minute the dark has him.

axle.text: A guild wagon down on one corner, the mule looking at the horizon, a carter on his back under the bed and a guard with a shotgun who watches you instead of the road. "Axle," says the carter, from under the wagon. "If you've got hands, I've got water. If you've got a gun, he's got a bigger one."
axle.again: "Still the axle," says the carter, from under the wagon. The guard still watches you instead of the road.

options.text: (Get under and look at the axle.)

mods.why: you have had worse things apart

fixed.text: A split block and a bent pin; an hour with a bar, a wedge and a lot of the carter's opinions, and the wagon stands up. He pays like a man who has been told to: ten Tolls and two waters, counted twice. "Guild thanks you for your custom." The guard lowers the gun a finger.

decision.text: You put a guild wagon back on its wheels on the road.

fix_no.text: The block is split through and the pin is not coming out for anyone without a forge. You get grease to the elbow and the carter's respect, which is worth nothing. "Post will send a wagon," he says. "Eventually."

again.text: "Still here." The mule has not moved either.
again.again: The carter nods. The mule, still, does not.

wheel.text: The wagon stops the way a wagon stops when it has decided to: a crack, a lurch, and the left rear wheel leaning out from the axle like a drunk from a doorway. Girma is already under it. "Pin's sheared. I've a spare pin and no spare hands. Lift, or wait for somebody who can."

mods.why: you have had your hands in worse

options.text: (Take the weight while he sets it.)

fixed.text: The pin goes in on the second try and the wheel comes true. Girma wipes his hands on the salt sacks. "Kin would have charged me for that." He looks at you. "I'll tell her you didn't."

lifted.text: You take the corner of the bed on your shoulder and the world goes red at the edges for the length of a held breath, and then the pin is in and Girma is saying "down, down, down." He does not thank you. He hands you the water first, which is the same thing.

fail.text: The pin goes in crooked and comes out again, and the second time it bends. Girma says nothing, which is worse. In the end it is a Tollmen guard off the guild's wagon who sets it, and writes something in a book.

waited.text: Four hours of salt and sky. A guild guard comes back down the line at last, sets the pin in a minute with a tool made for it, and tells Girma the Wheel owes the guild a favour. Girma says the Wheel owes nobody. The guard writes it down anyway.

halt.text: Two of them, on foot, from behind the cut where the road bends: scrap plates, one carbine between them, and the easy manner of people who have done this before. "Salt." Thistle nods at the wagon as if introducing it. "Salt pays. Forty, and the road's yours."

options.text: Kessler counts you. Does Kessler know you're out here collecting?
The Wheel feeds Dogs when the tribute's late. You want to be the one who ended that?

kin.text: Thistle's manner goes somewhere else. "He doesn't." Nettle has already stepped off the road. "Didn't see a wagon. Didn't see you." They are gone into the cut before Girma has finished reaching for the gun under the seat.

talked.text: It lands. Nettle looks at Thistle; Thistle looks at the salt; the salt does not look back. "Go on, then." He steps aside with a flourish that costs him something. "Tell the old woman the Dogs let her through."

talk_no.text: "Forty," Thistle says, as if you had not spoken, and Nettle's hand finds the carbine's strap.

paid.text: The Tolls go into a plate pocket. "Pleasure." They are off the road and gone. Girma, from the seat: "That's the Wheel's forty. Tell her, not me."

intro.text: A woman with a burn down one side of her face and a coil of green wire over her shoulder, halfway up the last tower with a pair of cutters. She looks down at you the way the towers do. "Copper's mine. Say what you're here for from down there; I'm not coming down for a face."

passives.text: She is stripping the wind-generator coils, not the pump wire. Somebody is paying for coil copper, which means somebody is winding motors.

options.text: The ruts going east. The Wheel?
A drifter on the road said a kite came down on the pan.

again.again: The cutters go snip, somewhere above you. "Go on. I can cut and listen."

options.text: The ruts going east. The Wheel?
A drifter said a kite came down on the pan.

pumps.text: "Nothing killed them. Somebody turned them off." She taps the tower with the cutters. "Vanes are locked, not seized. Brakes set from the valve house, all six, same day. Water went down the pipe to somewhere that mattered more, and the troughs went dry, and the farm that was here walked to Shale and became Shale." A shrug. "Sixty years. The game still comes at dusk. Habit."

interject.text: Tamsin looks at the dry troughs a long time. "Sixty years, and the game still comes," she says. "Even the animals keep the schedule."

wheel.text: "Forty-one wagons and a woman called Sefa who could sell sand to the pan. They camp east, in the lee of the hill, a week at a time, and they buy my copper and sell me back the horseshoes it came from." She almost smiles. "Go with something to trade. Go without the guild's paper. And don't touch the horses."

copper.text: "The Wheel, for the shoes. And a man at Tollhouse 9 who doesn't write it down, for Tolls, and he sends it east, and east of that I don't ask." She winds the coil tighter. "Someone's building motors. Someone always is."

kite.text: She stops cutting. "South. On the white. I saw it come down." She comes down the tower after all, slowly. "It sat two days and then it went up again, and where it sat there's a truck now that wasn't there before, and I don't go near it, and nor does the game." She points, south and west, across the pan.

hostile.text: She is behind the tower with the zip gun.
hostile.again: Still behind the tower. The zip gun is still on you.

look.text: A windpump: a lattice tower, a vane the size of a door locked side-on to the wind, a rod down the middle that has not moved in sixty years. At the foot, a pump head with its brake set and a brass plate: NETWORK 4 — FIELD 2 — No. 3.
look.again: The tower, the vane locked side-on, the rod that hasn't moved, the brass plate at its foot.

passives.text: The brake is a remote one. There is no handle. It was set from somewhere else.

view.text: From the top the pan is a sheet of hammered tin, and the hill east has a smudge of smoke in its lee, and south-west, far out on the white, something square that throws a shadow the wrong colour.

view_again.text: The pan from the top again: hammered tin, the smoke in the lee of the hill, and the square thing far out on the white, throwing its wrong-coloured shadow.

fall.text: A rung lets go and you learn the height of the second one from the ground.

look.text: A valve bank in a concrete box: six levers, all set the same way, each wired to a solenoid, and the solenoids wired to a cable that goes out through the wall and under the pan. A stencil above them: FIELD 2 — BRAKE — REMOTE.
look.again: Six levers, six solenoids, the cable out under the pan. FIELD 2 — BRAKE — REMOTE.

passives.text: The cable runs east along the pipe line, toward the pump station at Dry Wells and whatever is upstream of that. This field was switched off by the same hand that sets Shale's schedule.

mods.why: you have freed worse

released.text: Six levers, six solenoids forced, and outside, one after another, the vanes come round into the wind with a noise like a town waking up. The rods move. Nothing comes up the pipes; the water went somewhere else sixty years ago. But the troughs fill, slowly, from what is left in the ground, and by evening there will be game at them.

interject.text: "South-westerly," Ilya says, watching the vanes come round. "Steady. It'll hold all night." It is the most he has said all day.
Tamsin has her face turned up to the noise of the vanes. "Rust it," she says. "They were never broken. Only switched off."

decision.text: You freed the windpumps on the pan; the troughs fill again.

news.text: the dead windpumps on the pan are turning again

freed.text: Six levers thrown and six solenoids burned black. Outside the vanes turn in the wind, and the rods go up and down.
freed.again: The levers where you left them. Outside, the vanes still turn.

release_no.text: The solenoids are stronger than you are. One lever moves a hand's width and goes back.

look.text: In the middle of the ring: a machine the size of a big dog, sitting the way a dog sits, grey plates over a frame that is all angles, four legs folded under it, a head that is one lens and no mouth. Salt has drifted against its flank. It is not moving. It is not rusting either.

passives.text: The lens is not dark. Deep in it, something the colour of a pilot light is on, and has been on for a long time. It is not dead. It is waiting.

Pre-Burn, and not city work: a maker's mark on the shoulder plate, a crown over a gear. Military or something that bought from the military. The folded legs are a rest state: it sat down on an instruction, and it will stand on one.

again.text: The machine sits in its ring. The lens is on you now, and was not before.
again.again: Salt against its flank, legs folded, and the lens on you from the moment you step into the ring.

touch.text: Warm. Not sun-warm: warm from inside, like a sleeping animal. Under your palm something in the plates shifts the width of a hair and settles, and the lens, which was looking at the truck, is looking at you.

controller.text: The slab warms in your hand the moment it is in the lens's line, and a single point of light comes up under its surface and holds. The machine's head lifts an inch. It is listening to the thing you are holding, and through it, to you.

options.text: (Tell it to stand, and follow, and keep Shale.)

mods.why: the manifest names what it is
you know whose it was

options.text: (Tell it to stay. Keep the controller.)

decision.text: You left the machine on the pan sleeping and kept its controller.

woken.text: It stands. Four legs unfold with a sound like a gate, salt pouring off the plates, and it is taller than you expected and quieter, and the lens turns once around the whole horizon and comes back to the slab in your hand. It takes a step toward you and stops, exactly where a dog stops. It will walk at your heel to Shale and sit in the sheriff's yard and nothing will come into that town at night that it does not look at first.

interject.text: "It's looking at me." Tamsin has put you between her and it and doesn't pretend she hasn't. "Rust it. Tell it to look somewhere else."
"Shale's going to love that," Wren says. "Right up until it looks at them."

decision.text: You woke the machine on the pan and sent it to keep Shale.

news.text: a grey machine the size of a dog walked into Shale at the salt-cut stranger's heel and sat down in the sheriff's yard

wake_no.text: The slab goes dark in your hand. The head lowers the inch it had lifted. Whatever you said, it was not the word, and it has gone back to waiting for someone who knows it.

kept.text: The head settles. The light in the slab goes down to a point and stays. Somewhere east, you think, somebody has a slab like this one and is not using it, and does not know that you are.

text.text: The ring in the crust, empty. The salt is already drifting into the shape it sat in.
It sits in its ring, and will, until the guild's engineer comes with the slab you sold and says the word. You feel the lens on your back all the way to the edge of the pan.
It sits. The lens follows you. The slab in your pack is warm.

look.text: A guild truck on its side, the half-moon on the door, the cab crushed where it rolled and the trailer split. The skid behind it runs half a mile straight: it was going fast, in a straight line, away from something, and then it was not going at all. No bodies. Drag marks, two, toward the ring.
look.again: The truck on its side, the half-moon on the door, the long straight skid, and the drag marks going toward the ring and not coming back.

passives.text: The engine is whole; the cab is not. The truck did not fail. Something stopped it the way a hand stops a toy.
The drag marks go toward the ring and do not come back. In the crust beside them, prints: four-toed, each the size of your spread hand, pressed deep.

intro.text: A man on his knees at the foot of a tree with leaves on it, packing wet cloth round the roots with the care of someone dressing a wound. He does not get up. "Brother Anselm. You'll be from Shale, or through it. Mind the rows; the living ones are the ones with the cloth."

passives.text: Twelve living trees out of a hundred-odd dead: root-stock that survived the Burn under the ash, coaxed up over years. Nobody else in the Sallow is growing anything on a tree.

options.text: How do you keep a tree alive out here?
Sister Calla says something is robbing you.
You said they take the green ones. Who does?
There's a gap in the north wall with a Dog's plate dropped in it.

text.text: He is at the rows again, and the cloth is dry, and he looks up when you come as if he has been waiting to.
"Mind the rows."

again.again: He tucks the cloth tighter round a root before he looks up. "Go on."

options.text: How do you keep a tree alive out here?
There's a gap in the north wall with a Dog's plate dropped in it.

trees.text: "You don't. The tree keeps itself alive; you keep the ground from killing it." He pats the cloth. "Shade the roots, water them at dusk so the sun doesn't take it, and bury what dies at the foot of what lives. The Burn didn't kill the roots. It killed everything above them and then it killed the people who'd have waited." A breath. "The Choir waits. That's most of what we are."

interject.text: "We waited ninety years under a door," Tamsin says, under her breath. "Nobody called it a faith."

thieves.text: "Twice a week, since the fruit set. They come over the north wall and take the green ones, which nobody takes, because they're sour enough to take the skin off your tongue." He stands, finally, slowly. "Hanne heard them. Two, small. Dun says the prints are a Dog's, and Dun would know." He looks at the rows. "I don't want them hurt. I want them to stop. Those are two different things and I only know how to ask for one."

stakeout.text: "A Dog's plate." He turns it over in his hand as if it might be a seed. "Then it's what Dun said. Small, and from the overpass, and hungry enough for green fruit." He gives it back. "Wait for them, if you will. By the beds, after the lamps are out. I'll tell the novices to sleep through it." A pause. "Don't hurt them."

decision.text: You agreed to wait for the orchard thieves by the seedbeds at night.

text.text: "They're in Hanne's tent. The small one cried for an hour and then ate four." He shakes his head. "Two Dogs, under the open sky. The overpass will want them back, or it won't, and either way they eat. Thank you. I don't know yet what I've thanked you for."

"You took them back." He says it without blame, which is worse. "Then they'll come again when they're hungry, and someone with a gun will be waiting instead of you. Or they won't come, and I'll wonder what the Dogs do with children who get caught." He goes back to the cloth.

"The sheriff's cell." He looks at the north wall a long time. "She'll feed them. She'll send to the overpass. The overpass will say they're not theirs." He kneels again. "I asked you not to hurt them. I should have said what I meant."

"You let them go." A nod, slow. "With fruit, Hanne says. Then they'll come back, and I'll leave the green ones on the wall, and we'll call it a tithe and not a theft." He almost smiles. "The sky is open. So is the wall."

fruit.text: "Two." He counts them into your hand from his pocket, small and hard. "Sour. Eat them anyway; you'll not have had one. Tell Shale the Choir grew them, and tell them it took nine years."

seed_given.text: He opens it there in the rows, which Calla would not have, and holds a single seed up to the light between finger and thumb like a jeweller. "Bean." His voice goes. "Ninety years in the dark and it's a bean." He closes the case. "Tomorrow. The south beds. Pike will hear; let him hear it from the plants."

news.text: The Cistern's seed went into the Choir's beds.

decision.text: You gave the Cistern's seed to the Choir.

intro.text: A girl with her braid full of dust, thinning seedlings in a bed with a knife no longer than her thumb. "You're not Choir. You walk like a wall." She says it as a fact, not a complaint.
intro.again: "Still a wall." She doesn't stop thinning the seedlings.

options.text: Brother Anselm says you heard the thieves.

heard.text: "Two nights. Whispering, by the beds, and the wall scraping." She points with the knife. "North. One of them said Mote, run. So one of them is Mote." She goes back to the seedlings. "They took the green ones. You'd have to be starving. I was, once; I'd have taken the green ones."

choir.text: "Because they feed you first and ask what you believe after, and after goes on for a long time." A shrug. "Sister Calla took me off the road at Shale with a fever. I stayed. I'd have stayed for the fruit."

intro.text: A big young man hauling at the well rope, with the look of someone who was built for something else and is working at this one. "Dun. I draw the water. The well's forty feet and the bucket's thirty-nine, so I draw it twice."
intro.again: Dun lets the bucket down the first time. "Twice," he reminds you, and keeps hauling.

options.text: Anselm says you know a Dog's footprint.

prints.text: "Scrap-plate sole, two straps, the left one mended with wire. Kids' size." He lets the bucket down. "Kessler doesn't send kids over walls. Kids go over walls when there's nothing on the right side of them." He looks north. "Catch them and don't take them back. That's all I'll say."

dog.text: "Till I was twelve, and then Perpetua said I had a face for walls and gave me to the Choir with a sack of salt, as a trade." He draws the bucket up. "I don't go back. I don't say why."

interject.text: "Perpetua traded a boy for salt," Wren says, flat. "Sounds like her. She'd call it a kindness, and she'd be right."

look.text: A post with a board on it, and on the board, burned in with a wire: an open circle, and under it, THE SKY IS OPEN. Below that, smaller, in another hand: and the wall is low. Someone has left two green fruit on the ledge.
look.again: THE SKY IS OPEN, and the wall is low, and the two green fruit are still on the ledge.

bare.text: THE SKY IS OPEN. And the wall is low. The ledge under the board is bare where the fruit was.
bare.again: The board, the burned circle, the bare ledge.

look.text: A well with a windlass and a rope that has been spliced four times. The water, when the bucket comes up, is clear and tastes of stone, not pipe: this is not the network's water. It is the orchard's own.
look.again: The windlass, the four-times-spliced rope, and water that tastes of stone.

filled.text: Clean water, for once, for nothing.

look.text: A gap in the north wall where the stones have been taken down a course and put back wrong. In the rubble on the orchard side, scuffs, and a scrap of something that glints.

again.text: The gap in the north wall, the stones put back wrong. Nothing glints in the rubble now.
The gap in the north wall, and the glint still in the rubble.

passives.text: Two sets of prints, small, scrap-plate soles. They come at night and go the same way, north-west, toward the overpass road.
The glint is a Rust Dog's plate, the little kind they wear on a cord, snapped off its wire.

plate.text: A thumb-sized scrap of plate with a dog's head scratched on it, the way the overpass marks its own. A child's cord through it.

beds.text: Two shapes at the beds in the dark, filling a sack with green fruit, so intent that you are three steps away before one of them looks up. A boy with a shiv and a girl with the sack, neither of them sixteen, both of them all eyes. "Mote," the boy says. "Run."
beds.again: The two of them again, at the beds, with the sack. The boy sees you first this time. "Mote," he says. "Run."

options.text: Don't. Nobody here is going to hurt you. Put the sack down and sit.

mods.why: you can say Dun's name
the Dogs have heard of you

wren.text: "Kip." Wren does not raise her voice. "Mote. Your mother's Fen, under the third pier, and she thinks you're at the salt." The boy's shiv goes down. The girl starts to cry, silently, the way children do who have learned not to be heard.

grabbed.text: You have him by the collar before the shiv is up, and he goes limp the way a kid goes limp who has been grabbed before. The girl does not run. She will not leave him.

sat.text: They sit. The story comes out of the girl in pieces, with the sack in her lap: the overpass has been short since the tithe, the little ones eat last, the orchard has fruit on trees and nobody shoots at you here. "They're sour," she says, as if that were the crime. "We only take the sour ones."

interject.text: "They eat last," Ilya repeats. He has turned his back on the children to watch the wall, which is the kindest thing anyone has done for them tonight.
"The sour ones," Tamsin says, and has to look away. "Rust it. Give them the sack."

options.text: Stay. The Choir feeds you first and asks after. Ask for Dun; he was one of you.

decision.text: The two Rust Dog children who robbed the orchard stayed with the Choir.

news.text: two Rust Dog children are sleeping in the Choir's tents at the orchard
two of the overpass's children went to the Choir and did not come back

options.text: I'll walk you back to the overpass. Tonight. Whoever is short there can answer to me.

decision.text: You walked the orchard thieves back to the overpass.

options.text: The sheriff's cell, and she can send to the overpass for you.

decision.text: You handed the orchard thieves to Sheriff Vey.

options.text: Take the sack. Take the green ones, always, and nothing else, and go over the wall where the stones are loose.

decision.text: You let the orchard thieves go with the green fruit.

choir.text: The boy looks at the tents as if they were a trap with the teeth showing. The girl looks at the trees. "They've got fruit on them," she says, and that decides it.

returned.text: Four hours in the dark, the girl asleep on your back for the last one, and a lamp at the overpass gate that knows you. Whoever is short there will be shorter. But they are home, and the Dogs will remember who walked them.

cell.text: Ada does not ask you what they did. She looks at their feet and sends Jonah for blankets, and the boy says one word, which is a Dog's word for a cage.

interject.text: "A cage," Wren says, after, and nothing else all the way back.

go.text: They are over the wall before you have finished the sentence. The sack goes over first. In the morning Anselm will find two green fruit left on the shrine, which is a kind of receipt.

ran.text: They are gone over the north wall with the sack, and the stones come down behind them. You will not catch them tonight, and tomorrow they will know the beds are watched.

text.text: "Oh, it's you." A nod, almost a smile. "Dust's up. Mind the wells, they're slippy when they run."
"Hm." They look past you. "Don't know anything. Ask the sheriff."
"You're not from here." Not a question. "We get a few. Most go on east. Water's two a measure if you're asking."

hello.again: "Something else?" They're already half turned back to their day.

a0.text: "Office is the one with the flag that was a sheet once. Knock; she doesn't like surprises."

a1.text: "Mags has a room behind the saloon, if you've got ten and don't mind the noise. The Choir'll put you on a cot for nothing and pray at you for less."

a2.text: "Comes when it comes. Twice a year somebody turns a dial somewhere and it comes less." A shrug. "Nobody here knows where the dial is."

text.text: "Give us a hand with this?" They laugh. "No. Go on. You've done enough for one town."
"Two more loads." They don't stop. "Talk fast."

hello.again: They shift the load to the other shoulder. "Still two loads. Still talking?"

a0.text: "Scrap, salt, water, whatever's heavy. The guild pays by the load and weighs it light."

a1.text: "Work's work. Beats the overpass. Beats the road." They heft it. "Doesn't beat much else."

text.text: "Looking or buying?" The stall is three planks and a cloth, and everything on it has been owned before.

hello.again: "Still looking?" The cloth gets a twitch, so the lamp shows.

a0.text: "Odds. Wire, a lamp that works, a boot that doesn't. Pike has the real stock; I have what Pike won't touch."

a1.text: "Anyone with Tolls. Drifters, Dogs on a quiet day, the Choir when they've sold fruit. Guild scrip at a discount, and don't tell Pike I said so."

text.text: "Don't." They say it before you have asked anything. Then, softer: "Spare a water?"

hello.again: "Still here." They are looking at your water, not at you.

a0.text: "Somewhere with a name. It's gone; I'm not. That's the whole story, friend."

a1.text: "East, like everyone. Or west, if east doesn't want me." They look at the road. "The road doesn't care."

text.text: "The sky is open, friend." A grey scarf, clean hands, a look that is kinder than the place. "Are you hurt? We don't charge for asking."

hello.again: "Ask what you like, friend. The sky has time."

a0.text: "That the sky keeps no books. That what's buried under it is free. That's most of it; the rest is farming."

a1.text: "The tents by the west wall, with the sign on the pole. Sister Calla is there; she'll see to you before she sees to herself."

text.text: "Kessler's friend." A nod with no warmth in it, which from a Dog is warmth. "Don't steal anything. That's our job."
"What are you looking at." Scrap plates, a knife, a face that has been hit more than once. "Keep walking."

options.text: What is it like, under the overpass?

a0.text: "Dry. Loud. Nobody dies alone, which is more than Shale can say." They spit. "Kessler counts us. That's the deal."

text.text: "Move along." The carbine stays where it is, which is the courtesy. "Nothing to see. If there was, you'd have paid for it."

hello.again: "Anything else, or are you moving along?" The carbine stays where it is.

a0.text: "Quiet is the job. Loud is a report I have to write." A glance at the road. "Dogs came by last month. I wrote it."

text.text: "Horses first." They finish with the horse before they look at you. "Trade or go; the Wheel doesn't stop for talk."

hello.again: They have gone back to the horse. "Trade or go."

a0.text: "Where the water is. The mother decides; the rest of us find out at dawn." A shrug. "It's a good way to live if you don't need to know."

text.text: "Got a light?" They don't want a light. They want to know what you are, and they decide fast.

hello.again: "Still here?" They have already decided what you are.

a0.text: "Whoever's standing on it. Right now that's me, and I'm not selling, so."

text.text: "Wash it. Then come back." They say it without looking up, to anyone, about anything.

hello.again: "Still not bleeding?" They don't look up. "Then I'm still working."

a0.text: "Always. Dust in the lungs, salt in the cuts, the water doing what the water does. Sit if you're bleeding; otherwise I'm working."

intro.text: She does not get up. She looks at your boots, then your hands, then your face, in that order, and nods at the fire as if it were a chair. "Sit. You're a guest till you're not. Sefa Oduya; this is my wheel. Eat first; then tell me what you want from it."

options.text: Is there work on the road?

text.text: "Road-kin." She moves her stick so there is room by the fire. "Sit. What have you brought us from the places that don't move?"
"Guest." The nod again. "Sit. The water's been paid for."

again.again: Sefa feeds the fire a stick and waits for you to go on.

options.text: Is there work on the road?

wheel.text: "Nine families, seven wagons, four horses, no address." She counts it on her fingers like a thing she has said a thousand times, because she has. "We carry what towns want between towns that don't talk. Salt east, water west, letters both ways, people sometimes. We stop four days and move. Anyone who stops longer than four days is a town, and towns get taxed, and towns get Dogs. We don't."

interject.text: "No address," Tamsin says, as if it is the best word she has heard all year.

tollmen.text: "The Tollmen tax a road. We are not on a road; we are beside one. Pike pretends not to see the difference and we pretend not to see Pike." A thin smile. "That is the whole treaty. It has held thirty years."

join.text: "You don't. You ride with us until somebody says kin and nobody says no." She shrugs. "Share a road. Pay a debt. Don't steal. It isn't a secret; it's just slow."

text.text: "East, toward the Dry Wells pans, on the fourth morning. Then north under the orchard, then the overpass side, then back here by Shale. A ring. It's in the name."
"North, under the orchard, on the fourth morning. Then the overpass side, then Shale, then back to these pans. A ring. It's in the name."
"West, the overpass side, on the fourth morning. We don't go under it; we camp where the Dogs can see us and count us. Then Shale, then the Dry Wells pans, then back here. A ring."
"Shale, on the fourth morning. Then the Dry Wells pans, then under the orchard, then back here where the Dogs can count us. A ring. It's in the name."

turn.again: "Same ring as when you asked," Sefa says. "It's in the name."

job.text: "There's always work on the road, and most of it is walking next to a wagon with a gun and not shooting it." She looks you over again. "We've a wagon of salt going to Tollhouse 9 with the Tollmen's caravan. The guild's guards guard the guild's wagons. Ours needs its own. Sixty Tolls at the gate, and the Wheel remembers who rode."
job.again: "The salt is still going to Tollhouse 9," she says. "So is the work."

job_yes.text: "Then it leaves when you do. Walk the Tollhouse road from Shale and keep the wagon in your eye. If the road asks you for something, remember it's asking the Wheel."

son.text: "He does." She lets the fire have a moment. "He's right that a well that doesn't dry is worth more than a road that doesn't end. He's wrong that you can own one without owing somebody. I had a town once. It is under the salt now." She looks at you. "Don't tell him I said he was right."

intro.text: "You're the one from Shale." He has been watching the camp the way a man watches a room he wants to leave. "Dario. Hers." A nod at the fire. "Is it true the well there runs all year?"
intro.again: Dario has gone back to watching the camp, the way a man watches a room he wants to leave. "Go on."

options.text: It runs. The town fights over it.
Your mother's salt wagon. Tell me about the road.

well.text: "Everybody fights over everything. At least a well is worth it." He turns a cartridge over in his fingers. "We fight over which pan to stop on."

town.text: "I want a door. One that shuts." He says it quietly, because the ring has ears. "She thinks a door is a cage. She's not wrong about the old towns. But the old towns are gone and the salt took them, and Shale is still there." He looks at you. "You've lived in a place with a door. Is it a cage?"

interject.text: "It's a cage," Tamsin says, before you can answer. "A warm one, with a fridge that counts you." She looks at the fire. "Get a door anyway. Just keep the key yourself."

options.text: A door is a door. What you do behind it is yours.
Your mother kept nine families alive without one.

door.text: "That's what I think." He almost smiles. "Don't tell her you said so."

road_answer.text: "She did." He puts the cartridge away. "And she's tired, and nobody says so, and the Wheel will turn until it doesn't." He looks at the horses. "Four, now."

road.text: "Dogs on the road sometimes, when the tribute's late. A ford that isn't a ford after rain. And the Tollmen's own guards, who'll help you with a wheel and charge the Wheel for the help." He shrugs. "Keep the wagon in your eye. That's the whole job."

intro.text: "Not behind her." Mirren Tarrow doesn't look away from the horse. "Front, slow, hand out. There. Now she knows you." A nod. "Horse-master. I'm not selling."
intro.again: Mirren hasn't looked away from the horse. "Still not selling."

options.text: Could I ride one, if I needed to be somewhere fast?

horses.text: "Two pull, two rest, one dies every winter and I don't replace it, because there's nothing to replace it with. The Tollmen have mules. Mules eat less and think less. I'd rather have horses and think."

ride.text: "When you're kin, maybe. A horse is a road that carries you. We don't lend roads." She finally looks at you. "Ride with the wagon first. Then ask again."

intro.text: "Everything on the blanket walked here." Bisi Oduya spreads her hands over it: water, jerky, cartridges in paper, a lamp, strips of Holdfast. "So did the price. Looking or buying?"
intro.again: "Still all walked here." Bisi smooths the blanket. "Looking, or buying this time?"

letters.text: "To anywhere the Wheel stops and most places the Tollmen do. Write it at a caravan post; it rides with the next wagon. Replies come back the same way, when they come."

read.text: Two ledgers. The first is the Dry Well as everyone sees it: water in by the barrel, water out by the cup, rooms, Dust stakes, the barman's wages, the barman's shortfalls circled twice. The second is thinner and newer, and the figures in it are the first ledger's figures with the air let out of them.
read.again: The two ledgers, the fat one and the thin one, side by side as she left them.

passives.text: The second set isn't a thief's work; it's a lender's. Interest against the deed, compounding; a buyout line, signed, dated two months ago; the margins initialled in the Tollmen's half-moon hand. On paper the Dry Well is Factor Pike's. The town drinks here and does not know.
The numbers in the second book are the first book's numbers made smaller in the same places every month — not stolen, hidden. Hidden from whom?

options.text: (It is a buyout, and she is hiding it.)
