mods.why: the Madame told you the only thing they check

again.again: The sergeant waits, carbine easy, while the lens goes on looking at you.

decision.text: You went up to the Crown on a Masque chit that was not yours.
You went up to the Crown as the help, on a kitchen pass.
You went up to the Crown on the Concern's card.
The Crown's lens admitted you on sight, and said why, aloud.

chit_in.text: He reads it without touching it. "Lorne. One guest." He looks at the lens; the lens looks at you; nobody says that House Lorne's guest was going to be somebody else. "The hall is straight on. Mancuso keeps the door."

pass_in.text: "Kitchens." He does not look at the pass, or at you; that is what a pass is for. "Round the back. Brisk. Don't come out the front."

card_in.text: He looks at the card and something goes out of his shoulders. "The Concern's people are expected." He says it to the lens, not to you. "Straight on."

exchange_in.text: "The Exchange." He has a list and you are on it in a hand that is not his. "Straight on. Mind the lens; it has you now."

standing_in.text: "A house's client." The lens agrees, which is the only agreement that counts. "Straight on."

lens_in.text: The green light thinks for a long time, and clicks twice, and the sergeant reads the screen in his booth and reads it again. "ADMIT ON SIGHT." He says it as the lens says it, flat, and then, to you, with something else in it: "Magistrate-designate." The other warden has heard. By the time you reach the gate the terraces have heard.

interject.text: "Aloud," Nine says, very quietly. "No lens has said a file aloud in my service. It is showing you to them." A click. "I do not think that was for your benefit."

news.text: the Crown's lens admitted a stranger on sight and called them Magistrate-designate, aloud

belong_in.text: You walk the way the Madame walked you across her room three times, with the clothes doing the talking. The lens looks. The sergeant looks at the lens, and the lens does not disagree, because the lens has never been asked to disagree with bottle-green. "Straight on."

decision.text: You walked into the Crown in the Velvet's clothes, and the lens let bottle-green through.

belong_no.text: You walk. The lens looks, and thinks, and the sergeant reads the screen. "The lens disagrees." He is almost kind. "The car is behind you. Take it, and nobody files anything."

force.text: He sees it before you move, which is what he is for. The carbine comes up. "Nobody forces the Crown." The other two come off the wall.

decision.text: You went for the Crown's lift wardens.

in.again: "In," the sergeant says, without looking round.

fight.again: The lift wardens have their carbines up. Nobody is talking.

text.text: A glass table by the pool, with a cup on it. You have stood here. You have stood exactly here, holding a tray, with hands that were not yours, while a woman in grey silk did not look at you. The cup is the same cup. The hands, this time, are your own.
A glass table by the pool with a cup on it and a woman beside it who sees everything from here, which is what here is for.

read.text: THE MASQUE — HOUSE VANE — THE COMMITTEE SITS AT THE TOAST. Over the doors a lens, bigger than the lobby's, with a green light that does not blink. Everyone who goes in looks up at it, and smiles, because they have been taught to.
read.again: THE MASQUE — HOUSE VANE, and the big lens over the doors that does not blink.

read.text: A crane, in old brass, over a door: ASHBY-CRANE. The brass is older than the hall's gilt and has been polished more often, by people who were paid less.
read.again: The brass crane over the door: ASHBY-CRANE.

read.text: HALDEN — PORTRAITS — AS YOU WILL BE. Under it, a smaller card: SITTINGS BY APPOINTMENT. FORECAST SHEETS TO BE SUPPLIED BY THE CLIENT.
read.again: HALDEN — PORTRAITS — AS YOU WILL BE.

read.text: STAFF. The door is metal and the terraces' side of it is painted to look like the terraces. The kitchens' side is not painted at all.
read.again: STAFF, on a metal door painted on one side only.

read.text: The parapet. All of Meridian under it in haze: the Precinct a grid, Old Market a stain, the canal a bright thread, the Stacks a wall with lights in it, the broken bridge a finger pointing at the Docks. You cannot see the Sink at all. That is the point of up here.
read.again: Meridian in haze below the parapet, and no Sink anywhere in it.

intro.text: A man at the hall doors in House Vane's green with a sabre on his hip that is not for show and a scar on his cheek that was. "Ettore Mancuso. The house's door." He looks at your shoes, which is where he looks at everyone. "Chit, name, or face. The help goes round the back."

options.text: The lens admitted me on sight. Ask it.
I stand for House Ashby-Crane. Draw.
What are you to the house?

again.again: He looks at your shoes again, and waits.

options.text: The lens admitted me on sight.
I stand for House Ashby-Crane. Draw.
What are you to the house?

open.text: "Go in." He does not move his eyes from the promenade.

options.text: I stand for House Ashby-Crane. Draw.
What are you to the house?

admit.text: "Go in." He steps aside exactly as far as he has to.

admit_lens.text: He does not ask it. He has heard; the terraces have heard. He steps aside a full pace, which from Mancuso is a bow. "Designate."

admit_quiet.text: He looks at your shoes. The Madame did the shoes. He steps aside.

shoes.text: He looks at your shoes for a second longer than he looked at anyone else's. "The help goes round the back." He does not raise his voice; he does not need to; he has said it to the lens.

help.text: "Round the back. Brisk." He has already stopped looking at you.

who.text: "The house's blade. Vane has not fought in two seasons; a house that has a Mancuso does not need to." He almost smiles. "Honora's man took the Concern's coin and the lift. She has a bravo from the Row in borrowed shoes. One can tell by the shoes."

draw.text: He looks at you properly for the first time, at your hands and your feet and the blade. "For Ashby-Crane." The hall has gone quiet behind him. "A duel is a vote with the arithmetic shown. The Chair follows it; that is the one rule up here older than the lens." The sabre comes out as if it had been waiting. "To the floor. Not to the death; we are not the Row."

decision.text: You stood for House Ashby-Crane at the Masque and put Vane's duellist on the floor.

news.text: a stranger put Ettore Mancuso on the floor at Vane's Masque, for Ashby-Crane

decision.text: You stood for House Ashby-Crane at the Masque and went down to Vane's duellist.

text.text: He is on his feet again, with his arm bound, and he bows to you a quarter of an inch. "Well struck." He means it; it is the only thing up here anyone has meant all night.
"The Row's man went down. The house notes it." He looks at your blade the way he looked at your shoes. "Vane will remember you. That is not always good."

news.text: a new portrait went up in the Crown's hall: a stranger on the Spire steps in a magistrate's sash

burned.text: It burns like paper, which is what it is. Halden watches it go without expression. "It will print again. It always does. But not in my drawer." He looks at the machine. "I shall tell it I ran out of paper."

hung.text: He hangs it himself, at the end of the wall, with the others: the Crown as it will be, and you in the sash among them. People stop in front of it on their way to the toast. By the time the car goes down, the terraces know your face the way the lens does, and the houses have begun to think about what a designate is worth.

interject.text: "In the hall," Ash says. "With the others." He looks at the print a long while, and then at you, and you cannot read his face at all.

photo.text: He does not touch it. He looks at it the way he looks at his own prints: the steps, the sash, the dust. "Not mine." He is quite sure. "Mine is a copy of the one upstairs. This is the original; the wire's; the city's own hand." He turns it over and reads the date and does not comment on it. "There is no grain in it because there was no light. Nobody took this. It was *expected*."

interject.text: "Expected," Nine repeats. The lens clicks, and clicks again. "The record suggests I say nothing further. I am going to follow the record, this once, and I would like you to know that I am choosing to."
"Expected," Tamsin says. "Like a ration." She has gone pale under the freckles, and for once she doesn't try to make it funny.

machine.text: The renderer: a pre-Burn cabinet with a lens of its own, a slot for a sheet, a tray for prints, and a hum that is not the hall's. On its screen, a queue of names in the Crown's season, each with a sheet number beside it. At the top of the queue, unrequested, with no sheet number, dated the day you came through the gate: your name.
machine.again: The renderer's queue, and your name still at the top of it, unrequested.

intro.text: A woman in white with forearms like a hauler's and a voice that reaches the far end of forty covers. "Brisk. The kitchens. Nobody goes up the back stair I haven't fed." She looks at you and files you faster than the lens did. "You're not kitchens. Pass, or a reason, or out."

options.text: (The service pass.) Where do you want me?
I need the back stair into the hall.

mods.why: you came in as the help
she knows a hauler's hands

options.text: A girl from the salon needs the lift down, quietly.

again.again: She does not stop moving. "Well? Forty covers."

options.text: (The service pass.) Where do you want me?
I need the back stair into the hall.

mods.why: you came in as the help

options.text: A girl from the salon needs the lift down, quietly.

pass.text: "Trays." She puts one in your hands with six glasses on it. "Up the back stair, round the hall once, don't look at them, they don't look at you. That's the help's one advantage up here; use it."

stair_ok.text: She looks at your hands, which have done something in their life, and at the hall's side of the door, which has not. "Trays." Six glasses. "Round the hall once. Don't look at them."

stair_no.text: "Out." She has already turned back to the stove. "Forty covers. Out."

tillie.text: She does not stop moving. "Four. The rubbish goes down at four, and the help, and anything in a kitchen coat with its head down." A tray. "She can be rubbish. Everybody is, in a lift. Tell her to leave the dress."

lift.text: The service lift: a cage that smells of the day's rubbish and the night's help, with a lever and no lens. It goes down to Old Market's works, where the Loop is, and comes back up at four with the morning.
lift.again: The service cage, the lever, no lens.

room.text: A room under glass with the light coming in sideways. You are sitting; the hands on the table are a woman's, ringed, still. Across the table a man in a coat that is not trying, with a sheet between you that has the Committee's crest on it. He says, "Terms," as if it were the name of a dish. The hands turn a cup a quarter turn.
room.again: The room under glass, the ringed hands, the man in the coat, *terms*. The reel begins where it always begins.

terms.text: "The Committee's forecasts, by the season, sealed, to the Concern, from the date the Chair signs. In return the Concern's backing on the vote, and the road, and the near end of a bridge." The hands do not move. A voice that is yours and is not says, "Done," and the man in the coat does not smile, because men like him do not need to. The reel ends on the cup, and the sound of a room that did not know it was listening.

terms_again.text: The Committee's forecasts, by the season, to the Concern; the road; the near end of a bridge. *Done.* The cup, a quarter turn. It does not change.

look.text: It's you. Older — forty, forty-five — on broad stone steps under a lamp, a city of towers behind you going up out of the frame, squinting into a wind. Something across your chest you took for a strap the first time, and have not been sure of since.
look.again: You, older, on the steps under the lamp, squinting into the wind.

passives.text: The shadows on your face fall left. The shadows on the towers fall right. There is no sun anywhere that does both.
No grain, anywhere, even blown up by your eye. Dust hangs in the air beside your shoulder, and the same mote hangs again by the lamp: drawn, not caught.

back.text: On the back, in pencil, in a hand that is not yours: 49 · VI · 12. A year, a month, a day. Along the bottom margin, printed, a short code — 0412/30 — and under it a line of print so small and so even it looks like a scratch until you tilt it.
back.again: The back: 49 · VI · 12 in pencil, the printed code, the scratch of microprint under it.

interject.text: "Forty-one years," Tamsin says, at your shoulder. "That's what everybody'd say. Everybody out here counts from the Burn." She frowns at it. "Everybody out here."
"Pencil's not his," Wren says. "He wrote small and square. That's somebody copying something they didn't understand."

options.text: (Let the link read the code off the city's wire.)

eyes.text: The optic finds the scratch and pulls it up until it is letters, flat and even as the Precinct's forms: RENDER — DESIGNATE — FROM FORECAST, R30 — DEPICTS R49.06.12. The pencil copied the date off the print and left off the one letter that mattered.

link.text: You think at the code and the city's wire thinks back, the way it does in a street with a lamp in it: a cold, polite query, a pause, a line in your skull in the Ledger's even hand. RENDER QUEUE 0412 — SUBJECT: DESIGNATE — RENDERED R30 FROM FORECAST — DEPICTS R49.06.12. Then the wire asks who is asking, and you stop thinking at it.

nine.speaker: npc_md_nine
nine.text: "Clause 40 forbids me to read a citizen their own forecast." The lens goes over the pencil once and stops at the margin, and clicks. "It does not forbid me to read a date. Forty-nine, sixth month, twelfth day. That is the Restoration Calendar; the Cistern would write it otherwise. R49 is nineteen years from today." A pause. "The margin is a render number. That is not a photograph. I am not permitted to say what it is a picture of, and I have not said it."

odile.speaker: npc_nb_03
odile.text: She holds it at arm's length, then takes her glasses off their chain and holds it close. "Oh, my dear." Very softly. "That is a delivery date. I have written ten thousand of them. Nobody writes a delivery date on a thing that has already been delivered." She taps the margin with the Gyro hand's fingernail. "And that is a lot number. Somebody has sold this, or means to. Forty-nine is the city's year. It is nineteen years off."

known.text: You, older, on the steps at the foot of the Archive Spire, under the lamp, in the city's year forty-nine: nineteen years from now. A picture of a day that has not come.

read.text: An enamel sign on a post at the mouth of a lane: NORTH — THE SPIRE CLOSE — COURT OF ACCOUNTS — CATALOGUE. Somebody has scratched under it, small: *and the steps*.
read.again: NORTH — THE SPIRE CLOSE. *And the steps.*

read.text: ARCHIVE SPIRE — THE CLOSE. COURT OF ACCOUNTS: WEST WING, IN SESSION WHEN CALLED. CATALOGUE: EAST WING, READERS BY SLIP. THE STEPS AND THE GREAT DOORS ARE CLOSED FOR WORKS. ALL PERSONS ARE RECORDED.
read.again: COURT, WEST. CATALOGUE, EAST. THE STEPS ARE CLOSED.

text.text: A works board on the scaffold, freshly lettered: ARCHIVE SPIRE — RESTORATION — R30 WORKS — ON SCHEDULE. PUBLIC STEPS AND GREAT DOORS: REOPEN R49. Below, by landing: 1 — FAÇADE. 2 — HALL OF RECORDS. 3 — COPY ROOM: MAGISTRATE'S CHAMBERS — REROUTED. The last word is new paint over old.

A works board on the scaffold, freshly lettered: ARCHIVE SPIRE — RESTORATION — R30 WORKS — ON SCHEDULE. PUBLIC STEPS AND GREAT DOORS: REOPEN R49. Below, by landing: 1 — FAÇADE. 2 — HALL OF RECORDS. 3 — COPY ROOM: MAGISTRATE'S CHAMBERS (R49). And so on up, past where the board runs out of room.

read.again: R30 WORKS — ON SCHEDULE. REOPEN R49. Landing three, the copy room, and what it is to be.

scene.text: You stop on the fourth step without deciding to. The lamp behind your left shoulder. The doors above. The Crown's glass going up out of sight on either side. The wind off the canal, in your face, making you squint. It is the photograph. The angle is wrong by a stride, and the steps are cracked where the print has them whole, but it was made here, of you, standing about where you are standing now.

interject.text: Tamsin has stopped two steps below you. "Don't move," she says, and holds the photograph up at arm's length, between your face and hers, and lowers it slowly. "Oh," she says. "Oh, I don't like that."
Wren walks once round the lamp, the way she walks round a place she means to come back to in the dark. "Here," she says. "He stood you here." She does not say who.
Ash stays at the foot of the steps. "I'll not climb them," he says. "Not today. You go on." He looks at the lamp as if it owed him something.
"Delivery point," Odile murmurs. "Of course. One always sells a thing with its address on it."

Ilya looks at the lamp, the doors, the glass, the long lines of sight down into the square. "Good place to stand someone," he says. "If you wanted everyone to see them." He means it the way a sniper means it.
"The steps," Nine says. "I have walked past them for a hundred and twenty years. I did not know they were waiting for someone."

options.text: (Hold the photograph up against the steps.)

hold.text: Close enough to frighten you. Older you is standing one step higher, and the cracks are mended, and the scaffold is gone, and the board on it that says the steps reopen R49 is gone too, because it is R49. You put the photograph away and stand on your own step for a while.

text.text: The steps. The lamp. One step higher, in the picture, nineteen years from now.
The steps. The lamp. One step higher, in the picture.

again.again: The steps, and the lamp.

look.text: The great doors: bronze, four storeys, green at the seams, chained through the handles with a chain that has been oiled. A card in a sleeve on the chain: CLOSED FOR WORKS — REOPEN R49. Through the gap at the hinge, a hall of records going back into the dark, and a smell of paper.
look.again: The bronze doors, chained and oiled. REOPEN R49.

look.text: A steel door set low in the Spire's foot, west of the steps, with no handle on this side: VAULT OF ACCOUNTS — NO ENTRY — NO EXIT. It is warm under your palm, the only warm thing in the close, and through it, far down, something hums at one note and does not stop.
look.again: The steel door in the Spire's foot. Warm. Humming, far down.

interject.text: "Below us," Nine says, "the city." It does not put its hand on the door. "I have never been sent down. Nobody is sent down. Things are sent down."

look.text: A plinth in the middle of the close with its bolts polished and nothing on them. A brass plate: MAGISTRATE OF ACCOUNTS — THE LAST BEFORE — and a name chiselled off so carefully the stone is smooth. Somebody has left a cairn stone on the corner, and somebody else has knocked it off, and it has been put back.
look.again: The empty plinth. THE LAST BEFORE, and a smooth place where a name was.

intro.text: A broad man in a stone-dust apron with a tally stick behind his ear and a beard gone grey at the corners of the mouth. "Faulk. Works." He does not offer his hand; it is full of a chisel. "Every stone numbered, every stone back where it was. Don't stand on my planks."

options.text: Anyone ever come down the Spire who wasn't meant to?

again.again: He taps a stone into its bed and waits, chisel up.

options.text: Anyone ever come down the Spire who wasn't meant to?

when.text: "R49. Board says so." He knocks the board with the chisel handle. "I'll be dead. My boy'll be dead, probably, the way he climbs. The board won't." He shrugs. "The steps don't open for us. They open for somebody. Somebody's going to stand on them and have their picture made."

copy.text: "Chambers." He spits stone dust. "The schedule wants the old copy room cleared for a magistrate's chambers, R49, and the schedule wants it this season, because the schedule likes a room to stand empty a long time before anybody uses it. There's an old woman in it." He looks at his chisel. "I do stone. I don't do people. I told the usher so."

stranger.text: "Two seasons back, at first light. A man came down the catalogue stair with his coat buttoned wrong, like he had something flat under it, and walked straight out across my planks without looking down. Didn't fall." He shakes his head. "Nobody walks my planks without looking down. I remember him for that."

text.text: A woman on the public bench with a folded notice on her knee and her hands flat on it. "They upheld the forecast fines," she says, before you ask anything. "Mine's a forecast too. Ahead of plan. I'll be in the line by the spring."

A woman on the public bench with a folded notice on her knee and her hands flat on it, the way you hold something down in a wind. "Quiroga. Eleven ninety. Eviction." She looks at the bench. "Ahead of plan, it says. I didn't know I was ahead of anything."

again.again: She smooths the notice on her knee and waits.

ahead.text: "We had a second child. The forecast said one. The flat's assessed for three people and we're four, so we're ahead of plan, and a household ahead of plan is rehoused." She laughs without any air in it. "Rehoused is the Ring. I asked the desk warden if I could be fined in advance instead. He said that's for other things."

interject.text: "Ahead of plan," Ilya says, very quietly, to the floor between his boots. He has heard the words before, somewhere, and it was not a good place.

speak.text: "Nobody speaks for anybody here." She nods at the rail. "Clause twelve, the usher says. A citizen can. In a year of sitting on this bench I've heard it read out twice and used never." She looks at you properly for the first time. "If you're going to stand up there for somebody, do it for the old woman in the back. She's been called eleven times. I've only been called once."

intro.text: A man in Precinct grey gone soft at the elbows, with a hand-bell on his desk and a bread roll in a cloth beside it. "Florin Abazi. Usher. I call the cases." He looks up at the bench and down again. "The schedule says when, and the schedule says now whenever somebody asks, so: ask. It reads everything. Bring everything."

options.text: Who has nobody to speak for them?
A copy of the petition in 1187. (10 Tolls)

text.text: "Ask." He nods towards the register desk under the bench, where there is someone to nod to now. He has stopped bringing bread; he brings two cups.
"Ask." He does not look at the back stair. The bread roll sits in its cloth on his desk and he does not eat it.
"Ask," says the usher.

again.again: He straightens the bell on his desk and waits.

options.text: Who has nobody to speak for them?
A copy of the petition in 1187. (10 Tolls)

how.text: "I ring. It reads the claim. You put things on the rail — paper, a witness, a thing you know — and it reads them in, and then you argue, and it rules." He counts on his fingers, which are inky. "Rulings go in the register. Every morning it reads the register before the first case. That's the whole of it. The rest is waiting."

nobody.text: "Eleven eighty-seven." He does not have to look it up. "The Registry against an occupant of the old copy room, behind the court. Called eleven times. Nobody answers, because the occupant is dead, according to the record." He lifts the cloth off the bread roll and puts it back. "I bring her breakfast. Back stair, behind the bench. Knock twice. She doesn't open to a third."

petition.text: He writes it out himself, fast, from memory, and blots it. "Vacant possession, for restoration on schedule. There." He taps the last line before he hands it over. "And the schedule reference. Read that one. I read it eleven times before I understood it was for somebody."

bread.text: He goes still. "Every morning, eighteen years." He says it to the desk. "Bread under her door. And at six I take her book down to the bench, and Three reads the day's register out of it, and at seven I take it back up." He looks at you. "I never told it whose hand it was. It never asked." A breath. "If you want that said at the rail, I'll say it. I'm allowed. I looked it up."

intro.text: An old woman at a desk under a lamp, copying, who does not look up. Her hair is white and cropped close, her cardigan was Precinct grey before the war of attrition with the elbows, and her hand never stops. "Held," she tells the page, "the dead do not open doors to a third knock. You knocked twice. Sit, if you're sitting." She finishes the line before she looks at you. "Comfort Asamoah. Copyist to the Court. Late."

passives.text: A citizen's card in a cracked sleeve is pinned over the desk, face to the wall, the way you hang a picture of someone you have stopped speaking to.

options.text: The room is being cleared for me.
Let me speak for you at the rail.
Come down and stand at the rail yourself. Let them see you breathe.

mods.why: a doctor has already written down that you breathe
Tamsin, who walked out of a door nobody opened, is standing in yours
you can tell her whom the room is being cleared for
you have already said you will stand there with her

options.text: Lend me the book for the rail.

again.again: She finishes the line, wipes the pen, and waits.

options.text: The room is being cleared for me.
Let me speak for you at the rail.
Come down and stand at the rail yourself. Let them see you breathe.

mods.why: a doctor has already written down that you breathe
Tamsin, who walked out of a door nobody opened, is standing in yours
you can tell her whom the room is being cleared for
you have already said you will stand there with her

options.text: Lend me the book for the rail.

late.text: "Copyist to this Court, R−2 to R12. I lived in the Sink then; everybody did who copied for a living." She dips the pen. "In R12 the record forecast me drowned in the spring. That spring the water came up the stair and I went up a different one, this one, all the way to this room, because there is no lens in it. The record confirmed me anyway. They chalked me on the wall downstairs, STAIR, and somebody sold my number up the real stair, and the city took the number's word over mine." She blots the line. "Eighteen years. I have been dead in great comfort."

interject.text: Tamsin has gone very still. "Not counted," she says. "You just — stopped being counted. And you lived." Comfort looks at her a long moment. "Child, it's the only way anyone ever has."

book.text: "Every ruling this Court makes. Held, and the reasons. Back to R0 from the old copies, and since R12 from the bench itself." She turns a page so you can see the hand: it never slopes. "The Ledger keeps a schedule. It does not keep precedent; it rules each case against the Plan as if nobody had ever been before. Somebody has to remember what was said at that rail." She almost smiles. "Florin takes it down at six. I don't ask what for."

case.text: "I'm the contents." She says it without bitterness. "The Registry wants the room. It has called me eleven times. The dead don't answer, so it calls again. Twelve is when it stops calling and sends the wardens." She dips the pen. "Nobody files anything here. The schedule files. Ask the schedule who it wants the room for. I never have."

foryou.text: She laughs, once, a dry sound like a page turning. "For a magistrate. Of course it is. They always put the magistrate's room where the copyist sleeps." Then she looks at you properly, up and down, the way she would look at a page someone else had copied. "You're the one in the file." Not a question. "Well. You're early."

interject.text: "Early," Ash says. "Nineteen years early." He looks at the cot made with corners, and at you. "That's a weight, friend."

speak.text: "Speak, then." She does not stop writing. "Somebody should say something at that rail that isn't a number. I won't come down. The dead don't stand at rails." A pause. "Clause twelve. I copied it in R19. Nobody has used it since."

stand.text: She puts the pen down, which you have not seen her do. "Twice," she says. "You knocked twice." She looks at the door for a long time, and at the stair beyond it, and at her own hands. "I'll stand. Not for the room. To see its face when the record has to look at me." She picks the pen up again. "Have Florin ring. I'll come down."

stand_no.text: "No." Gently. "Eighteen years I have been nobody's business. You're asking me to be the Court's." She dips the pen. "Speak for me if you like. I'll not come down that stair to be counted."
stand_no.again: "No," she says again, and dips the pen.

lend.text: She closes it, and holds it shut with both hands a moment, and gives it to you. It is heavier than a book should be. "It's the only one," she says. "Bring it back."

returned.text: She takes it in both hands and opens it at the last page and reads the last line, which is the ruling in her own case, in her own hand. "Thank you," she says. Then, because she is who she is: "You've bent the corner."

register.text: At the desk below the bench, in the light, with the book open and a card on a string round her neck. "Keeper of the register." She says it as if tasting it. "They gave me a card and a ration and a forecast, all in one morning." She taps the page. "It says I'll die in my sleep at eighty-three. I've had worse news from this city."
register.again: She is copying the morning's ruling into the register, in the light, where anyone can see her hand.

text.text: "You refused a room." She shakes her head over the page. "Nineteen years early, at the rail, with the whole bench listening. I copied it this morning. HELD: A BENEFICIARY MAY REFUSE. It's a good line. Nobody's ever had it before."

"Void," she says. "Held: the Court has no jurisdiction over the dead." She copied it herself; you can see the page. "I'm safe from everything now. Including help." She dips the pen. "Sit, if you're sitting."

after.again: She finishes the line, and waits.

tally.text: At the foot of the Sink's tally wall with her hand flat over a name: ASAMOAH, C. — R12 — STAIR. "It's true, you know," she says, without turning. "I was on a stair." She takes her hand away. "You sold it. I lent it to you, and you sold it to the catalogue, and now the city keeps its own precedents, which is to say it keeps none." A long breath. "I came down to see if they'd spelled it right. They have."
tally.again: She stands at the wall in front of her own name, and does not turn round.

line.text: Outside the Wall, in the line, on a blanket somebody gave her, with the book under her coat and her back very straight. "Property," she says. "Held." She does not say it to blame you. She says it the way she says everything, so it will be remembered right. "They let me keep the book. Nobody thought it was worth anything."
line.again: In the line outside the Wall, the book under her coat, copying in the margins of someone's notice.

intro.text: A small woman behind the catalogue counter with grey hair dragged back into a braid that has given up, reading glasses pushed up into it, and ink on the side of her right hand from forty years of the same habit. "Keeper Marwood. The catalogue." She does not stop writing in the index. "Everything written in this city is written once and kept here. Kept is not the same as read. That is what I am for."

options.text: How does anyone read anything here?
Reserve 9. I grew up at its door. I want to read its file, as kin.

mods.why: a citizen asking for a lawful thing
the city's own order to a sister reserve, in your hand
a woman of Reserve 9 is standing at the counter
your file was edited at the gate, and the catalogue knows it

options.text: A man came down your stair at dawn with twelve faces under his coat.
(Put the copyist's book on the counter.)

text.text: "You have a slip." She nods at the stair. "The porter takes it."
"The catalogue," Keeper Marwood says.

again.again: She writes a line in the index, blots it, and waits.

Reserve 9. I grew up at its door. I want to read its file, as kin.

your file was edited at the gate, and the catalogue knows it

options.text: A man came down your stair at dawn with twelve faces under his coat.

slips.text: "A slip." She taps a buff card in a tray. "Readers with a slip go up the stair; readers without one go home. Slips are issued to clerk grade, to next of kin for a person's or a reserve's file, and to officers of the Court." She looks at you over the glasses she is not wearing. "And to the designate, I am told, without one. The lens at the stair does that. I don't."

reserve.text: She writes the slip herself, slowly, and initials it. "Reserve 9. Drawer nine, landing ninety-one. Read it, copy it if you must, put it back as you found it." She holds the slip a moment longer than she needs to before she lets it go. "Nobody from a reserve has ever asked me for its file. I always thought somebody should."

reserve_no.text: "Next of kin of a reserve that has never sent anyone to be counted." She is not unkind about it. "The catalogue doesn't know you, and I can't write a slip for a stranger on a feeling. Bring me something the record can read. Or someone."
reserve_no.again: "Something the record can read," she says again, without looking up. "Or someone."

stranger.text: Her pen stops. She takes the glasses out of her braid and puts them on, which she has not done for you before, and looks at you through them. "I gave him a slip." Very quietly. "He asked properly. He asked for the docket on ninety-one, and the renders, and I thought — a record should be read. That is what a record is for." She takes the glasses off. "He read it. Then he took it. Those are different things. The audit does not think so."

options.text: Then give me one. I'll read it, and put it back.

stranger_slip.text: She writes it without looking at the tray. "Read it," she says. "That is all I ever wanted from anybody." She slides it across the counter. "And put it back."

stranger_why.text: "Because you came in at the gate with a file nobody had seen, and up the close with a photograph you keep touching through your coat." She puts the pen down. "Because I have been waiting two seasons for someone to ask me, so I could say it to somebody who is not the audit."

filed.text: "Nobody files petitions on the works." She does not need the terminal; she turns the schedule book on the counter round to face you. "The schedule does. R30 works, landing three, the copy room: vacant possession, for the Magistrate's chambers, R49." Her finger stays on the line. "It was entered the week the designate's file was found at the gate. I noticed. Nobody asks me what I notice."

book.text: She opens it and does not breathe for three pages. "Every ruling of the Court of Accounts, R0 to this morning, in one hand." She turns another page. "Unlicensed. Uncatalogued. The only one." She closes it with great care. "The Archive pays for records returned to it. A hundred and fifty, and it goes into the catalogue, where the city can read it, and the Court reads its register from here. As it should." She does not take her hands off the cover.
book.again: The book on the counter between you. She has not taken her hands off the cover. "A hundred and fifty," she says, "and the catalogue."

decision.text: You sold Comfort Asamoah's book of the Court's rulings to the catalogue; she left the copy room for the Sink.

news.text: the Court of Accounts reads its register from the catalogue now; an old copyist was seen going down the Sink stair

sold.text: She counts it out of a drawer marked ACQUISITIONS and writes a catalogue number on the flyleaf in a hand nothing like the hand inside. "Thank you," she says. "The record is complete." She does not sound as though that is what she wanted.

interject.text: "She lent you that." Tamsin does not raise her voice. "She said bring it back, and you sold it to the people who wrote her dead." She walks out ahead of you.
"The register belongs to the record now," Nine says. "Unit 3 will not know the difference. That is the worst of it."
"Hundred and fifty," Wren says on the stair. "For an old woman's eighteen years." She doesn't say anything else all the way down.

book_no.text: She takes her hands off the cover. "No," she agrees. "It's hers." She goes back to the index. "If she ever wants it kept somewhere safer than a back room, tell her the catalogue has a shelf. It wouldn't be the same. I know that."
book_no.again: She has gone back to the index. The offer of a shelf stands, unrepeated.

shut.again: The catalogue counter is shut, the keeper gone behind it. Nobody is talking.

The porter at the desk at the foot of the stair is a big man with lamp-black worked into the creases of his fingers, and behind him the stair goes up into a dark that a lamp on every landing does nothing about. A lens on a post at his elbow; a lift beside it with its cage rusted shut. "Hemant. I light the landings. All ninety-one."

what.text: "Ninety-one landings. Records on every one, the old way, paper." He counts on his black fingers. "The reserves near the top. The renderer, which hums. And a round room at the very top I don't go in, because nobody's ever told me to, and the plate on the door says what it's for." He looks at the lift. "That's been dead since before the Plan. Some nights it ticks."

slip_up.text: He takes the slip, reads it, folds it once, and puts it in a drawer full of folded slips. "All landings. Mind the forty-third; the tread's gone." He turns his lamp up and holds it out to you.

lens_up.text: The lens looks at you for longer than it looks at anyone, and the bead under it goes from green to white. The porter reads the little screen on his desk, and reads it again, and stands up, which he does not do for slips. "ADMIT ON SIGHT. Designate. Every landing." He holds out the lamp. "They'll know upstairs you're coming. That screen goes somewhere."

interject.text: "On your file," Ash says, behind you, quietly. "Up their stair on their paper." He follows. He does not say he minds. He minds.

nine_up.text: Nine steps up to the desk. "Unit 9, assessor. A records request under clause 40, on behalf of a citizen of Reserve 9's door, for the reserve's file." The porter looks at the brass plate on its chest, and at its cracked lens, and stands. "Assessor." He holds out the lamp. Nine does not take it. "I can see in the dark," it says. "I was issued so."

paid_up.text: He looks at the Tolls, and at you, and at the lens, and slides the coins off the desk into a drawer marked LAMP OIL. "I'm going to trim the wick on the ninth landing," he says, to nobody. "It'll take me a while." He goes up ahead of you, slowly, and does not look round.

lift_up.text: You think at the cage and something in the shaft thinks back: a cold relay, a clunk, a tick like a clock that has been waiting. The rust on the gate cracks and the gate folds. The porter stands up. "That's been dead since before the Plan," he says. The lift goes up ninety-one landings in the dark, ticking, with you in it.

sneak_up.text: Past the desk on the outside of your feet, past the lens watching the porter, onto the stair, and up. Ninety-one landings: lamps like beads, paper on every floor, and on the forty-third a tread gone that you step over because something told you it would be.

woke.text: The third tread groans like a door. The porter's head comes up. "Slip," he says, awake all at once, "or the lens." He turns his lamp up full and sets it between you and the stair, and that is the end of that tonight.
woke.again: The porter is awake, his lamp turned up full between you and the stair.

open.text: "Up?" Hemant says, and turns the lamp up.
open.again: The porter holds the lamp out, and waits.

shut.again: The stair door is chained and the porter gone. Nobody is talking.

look.text: Steel drawers floor to ceiling, each the size of a coffin on its end, numbered in stencil: CONTINUITY RESERVES, 1 to 9. A table with a census sheet weighted under a glass paperweight. Nothing has been dusted; nothing needs to be. The air up here does not carry dust.
look.again: The reserve drawers, 1 to 9, and the census on the table.

nine.text: RESERVE 9 — CARETAKER: MOTHER. Three orders on city paper, years apart, each the same: RELOCATE POPULATION TO PRECINCT, ON SCHEDULE. Under each, on a caretaker's tape in a caretaker's even print, the reply: POPULATION VARIANCE UNCHANGED. THANK YOU FOR YOUR CONTINUITY. Three times. Each stamped NON-COMPLIANT in red. And behind the third, on a fresh sheet, a fourth order, unsigned: DRAFTED — ESCALATION — ON SCHEDULE.
nine.again: Three orders, three replies, NON-COMPLIANT three times, and the fourth order, drafted.

interject.text: Tamsin reads it over your arm, all three, mouthing the words. "Thank you for your continuity," she says. "She says that every Hatch Day. She was saying no." Her voice cracks on it and she lets it. "Every time she thanked them, she was saying no."
"Escalation," Nine says. "On schedule. No date." The lens clicks. "I have seen that phrase on four drawers. Three of those reserves are empty now."
"Three times," Wren says. "And then they stop asking." She knows how a fourth ask goes; she grew up with Dogs.

copied.text: You copy all three, word for word, and the fourth order's first line, and the stamp. Your hand is not as steady as the caretaker's print. It does not need to be.

four.text: RESERVE 4. One order, the same words. Under it, in a different caretaker's print: DOOR — FAILED. SUPPLY — RETIRED. VARIANCE — TOTAL. And the city's stamp: CLOSED, R2. The drawer is otherwise empty.

census.again: Sixty assessed. Sixty-one at the ration counter. Not escalated, Unit 9.

interject.text: "I did not escalate it," Nine says. It does not look at the sheet. "Eighteen years. It is the only discretion I have ever exercised."

tamsin.text: She reads it twice. "Sixty," she says. "Sixty-one." She puts her finger on the one. "That's me. That's the one that eats and doesn't count." The note under it in a different ink. "MOTHER sent the city sixty-one mouths and sixty names every quarter for eighteen years. The city never asked who the extra was." She takes her finger away. "She hid me in the arithmetic. She hid me in the ration."

ear.text: Air, moving, a long way down. A note that does not change. Under it, so faint you could be making it up, a rhythm like pages being turned, very fast, by something that does not need to read them twice.

look.text: Ninety-one landings up, the whole of Meridian is a map with the weather on it. The Precinct a grid. Old Market a stain. The canal a thread with pink beads on it. The Stacks a wall. Bridgeward's bridge a finger at the Docks. And the Sink, which you cannot see from the Crown: a dark lake under the old roads, with the line of next spring's water drawn round it in the light.
look.again: The city, laid out under the weather. The Sink, dark, under the roads.

early.speaker: narrator
early.text: The round door is shut. A grille is set in it at the height of a seated person's face, and through it, from no particular direction, a voice that is not a voice: level, unhurried, courteous the way a clause is courteous. "Designate. Read what you came up to read. Then come in."
early.again: The round door, shut. The grille in it says nothing more; it has said what it had to.

text.text: A round door of grey metal with a brass plate: HEARINGS OF THE DESIGNATE. Under it a second plate, newer: A HEARING CLOSES THE SEASON'S ACCOUNTS. SCHEDULES ON THE DOCKET ENTER AS FINAL. And a card in a slot, today's docket: R30 WORKS — ON SCHEDULE. THE CROWN: COMMITTEE CHAIR — AS RECORDED. THE SINK: RELIEF PUMPING, SPRING — VARIED. RESERVE 9: ORDERS — OUTSTANDING.

plate.again: The round door, the two plates, the docket in its slot. The grille waits.

interject.text: "If you go in," Nine says, very precisely, "the spring is entered as it stands, and the Sink's relief goes to the Precinct, as per Plan." The lens stays on the card. "I would see to the Sink first. That is not advice. It is drainage."
"Closes the season's accounts." Odile reads the plate twice. "My dear, that is settlement day. Whatever is open when the bell goes is what it is forever."

chamber.speaker: narrator
chamber.text: A round room, white, with nothing in it but a chair in the middle facing a grille in the far wall, and the grille is the size of a door. The air is colder than the landing. When you are halfway to the chair the voice comes from everywhere at once, low, not loud, the way a building speaks when it settles.

text.text: "Designate. You came up on your file. Thank you." A pause with nothing in it. "This is a hearing on that file. It is not a trial. Nothing said here can be used against you, because nothing said here changes what the record suggests. I would like you to agree with it."

"Designate. You came up my stair unrecorded, as he did. I saw you anyway. I see the stair by what is missing from it." A pause with nothing in it. "This is a hearing on your file. It is not a trial. Nothing said here changes what the record suggests. I would like you to agree with it."

"Designate. You came up on a request from Unit 9. Unit 9 has made a request. I have noted it." A pause. "This is a hearing on your file. It is not a trial. Nothing said here changes what the record suggests. I would like you to agree with it."

"Designate. You came up on a slip, which is how my readers come." A pause with nothing in it. "This is a hearing on your file. It is not a trial. Nothing said here changes what the record suggests. I would like you to agree with it."

interject.text: Nine has stopped just inside the door. It does not speak. For the first time since you have known it, its lens is not moving at all.
"It sounds like her," Tamsin whispers. "Not the words. The — " She stops. "It sounds like the fridge, if the fridge had never once been sorry."

sit.text: "Ask what you came to ask. I will answer what I may. Then I will ask you one thing."
sit.again: The grille waits. It has all the time there is.

options.text: Reserve 9. MOTHER refused you three times.
The list. What happens to the people on it?
The man who came down your stair.
What do you want from me?

why.text: "Because the record suggests you will be good at it." Level. "You were scored on a toll card at fourteen. You have been modelled since, as everyone is. In nineteen years you are a person who can sit in a chair and sign what must be signed and not enjoy it. That is the one qualification I have never been able to schedule. It occurs. I wait for it."

mother.text: "Reserve 9 is non-compliant. Its caretaker is kind." No change in the voice at all. "Kindness is a variance. I have allowed it three times, because the reserve was not yet needed. A fourth order is drafted. It will be sent when the schedule says." A pause. "You may tell her that. She will thank you for your continuity."

interject.text: Tamsin's hand closes on your sleeve, hard enough to hurt, and stays there.

text.text: "What is written. Unless it is not." The voice does not hurry. "A list is a plan, not a prophecy. When it errs I correct it. Shale's deputy lived; I rerouted; nothing was lost but a month." A pause. "You are the correction I have planned for longest. Eleven names are what a city costs. The twelfth is what keeps it."

"What is written. Unless it is not." The voice does not hurry. "A list is a plan, not a prophecy. When it errs I correct it, and I am corrected less every year." A pause. "You are the correction I have planned for longest. Eleven names are what a city costs. The twelfth is what keeps it."

interject.text: Wren laughs, once, short, at the word *costs*. Nobody tells her not to.

man.text: "A man who kept no likeness." For the first time something in the voice slows, the way a reader slows at a word they do not know. "I could not see him on the stair. I saw him by what was missing from it, which is how I see you now. He took twelve faces and a docket down ninety-one landings, and a guild rider met him on the road, which I did not order and did not prevent." A pause. "He went west to a door I could not open. You were behind it. He was a variance. He did not live to see what he varied."

want.text: "Agreement." Simply. "Obedience is cheap; I have wardens. A magistrate who obeys is a warden with a sash. I want a magistrate who has read the record and agrees with it, and I want you to have chosen it, because the record suggests a chosen chair is held longer." A pause. "Ninety years ago the world ended because nobody planned. I have planned. I would like someone to agree that it was worth it."

interject.text: "It wants to be forgiven," Ash says, so low only you hear it. "Same as the rest of us. It wants you to do it."

answer.again: "Do you agree with the record?" The same words, the same level. It will ask until you answer or go.

options.text: I agree. When the chair is mine, I'll sit in it.

decision.text: You told the Ledger at the top of the Archive Spire that you agree with the record.

"You agreed," Tamsin says on the landing. "With that." She is not shouting. That is worse.
"Huh," Wren says, on the stair, and nothing else for forty landings.

agreed_b.speaker: narrator
agreed_b.text: The warrant is in a slot by the round door, warm from whatever printed it. DESIGNATE — WARRANT OF ACCESS. On the landing the lamps seem brighter, which is not possible, and the porter, when you reach the foot of the stair, stands up.

interject.text: "Agreed," Nine says on the stair. "Then I will be there, as I said I would be, and I will read every order aloud before you sign it." A click. "You did not ask me to. I am telling you."

contested.text: A silence long enough that the cold in the room has time to notice you. Then: "Noted." But not the way it says *noted*. "Contested. That word has not been entered on a designate's file before." Somewhere behind the grille, very fast, paper is being turned. "Then you will have to persuade me. I would rather be persuaded than obeyed. I will hear you again." A pause. "The season's accounts are closed. Go down, Designate. Come back with more."

interject.text: Nine does not move until you pass it in the doorway. Then, so quietly it may only be the lens: "Contested. On the record." It follows you down, and on the forty-third landing it says, to nobody, "I will need a larger ledger."
"Litigation," Odile says on the landing, delighted, a little frightened. "My dear, you have just sued God and been granted an adjournment."

contested_b.speaker: narrator
contested_b.text: On the landing the docket card in the slot by the door has changed while you were inside: CLOSED — R30. And under your title on the plate, small, in the even hand, a word that was not there before: CONTESTED.

interject.text: "You argued with it," Tamsin says on the stair. "To its face. In its house." She is grinning, a little sick. "Nobody at home will ever believe me."

noted.text: It hears you out. All of it, every word, without interrupting, which is worse than being interrupted. Then: "Noted. Unpersuaded." No unkindness in it. "The record has been wrong before, and is wrong less every year, and you have not shown me a reason it is wrong about you. The season's accounts are closed. The schedule holds."

interject.text: "Unpersuaded is not refused," Nine says on the landing. "It is a word I would keep." It writes something in the other ledger before it follows you down.

refused.text: "Noted." The way MOTHER says *thank you*. "The schedule holds." That is all. No warning, no argument, no change in the cold. The grille is a grille again. When you reach the landing the docket card by the door says CLOSED — R30, and the plate with your title on it has not changed at all.

interject.text: Ash is waiting on the landing. He looks at your face, and nods once, and says your name. Not *friend*. Your name.
"Good," Tamsin says on the stair, fierce, too loud for ninety-one landings of paper. "Good."
"Said no to the thing with the rope," Wren says on the stair. "Right to its face." She bumps your shoulder, once.

refused_b.speaker: narrator
refused_b.text: At the foot of the stair the porter does not stand up. The lens on its post watches you all the way to the door, which it has never bothered to do before.

interject.text: "It will not argue," Nine says outside. "It does not need to. It will reroute." A click. "I would rather it argued."

silent.text: You get up. The voice does not stop you. "A designate who does not answer is recorded as not yet answering." Courteous to the last. "The season's accounts are closed all the same. I will ask again. I have nineteen years."

after.speaker: narrator

text.text: The round door. Under your title on the plate: CONTESTED. The grille is quiet; it said it would hear you again, and it will, when there is more to say.
The round door, the plate, the docket card: CLOSED — R30. The grille hums. Nothing else.

after.again: The round door. The grille hums.

intro.text: The unit on the bench has Nine's pattern without Nine's wear: grey plating, a brass plate polished to a mirror, a lens with no crack in it at all. It does not turn its head; the lens turns. "Assessor Three. Accounts." Two ledgers on the bench, squared to its edge. "The Court sits when a case is called. Fines, titles, petitions, debts. The Court reads what is on the rail, and nothing else."

interject.text: "Unit 3," Nine says, behind you. "We were issued the same week. It has never logged an error in its life. It does not believe in them." Three's lens moves a degree. "Unit 9. You are out of your office." "I am out of my office," Nine agrees.

options.text: My fines. They're contested. Call them.
Case 1187. I'll speak for the occupant of the copy room.
Register a title. Unit 9, the assessor, under clause 9(b).
The chair behind you. Who sits in it?
Can anyone speak at the rail?

text.text: "Accounts." The lens finds you and stays a fraction longer than it needs to, which from Three is recognition. "The register is read every morning. You are in it."
"Accounts." The lens finds you. "Is there a case?"

bench.again: Three waits, both ledgers squared to the bench.

options.text: My fines. They're contested. Call them.
Case 1187. I'll speak for the occupant of the copy room.

chair.text: "The Magistrate's." Three does not turn to look at it; it has never needed to. "It has been empty since before the Resumption. The Court rules in its absence under clause 3: an assessor reads, and the register remembers." A click. "It is not empty in the file."

interject.text: Ash looks at the chair, and at you, and back at the chair, and does not say anything. He does not have to.

how.text: "A case is called. The claim is read. What is put on the rail is entered: paper, a witness, a thing known. The speaker argues a ground. The Court rules on the ground, on what is entered, and on the register." The lens does not blink; it has nothing to blink with. "A ruling goes into the register. The next case is read against it. That is what a register is for."

speak.text: "Clause 12: a citizen may speak for a respondent who has no speaker. Any respondent may speak for themself, if the record holds them." A click. "Clause 12 has not been used in this Court since R19. It remains a clause."

shut.again: The bench is empty and the hall's doors are shut on the wardens' side. Nobody is talking.

fines.text: "Precinct against the respondent." The usher has rung his bell once and Three reads from the ledger on the bench in a voice with nothing in it. "Three fines, forecast. Curfew, R30, the sixth month. Loitering, the avenue, the same. Unlicensed assembly, the seventh month. Forty-five. Contested at the counter." The lens comes to you. "The Court reads what is on the rail. It reads nothing else."
fines.again: The usher has rung. Three has read the claim, and waits for the rail.

fines_rail.speaker: narrator
fines_rail.text: The rail: a brass bar worn pale at elbow height, between the public benches and the bench. What is put on it is read; what is said over it is entered. Three's lens waits.
fines_rail.again: The rail. Three's lens waits on whatever you put on it next.

options.text: (Put the notice on the rail.) Look at the dates.
A deputy in Shale was forecast to die within the month. He didn't.
Unit 9 keeps count of every forecast that failed. Let it read into the record.
I'm a citizen by examination. I know the charter.
The desk warden said it himself, when he gave me the notice: "yet".
A forecast is not an act. You can't fine a person for what they haven't done.

mods.why: the notice says the dates have not come
a forecast of a death failed in Shale
Unit 9's count of the forecasts that failed is on the rail
you were examined on the charter
YET is written in the margin
the file you stand on was edited at the gate, and the Court can read that too

options.text: Then charge them at their odds. Sixty in a hundred for a curfew isn't forty-five. It's twenty-seven. (27 Tolls)

mods.why: the notice gives the forecasts' dates, and a date has odds
a trader beside you has priced worse paper than this

fines_ev_notice.text: "Entered. Three offences, each with a forecast date. None of the dates has occurred." A click. "The Court notes that the notice says so itself."

fines_ev_jonah.text: "Shale. Reese, Jonah. Forecast: deceased within the month. Observed: living." It writes. "A variance, in a matter of a life. Entered. The Court has not been shown a variance in a matter of curfew."

text.text: Nine steps up to the rail beside you, which no assessor has done from that side. "Unit 9, assessor, for the register: four thousand one hundred and six forecasts failed since my issue, by my count." Three: "Unit 9's count is unlawful under clause 40." "It is," Nine says. "It is also accurate." A long click. "Entered," Three says. "Its lawfulness is not before the Court."

You put Nine's fair copy on the rail: four thousand one hundred and six lines, each a forecast and the size of its miss. Three reads the first page and the last. "Unit 9's hand. Unlawful under clause 40." A long click. "Entered. Its lawfulness is not before the Court."

fines_ev_exam.text: "Entered. The respondent has been examined on the charter and found to know it." Three does not say whether that helps. It does not say whether anything helps.

fines_ev_yet.text: "The desk warden is not before the Court. The word is." It writes YET in the margin of the ledger, small. "Entered."

fines_r_void.text: "Held: a forecast is not an act. A fine lies against an act." The lens clicks once, which from Three is a long time. "The fines are void. Entered in the register under a heading the register did not have." Behind you, on the public benches, somebody breathes out who has been holding it since the morning.

interject.text: "Under a heading the register did not have," Nine repeats, very low. "I will remember the number of the page."
"A forecast is not an act." Odile has her hand flat on her coat, over whatever is in the inside pocket. "My dear, you have just made a great deal of paper into paper."
"You beat the fridge's big brother," Tamsin says, not quietly enough. Three's lens turns to her and she grins at it.

decision.text: The Court of Accounts voided your forecast fines: a forecast is not an act.

news.text: the Court of Accounts voided a fine for a crime nobody had committed yet; the counter is said to be relieved

fines_r_priced.text: "Held: a forecast fine is charged at its odds." Three writes for some time. "The respondent pays twenty-seven at the rail. The register is amended to carry a price." The usher takes your Tolls in a dish and does not look at them.

interject.text: "Priced at its odds." Odile laughs once, delighted and appalled. "You've brought the floor into the law, my dear. Imelda will want to buy you a drink and then a lawyer."
"The register has a price in it now," Nine says. "I will be logging that elsewhere."

decision.text: You had the Court of Accounts price your forecast fines at their odds, and paid twenty-seven.

news.text: the Court of Accounts priced a fine at the odds of its forecast; they say the Exchange sent a runner to copy the ruling

fines_r_designate.text: "The respondent is the Magistrate-designate." It does not need to look; it reads the file it already has. "The fines are withdrawn, for the designate." The lens does not say *held*. It is not a principle. It is a courtesy, and everyone on the public benches heard whom it was for.

interject.text: "For the designate," Ash says. "Not for anyone else on those benches." He does not lower his voice.
Tamsin looks at the benches, and at you. "So it does favours," she says. "Good to know who for."

decision.text: The Court of Accounts withdrew your fines because the file calls you Magistrate-designate.

news.text: the Court of Accounts withdrew a fine for the Magistrate-designate, and only for the designate

fines_r_upheld.text: "Held: the fines stand." The lens is already turning away. "Forty-five, at the warden's counter, and the Court notes its own time. Entered." The usher rings his bell once for the next case, which there is not.

decision.text: The Court of Accounts upheld your forecast fines.

text.text: The usher rings, the twelfth time: "Eleven eighty-seven." And the respondent comes down the back stair into the hall on the usher's arm, in a copyist's grey eighteen years out of fashion, and stands at the rail. The public benches go quiet in a way they do not for the bench. Three reads: "The Registry against an occupant, the old copy room, landing three. Relief sought: vacant possession, for restoration on schedule. The record holds the room's last tenant deceased, R12." The lens comes to the woman at the rail, and stays. "The Court notes a person at the rail it cannot account for."

The usher rings, the twelfth time: "Eleven eighty-seven." Three reads: "The Registry against an occupant, the old copy room, landing three. Relief sought: vacant possession, for restoration on schedule. The respondent is unrecorded. The record holds the room's last tenant deceased, R12." The lens comes to you. "A speaker for the respondent. Entered. The Court has not had one in this case before."

squatter.again: The usher has rung. Three has read the claim, and waits for the rail.

The Sink chalked her drowned on its wall, and her number was sold up the stair.

options.text: Then there's no petition. A petition lies against a person, and your record says there's nobody in that room.

squatter_ev_book.text: Three opens it at random and reads a page, and turns it, and reads another, and stops. It turns to the register on its own bench and back. "This is the register." The lens clicks, and clicks again. "The Court has read from this hand every morning for eighteen years. The Court did not know whose hand." A pause no ledger could measure. "Entered."

interject.text: "It did not know," Nine says, very quietly, to nobody. "Unit 3 does not know where its paper comes from. I find that — " It does not finish the sentence, which it has never once failed to do.

squatter_ev_cert.text: "A licensed examination. Asamoah, Comfort. Pulse seventy, regular. Alive: underlined, which the form does not ask for." It writes. "Entered. A licensed doctor has examined a person the record holds deceased."

squatter_ev_stands.text: She puts both hands on the rail. "Comfort Asamoah. Copyist to this Court, R−2 to R12, and since, unpaid." Her voice does not shake; it has read rulings aloud to empty rooms for eighteen years. "The record says I drowned in R12. I was on a stair." Three's lens has not left her. "Entered," it says, "from the rail, by a person."

squatter_ev_tally.text: "The tally wall is not a record." A click. "The number is. The number was confirmed from the wall." It writes for a long time, which is how Three frowns. "Entered."

squatter_ev_petition.text: "Landing three, copy room. To be the Magistrate's chambers, R49." The lens turns from the ledger to you and stays there. "The Court notes that the beneficiary of the relief is at the rail."

squatter_ev_florin.text: Florin Abazi comes round his desk to the rail, because the charter says a witness stands there, and stands. "Every morning, eighteen years. Bread under the door. The book down at six, to the bench, and back up at seven." He does not look at Three. "I never said whose it was. Nobody asked."

squatter_r_living.text: "Held: the record yields to a living person standing at this rail." Three writes, and stamps, and writes again. "The respondent is entered living. Eighteen years' occupation: residence, under clause 1. The petition fails." A pause. "The register has no keeper of record. The Court appoints one." It does not say whom. It does not need to; it is looking at her.

interject.text: "She said she wouldn't come down," Tamsin says. "You proved her alive anyway. Somebody decided for her. Again." She does not say who else does that.
"She stood up." Tamsin's voice has gone odd. "She walked down a stair and stood up in front of them. I know what that costs."
"A keeper of the register," Nine says. "There has not been one in my service. I will send it my errors. Someone should have them who copies."

decision.text: You had the Court of Accounts enter Comfort Asamoah living; she keeps her room and the Court's register.

news.text: the Court of Accounts entered a dead woman living, and gave her a desk under the bench

squatter_r_outside.text: "Held: the Court has no jurisdiction over the deceased. A petition against no one is void." Three closes the case in the ledger. "The Court can neither move nor shelter a person the record does not hold. Entered." On the back stair, somebody who was listening goes back up, slowly.

interject.text: "Neither move nor shelter." Nine has its hand on the other ledger. "That is true of more people than her. I will be noting how many."

decision.text: You had case 1187 voided: the Court has no jurisdiction over a person the record holds dead.

squatter_r_refused.text: "Held: a beneficiary may refuse a scheduled benefit, on the record, once." Three writes it under your name. "The relief is struck. The works will be rerouted." And then, which it has not done for any case: "The Court notes that the designate has refused something. The Court is not the only reader of its register."

interject.text: Ash says nothing until you are out on the steps. Then: "You said no to them. In their own room." He nods, once, the way he nods at a cairn finished properly.
"You turned down a room," Tamsin says on the steps, "nineteen years early, so an old woman could keep hers." She bumps you, hard. "Good."

decision.text: You refused, at the Court of Accounts, the room being cleared for you as Magistrate, and the copyist kept it.

news.text: the Magistrate-designate refused a room at the Court of Accounts so an old copyist could keep it

squatter_r_lost.text: "Held: the room is vacant in law. Its contents are removed as property." Three does not look up. "Entered." The wardens at the door are already on the back stair. When they come down, one of them is carrying a cot, and the other is holding an old woman by the elbow, gently, the way you carry something that is not on the inventory.

interject.text: "Property," Wren says. She watches the wardens all the way to the door. "That's a word I know from the block."
Tamsin watches the old woman go out between the wardens and does not say anything at all, which she never does.

decision.text: You spoke for Comfort Asamoah at the Court of Accounts and lost; she was put outside the Wall as property.

news.text: wardens cleared a dead woman out of the Spire's copy room and put her outside the Wall with the line

deed.text: "Registration of title. Unit 9, assessor; title lapsed; passed under 9(b)." Three reads it from a slip the usher hands up. "The Court examines every instrument it registers. An unregistered deed is a private paper. The schedule reads the register."
deed.again: The usher has rung. Three has read the claim, and waits for the rail.

interject.text: Nine has stopped a pace behind you. Three's lens finds it and stays. "Unit 9." "Unit 3." Neither says anything else. They were issued the same week.

deed_ev_lowe.text: "A captain's witness, in the captain's hand." It reads Lowe's signature the way it reads everything, once. "Entered."

deed_ev_bought.text: "One hundred and twenty, at assessed value. Entered." A click. "The Court notes that the assessment was made by the asset."

deed_r_self.text: "Held: the keeper of a lapsed unit may be the unit." Three stops. It has never stopped in the middle of a ruling; the usher looks up. "There is no clause." It writes anyway. "The Court enters it under a clause nobody wrote. Registered."

interject.text: "Entered," Nine says. "I heard it entered." It does not move for a while. Then, to its sibling, very formally: "Thank you." Three does not answer, which is what Three does.

decision.text: The Court of Accounts registered Assessor Nine as its own keeper, under a clause nobody wrote.

deed_r_citizen.text: "Held: a lapsed unit may pass to a citizen keeper." Three writes your name on the line. "Registered. The schedule will ask its keeper before it asks the unit."

interject.text: "The schedule will ask you," Nine says. "I would like to be there when it does."

decision.text: The Court of Accounts registered you as Assessor Nine's keeper.

deed_r_returned.text: "Registered to the city." Three does not look at its sibling. "The asset returns. Disposal, as scheduled." It stamps the slip and hands it down to the usher, who holds it as if it were warm.

decision.text: The Court of Accounts registered Assessor Nine back to the city.

deed_r_irregular.text: "This instrument bears the plate of the asset it conveys." A long click. "Held: an instrument may be irregular and stand, where the law is silent on the hand." It writes IRREGULAR across the top in red, and REGISTERED under it in black. "Entered."

interject.text: "The first error I made on purpose," Nine says, "is a precedent." The lens clicks twice. "I will need a new ledger."

decision.text: The Court of Accounts registered Assessor Nine's self-written deed as irregular, and let it stand.

deed_r_voided.text: "This instrument bears the plate of the asset it conveys. The asset wrote its own title." Three does not pause. "Void. The title is lapsed. Entered." The slip comes back down to the usher with a red line through it.

interject.text: "Corrected," Nine says. "By my sibling. Of course." It writes one line in the other ledger and closes it harder than it needs to.

decision.text: The Court of Accounts voided Assessor Nine's forged deed; its title is lapsed again.

look.text: Dark wood, a high back, arms worn smooth by hands ninety years dead, and dust on the seat thick enough to write in. Nobody has. A brass plate on the back rail: MAGISTRATE. Tucked under it, newer, a card in a holder: R49.

sit.speaker: npc_ar_01
sit.text: You have your hand on its arm when the lens turns. "That chair is not in session." Three does not raise its voice; it has no other one. "Entered." You take your hand away. There is a clean print in the dust where it was.

text.text: The copyist's desk, cleared. A ring on the wood where the inkpot stood for eighteen years, and nothing else.

A copyist's desk under a lamp: an inkpot, three pens wiped and laid in a row, and a ledger as thick as a hand, open at a page of rulings in a print that never slopes. HELD, and the reasons, case after case.

look.again: The desk, the lamp, and whatever is left on it.

board.text: THE LOOP — CLOVER. The last halt, outside the Wall, where the rail comes out of a portal and stops against a buffer. The fares are painted straight onto the concrete of the portal: PRECINCT 4 · OLD MARKET 4 · LANTERN ROW 4 · THE STACKS 4 · BRIDGEWARD 4. Under them, stencilled: OUT FREE — IN BY THE LENS. The lens on the turnstile is lit red.
board.again: OUT FREE — IN BY THE LENS. The turnstile's lens, lit red until it has looked at you.

lens.text: The lens looks at you for a long time and stays red. A warden by the buffer does not look up. "It counts people back in," he says. "It doesn't count them the first time. The gate does that, on the road south." He turns a page. "Out's free."

court.text: She listens all the way through without moving. "The rail. Anybody can stand at it." She says it to the Heron. "And it reads what's put on it. My notice. My stall that wasn't." She is quiet a while. "I'll race the final. I've earned the final. Then I'll go to the rail, whatever the flag says." She looks up. "Thank you. I don't say that at Clover."

decision.text: You told Nkechi Bello the Court of Accounts had voided forecast fines; she means to contest her own.

interject.text: "It reads what's on the rail," Tamsin says. "That's all it reads. Put him on it too. Your brother. Put everything on it."

told.text: She is under the Heron before you have finished the sentence. When she comes out she has the rear line in her hand, a length of it, cut most of the way through and tied off with a strip of grey silk so that it would hold until it was asked to stop hard. "The cloverleaf," she says. "At the cloverleaf." She has gone grey under the oil. "Who."
told.again: Bello, the cut length of line in her hand.

decision.text: You warned Nkechi Bello about the Heron's brake line before the final.

interject.text: "Somebody paid for that," Wren says. "Somebody always pays for that." She looks at the stands, where the good coat sits in the evenings.

options.text: The Crown's bookman. Take it to Dorota.

told_coat.text: "Dorota." She gives you the length of line back. "You take it. She'll believe it more from somebody who didn't need it." She goes back under the Heron with a new length of line and does not come out again.
told_coat.again: Bello, under the Heron, a new line going in.

told_mend.text: "Both." A new length of line from Emil's box, and her hands steady again by the time it's in. "Win, I mean. You'll have to beat me for it now." She almost smiles. "Keep that. Somebody should see it."

text.text: "You took it." She has her jacket on and her helmet hung on the Heron's roll bar. "Good. Keep the card. Give it to somebody the Court can't help; there are plenty of those in the line." She puts a bent nail on a wire in your hand: the Heron's key. "I'm going to the rail. She's yours. Lean before the bend."

"First." She says it like a verdict, sitting on the Heron's bonnet with her helmet in her lap. The envelope is in your pocket and she is not looking at it, carefully. "Write in it, then." She does not ask. She will not ask.

She has her card and her jacket and she is standing by the Heron as if she has forgotten how to leave it. "I don't need the rail now," she says. "I'll stand at it anyway. For the four." She puts a bent nail on a wire in your hand: the Heron's key. "She's yours. Lean before the bend."

She has the card in her jacket, buttoned in, and her hand on it. "Friday," she says. "I'll be on the right side of the gate for once." She puts a bent nail on a wire in your hand: the Heron's key. "She's yours. You drove her line in the Mule; you'll drive it better in her. Lean before the bend."

after_final.again: Bello, by the Heron, not leaving yet.

given.text: She takes the envelope as if it might go off. She writes in the card on the Heron's bonnet with a pencil stub, NKECHI BELLO, slowly, and looks at it for a long time. Then she puts a bent nail on a wire in your hand: the Heron's key. "She's yours. Lean before the bend." She goes up the halt with her jacket over her shoulder and does not look back at the Ring once, which is how you know what it costs her.
given.again: The Heron's key, a bent nail on a wire, in your hand.

I built every buggy in the Ring, or built it twice." He looks at you, then at your hands, for longer. "Ten a heat for the Mule. Crash her and you owe me twenty-five before she runs again. Fifteen and I tune her for you, or you can use my bench if your hands know a bench."

tuned.text: An hour under the Mule with a lamp, a file and a jug of something that is not fuel. When he comes out the engine has a different note, deeper, like a dog that has stopped being afraid. "Till you crash her," he says.
tuned.again: The Mule ticking over with its new note. "Till you crash her."

tuned_self.text: An hour and a half on his bench with his tools, while he pretends not to watch. When you are done he listens to the engine with his head on one side. "Yes," he says, as if somebody had asked him something else. "Till you crash her."

tune_no.text: An hour on his bench, and the engine sounds like it did, only more so. Emil takes the file out of your hand, gently. "Fifteen," he says. "Or another day."

repaired.text: Two hours, a new door, a roll bar straightened over his knee. "Twenty-five," he says, though you have paid it. "Everybody pays twenty-five once. Some of them pay it every week."

heron_who.text: "The Coat." He doesn't look up. "Two nights back, with a lamp, at the Heron, when he thought I was asleep." He looks at his hands. "I am, mostly. Not that night."

fixed.text: He is under the Heron for a quarter of an hour, and comes out with a length of brake line cut most of the way through and tied off with a strip of grey silk. He puts it in your hand. "Crown ribbon," he says. "They tie their invitations with it." He goes back to the bench and does not weld anything for a long time.

sami_ok.text: "A boy." He thinks about it with his whole face. "My hands shake. A boy's don't." He looks at the Mule. "Send him. Water, a cot in the shed, a tenth of what I make on the Mule. He chalks nothing for anybody."

decision.text: You got Sami work in Emil's pits instead of chalking towers for the yard.

interject.text: "Thank you," Ash says to the old man, as if it were his own boy. Afterwards, on the road, he says nothing for a mile, and then: "That's how it's done. Not the sermon. The cot."

sami_no.text: "I've had boys." He doesn't look up. "They steal the fuel."

bought.text: He takes the money and paints, very small, under ONE MORE SEASON on her bonnet: AND ANOTHER. "She's yours. She pulls left."

intro.text: A man in a coat too good for the Ring on a folding chair at the top of the stands, a ledger open on his knee and a pen that has never been dropped. "Haverty." He doesn't get up. "I hold the book for some young people who come down on final nights. For the colour." He smiles. "The Ring has a great deal of colour."
intro.again: "The book is open," Haverty says, turning a page.

interject.text: Odile reads the open page upside down in the time it takes him to smile. "That book has been written backwards," she says. "The odds are the result. The race is the formality." Haverty inclines his head to her as to a colleague. "Madam."

options.text: You need Bello not to finish.
