book.text: "The final." He turns the ledger so you can see a page of names in a good hand, and beside every name the same word: BELLO. "They've all backed her. Every one of them. A woman from the Ring who wins her way back inside the Wall: it is a lovely story, and they are young." He turns the ledger back. "If she wins, I pay them out of a book my house holds, and my house will want to know why it backed a story." He says it pleasantly. "I owe my house a great deal. My own card is in this book."

offer.text: "I need the book to balance." He doesn't lower his voice; nobody on the stands is listening to a man in a good coat. "A hundred and fifty, for the Heron not finishing. You needn't touch it. You need only say nothing about anything you see in the pits between now and the flag." He slides a purse half out of his coat, and leaves it there.

decision.text: You took the Crown's bookman's money to say nothing about the Heron before the final.

taken.text: "Splendid." The purse is in your hand and his pen is moving. "You have seen nothing, then, either way." He does not watch you go; he is writing your name in the book, on the side of the page where the money goes out.

interject.text: Wren waits until you are off the stands. "A hundred and fifty," she says. "For a woman going into the tyres at the cloverleaf." She keeps walking. "I keep count."
"You took it," Tamsin says, not loud. "For her not finishing. You know what not finishing is here. You heard Dorota." She doesn't walk beside you for a while.
Ash says nothing at all on the stands. On the road, much later: "There's a price on everything out here, and you just learned yours." It is not said kindly, and it is not said to hurt.
"Right," Ilya says, and it means only one thing, and the thing is not good.

refused.text: "Then you have seen nothing either way," he says, as pleasantly as before, and the purse goes back into his coat. "It comes to the same, you know. It nearly always does." He writes something in the book.
refused.again: "It comes to the same," Haverty says.

card.text: He looks at the envelope and his whole face changes, briefly, into somebody's who has been let off. "A hundred and fifty." He counts it out of a different purse. "It will go back up the Loop and be given to somebody's cook, who will be very grateful, and say so, and be a citizen." He tucks it into his coat. "Thank you. You have saved me a conversation."

decision.text: You sold the Crown's card back to its bookman for a hundred and fifty.

interject.text: "Above its value to him," Odile says, when you are down off the stands. "He would have paid two hundred. Still. Clean." She does not look at the pits.
Wren looks at the pits, where the Heron is, and then at you, and says nothing about it, then or after.

door.text: Leven's door: a steel door propped open on a brick, with a number painted out (11) and a name painted in (LEVEN). On the steel at shoulder height, in white chalk, a mark: a ring with a bar through it. Fresh. Somebody inside has tried to rub it off with a wet hand and made it a smear of the same shape.

again.text: The ring with a bar on Leven's door, chalked again, darker than before.
The ring with a bar on Leven's door, and the smear of a hand that tried to rub it off.

passives.text: The same mark, fainter, on the door frame, and under it older chalk: scrubbed off, and come back, and scrubbed off.

barred.again: LEVEN, and 91, in white over the smear.

I keep the count." She makes a tick. "Ninety-one. If you're staying the night, say your name and it's ninety-two."
intro.again: "Ninety-one," Ha-eun says, finishing a line before she looks up.

interject.text: Tamsin is looking up the stairwell, where people are living on every floor of a building that is open to the weather and has never been sealed. "Ninety-one," she says. "Inside, we were sixty, and we had a machine to count us." She looks at the ledger. "This is better."

mark.text: "A ring with a bar." She puts the pencil down. "It comes on a door, and the tower burns before the rains. Tower Six had it, and Nine, and Three. Nobody was counted dead in any of them. count.text: "So that when they say nobody died," she says, "I can say who." She turns back a page and runs her finger down it, a woman checking a sum. "The Wall says the Ring burns and they count. They count the fires. I count the people."

"The chalk's back," she says, without looking up from the count. "Darker than before." She makes a tick. "Ninety-one."

intro.text: A big man at a table in a steel container, with a ledger, a mug, and a length of pipe across the table where another man would keep a gun. "Ruben. The yard." He looks you over the way he looks at a girder. "Steel's weighed at the gate. If you're selling, sell. If you're buying by the ton, you're the Crown, and you're not."

towers.text: "Dead towers." He drinks from the mug. "The Ring's nothing but dead towers, and a tower nobody lives in is steel. That's all a tower is, out here. Cut it, weigh it, sell it." He puts the mug down. "Somebody inside the Wall is building something. They don't ask where it comes from."

leven.text: "It has." He doesn't pretend; it is the thing you will remember about him. "Sixty families eat off this yard. Twenty of them sleep in Leven, as it happens." He taps the ledger. "There's a road going in at the near end of a bridge in Bridgeward, and the Crown wants steel for it by the ton, no questions about how it came down. A tower that burns comes down lawful. There's no law out here to say otherwise." He looks at you. "Nobody's ever died in my fires. Ask the Wall. It counts."
leven.again: "Nobody's ever died in my fires," Ruben says. "Ask the Wall."

price.again: "Sixty," Ruben says. "I wasn't going to ask leave."

paid.text: The money comes out of a tin under the table. "You never came in." He goes back to the ledger. On the last page you can see LEVEN, and beside it he writes a date that is not a date: AFTER THE COUNT.

dug.text: Maren stands at the end of the row with her coat open and says the eleven names, slowly, and then the Shift says them back. Then she hands you a lamp tag of your own, blank. "That was a shift in the mine," she says. "You're Shift now, if you want it. The tag says so."

rafe.text: For a moment she says nothing at all. "Six cases." The rag goes into her fist. "Rafe lost Ivo under that roof. I'd want the car too." She stands up. "But the car has a crew in the cable house, Shift people, and the Clean will come down Cascade with rifles the morning after. I'll take the powder off him. He won't thank either of us."

decision.text: You told Maren about Rafe's powder. She took it off him.

scabs.text: "Twenty of them." She knew. "Off the guild's block at Ninebridge, on Concern paper. Debtors, same as us." She folds the rag. "We don't beat debtors off a platform. We feed them, if they'll sit down. If they go down Six, holding is starving, and the vote goes to Rafe." She looks at you. "Turn them, or buy their paper at the Letter's counter. Then call the vote."

Stop the car and the hill eats what it's got. Six cases says it stops tonight. The room turns its head from one to the other, and then, one by one, to you.

dawn_won.text: At dawn Corwin Dysart knocks on the Lodge door with his hat in his hand and a paper in the other. Nobody else has dug Six for eleven days and twenty men on the platform would not; the quarter's tonnage is a number with nothing in it. The Concern's terms, as written: Six East opened by the Concern's crew and the dead returned to kin; the debts of the eleven void under Clause 11; a steward with a stop. Maren reads it twice, and signs, and gives him back his pen. He takes the noon car up the hill and does not come down.

dawn_broken.text: At dawn the cage goes down with the men off the Line in it, past the picket, with the Clean either side of them, and the winding engine starts for the first time in eleven days. She goes with them without a word. In the morning she is on the post at Footgate, and the Concern's notice is nailed under her feet.

Then they cut them, a bit a week. The roof started talking on the Tuesday. Ivo said it was talking and Mr Dysart's man said get on. I was at the door. When it went I let go of the door and ran, and Yusuf didn't." He wipes his face with a black hand. "I'll say it. At the Letter's counter, if Maren wants. I'll say it."

interject.text: Tamsin crouches down to his height without being asked. "You ran," she says. "That's what the door was for. Somebody had to come out and say it." Pim looks at her as if nobody has said that to him in eleven days.

text.text: Pim on the slope by the eleven graves, with a lamp of his own on his belt now. "Steward says I can work the door again," he says. "If I want. I don't know if I want."
Pim, picking at his nails. "I said I'd say it." He doesn't say geological.

intro.text: An old man with a grey plait down his back, sitting on an oil drum beside the winding engine with his hand on its housing as if it were a horse. "Orrin. Thirty years on this winch." He pats it. "She doesn't move without me, and I don't move her without the Shift. The Clean know it. That's why they sit on the gate and not on me."
intro.again: Orrin, with his hand on the winch.

options.text: Maren says the roof talked before it went.

text.text: "Winding again." Orrin has oil to his elbows. "Where to?"
"Still here," Orrin says, "and so is she."

again.again: Orrin and the winch.

options.text: Maren says the roof talked before it went.

talk.text: "Talked all the Tuesday." He looks at the shaft. "A roof talks when you take its legs out from under it. Good ground doesn't talk; it doesn't need to. I heard it up the shaft. I rang the bell. Nobody came up." He takes his hand off the winch for the first time. "Geological, they wrote."

day.text: "Not with the Clean sitting on the gate." He nods at them. "After dark. One of them sleeps. Come back when the lamps are lit and I'll put you down like a parcel."

text.text: Grey that stays clean, a lens on the shoulder that turns to you on its own. A small green light on it. "Citizen-grade implant," the guard says, to the lens as much as to you. "You may stand here." Then, as if correcting himself: "For now."
Grey that stays clean, a carbine held across the chest, and a lens on the shoulder that has not stopped moving since the cable house went. "Back," the guard says. "Nobody comes near the station."
Grey that stays clean, a lens on the shoulder that turns to you on its own, and a face behind it that has decided not to have an expression. "Face to the lens."

face.again: The lens turns to you on its own.

hill.text: "Halcyon." As if that answered it. "Contracts and the Board's guests."

name.text: "Contract number." He tells it to you: eleven digits. Then, after a moment, as if it had got out on its own: "My mother was from Nursery."
name.again: He does not say anything else.

intro.text: Twenty men on the platform with their bags at their feet, and a big one at the front with a shaved head and salt-cracked hands. "We were bought," he says, when you come up, as if you had asked. "We work. That's what bought means. Nowak. From the Sallow."
intro.again: Nowak, and his twenty, and their bags.

interject.text: Wren looks along the twenty of them, face by face. "Ninebridge," she says. "The block." Nowak looks at her. "You know it?" "I know the counter," Wren says.

options.text: Six East came down on eleven men under robbed pillars. That's the pit you're here to dig.

mods.why: you saw the pillars yourself
the pillar log, passed down the line of them
Wren tells them what the block's counter is
eleven tags out of the fall
the boy who worked the door will tell them

decision.text: You turned the men off the Line: they sat down on the platform and would not go down Number Six.

news.text: the twenty men the Concern brought up the Line sat down on the platform at Two-Twelve and would not go down Number Six

again.again: Nowak, and the twenty.

options.text: Six East came down on eleven men under robbed pillars. That's the pit you're here to dig.

mods.why: you saw the pillars yourself
the pillar log, passed down the line of them
Wren tells them what the block's counter is
eleven tags out of the fall
the boy who worked the door will tell them

decision.text: You turned the men off the Line: they sat down on the platform and would not go down Number Six.

news.text: the twenty men the Concern brought up the Line sat down on the platform at Two-Twelve and would not go down Number Six

who.text: "The Concern, off the guild's block at Ninebridge. Twenty papers in one lot, cheap, because there was a strike on and the guild knew it." He shrugs. "We dig or we're in breach, and breach goes to the Weighhouse. That's what the paper says. None of us can read past page two."

turn.text: He hears it out. Then he passes it down the line of them, and you watch it go from man to man, and at the end of the line somebody sits down on his bag. Then the next. Nowak is the last one standing. "Eleven," he says. "Under the legs of the roof." He sits. "We dug salt in the Sallow. You don't take the legs out of a salt roof either." He looks up at you. "They'll put us in breach." "Then sit in breach," says a voice behind you, and it's Maren, with a pot of soup.
turn.again: Twenty men sitting on their bags, and Maren with a pot of soup.

interject.text: "That's the first lot off that block I ever saw sit down," Wren says. She says it to the soup, not to you, but you hear it.

no.text: "We were bought," he says again, and the twenty pick up their bags.

turned.text: Nowak at the long table in the Lodge, with Shift soup in front of him and a borrowed coat on. "In breach," he says, and almost smiles. "First time I ever sat down."

through.text: Nowak at the pithead with coal on his hands that isn't salt. "We dig," he says, and doesn't look at the picket. "That's what bought means."

text.text: The car hangs a little way up its track with its doors open and its cable lying down the station like a dead snake. The board says SERVICE SUSPENDED. Nobody has changed it, and nobody needs to.

The car at the bottom of its track, a long glass box on rails as steep as a ladder, its doors open and its crew in grey at the controls. The board: SERVICE — CONTRACTS AND THE BOARD'S GUESTS. A clerk with a list at the doors. Your name is on the list. It will be your appointment when you choose it.

The car at the bottom of its track, a long glass box on rails as steep as a ladder going up into the rock, doors shut, crew gone. SERVICE SUSPENDED — INDUSTRIAL ACTION. Through the glass, on a seat, somebody's forgotten scarf in a colour nobody in the Skirts can afford.

again.text: The car, hanging, the cable down the station.

interject.text: "The Express," Kes says. "I rode it once, up and down, at sixteen. The gardens at the top smell like rain that came out of a pipe." She stops. "Obviously I don't think about it."

text.text: Where the cable house was: a black room with no roof, two drums the size of rooms thrown off their mountings, and the smell of powder and burnt grease. Someone has put eleven lamp tags and one new one on the sill of the window that is no longer there.

The cable house behind the station: two winding drums the size of rooms, the cable going up through a slot in the roof into the rock, oil on everything. Two cots against the wall where the car's crew sleep when the car runs late. Shift people: they walked out with the pit.

look.again: The cable house.

text.text: The post at Footgate. They left her a day, for the slope to see, with the Concern's notice nailed under her feet. Now there is nothing on it but a folded rag tied to the crossbar, and under it, nailed in a row, eleven lamp tags and a twelfth, blank.

A post with a crossbar beside the gate, in sight of every door on Cascade, and a notice nailed to it in clean print: ACTION IN BREACH OF CONTRACT BY ANY PARTY ON THIS SLOPE IS SABOTAGE. SABOTAGE IS ANSWERED AT FOOTGATE. Nothing on it now. Old rope marks on the crossbar.

look.again: The post at Footgate.

interject.text: Ilya looks at the post a long time. "Right," he says, which is what he says instead of everything else.
Wren looks at the rope marks on the crossbar and then at nothing, the way she does. "They all have one," she says. "Every place that keeps a count."

cage.text: The cage at the bottom of the shaft, a bell-pull beside it. Pull once to go up. A long way above, a square of grey that is the night.

look.text: A survey board nailed to the rock in a niche off the heading: the east gallery's plan in a surveyor's neat hand, pillars numbered one to thirty, and a log of their widths, week by week. From fourteen to twenty-two the widths go down: four paces, three, two, one. Across the last column, in chalk, in a different hand: RETREAT — D.
look.again: The survey board. Widths going down. RETREAT — D.

passives.text: The widths are in the surveyor's hand, careful and regular. The chalk is not. Whoever logged the pillars was measuring them being cut, and writing it down, as if somebody would read it.

options.text: (Tear the log sheet off the board.)

taken.text: The sheet comes away with the nail through it. You fold it round the nail.

look.text: A wooden door in a timber frame across the heading, with a cord on it that runs back to a stool in a niche. Somebody sat here twelve hours a shift opening it for the carts and shutting it for the air. On the stool, a lunch tin, never opened.
look.again: The trapper's door, the stool, the lunch tin.

interject.text: "Pim's," Kes says. She picks up the lunch tin and puts it in her jacket without opening it. "His mother'll want it back. Obviously."

look.text: Pillars fourteen to twenty-two: columns of coal left standing to hold the roof, the way the ones you walked past are four paces across. These are cut back to a waist. Fresh pick marks, bright on the black. Chalk on each: a number, and RETREAT, and a long D. Above them the roof has sagged into a belly, and somewhere in it, very quietly, something ticks.
look.again: Pillars cut to a waist. RETREAT — D. The roof ticking.

passives.text: Retreat mining: you take the pillars on your way out of a worked gallery, last thing, for the coal in them, and you let the roof come down behind you. You never do it with a crew still working the face beyond. Whoever cut these knew there were people past them.

interject.text: "Somebody did that with a plan," Ilya says. He touches a pick mark with one finger. "A bit a week. Right."
Wren listens to the roof with her head on one side. "Don't talk," she says, very quietly. "It's talking."

look.text: The fall: the roof come down across the gallery from wall to wall, slabs and slack and broken props, piled to where the roof used to be. At its edge, half in the rubble, the glass of a lamp. Then another. Eleven people are on the other side of this, and none of them are waiting any more.
look.again: The fall, and the lamps at its edge.

options.text: (Dig carefully to the lamps at the edge.)

mods.why: Wren reads the roof for you
Kes holds the lamp where you need it

tags.text: An hour on your knees with the roof ticking over you. The lamps first, then the belts they hung from, and on each belt a brass tag with a number. Eleven. You leave everything else where it lies. Bringing them up is for more than one pair of hands.
tags.again: The edge of the fall, dug back.

talks.text: You get one slab off and the roof answers: a crack like a door slamming, a shower of slack down your collar. You are back at the pillars before you know you have moved. Nobody digs that alone.
talks.again: The fall. The roof still ticking.

open.text: The fall dug back to a passage the width of a man, propped with new timber. Beyond it the gallery is empty. The Shift took everything they found up the cage, and chalked on the last prop: UP.

text.text: The wall on Cascade, three deep in paper. In the middle of it, nailed through all four corners so nobody can take it down, a page of the Weighhouse book: NAME — DEBT — YIELD — SERVICE. Somebody has written beside the yield column, in big letters, what K L C H stand for.

The wall on Cascade, three deep in paper: lost, found, for sale, a room, a goat, a pair of boots in good condition. NO LAMPS DOWN in red over all of it. And one notice newer and neater than the rest, pinned at eye height by somebody who comes back every day to straighten it.

options.text: (Nail a page of the Weighhouse book to the wall beside it.)

saba.text: DAWIT MEKONNEN, MINER, NUMBER FOUR, WENT TO THE WEIGHHOUSE TO CLEAR HIS PAPER. THE WINDOW WROTE DISCHARGED IN SERVICE. HE HAS NOT WRITTEN. IF YOU HAVE SEEN HIM UP THE HILL TELL SABA, NURSERY, THE SECOND ROW. HE IS TALL AND HE HUMS.
saba.again: HE IS TALL AND HE HUMS.

rest.text: A goat, two scrip a day for its milk. A room on Nursery, no cough. CONTRACT FOR SALE, TEN YEARS LEFT, GOOD TERMS, ASK AT THE POND. A child's drawing of an orange tree. And small, in the corner, chalk: THE LEDGER CAN'T SEE US. GOOD.
rest.again: A goat, a room, a contract for sale, an orange tree.

pin.text: You nail the page up beside Saba's notice and stand back. It takes an hour. First one person stops, then four, then the whole of Cascade is reading it over each other's shoulders, and somebody who can read the letters says them out loud, and somebody else says what they stand for. By dark there are three hundred people outside the Weighhouse. By midnight there are none inside it.
pin.again: The page, nailed up beside Saba's notice.

decision.text: You nailed a page of the Weighhouse book to the wall on Cascade. The Skirts read it, and shut the Weighhouse.

news.text: the Skirts shut the Concern's Weighhouse after its book went up on the wall: the debtors it sent up the hill were weighed for parts

interject.text: "There's a weight to that," Ash says, watching them read. "Now it's everyone's."
Tamsin reads it with them and then turns round to you with a face like a slammed door. "Bits," she says. "They weigh them for bits."
"That's a block," Wren says. "With a doctor at the counter." She doesn't say anything else for an hour.

intro.text: A woman straightening a notice on the wall that does not need straightening. "Have you been up the hill?" she says, before anything else. "Dawit. He's tall. He hums when he works. He went to the Weighhouse to clear his paper and they wrote that he's in service."
intro.again: Saba, straightening her notice.

again.text: "Anything?" Saba says. She already knows the answer from your face.
again.again: Saba waits.

what.text: "His paper crossed the line after the winter. The cough took two months' tally. You go to the Weighhouse when you cross the line; they weigh you and offer you service, and service clears it all, and the family gets a settlement." She says it like a lesson. "He went on a Tuesday. On the Friday the Window gave me forty scrip and his boots, cleaned. Nobody comes back from service. Everybody says they're in the gardens." She looks at the notice. "He would have written."

boots.text: She brings them out of the shack: a miner's boots resoled twice, cleaner than any boot on the slope. "Take them," she says. "Find out. I can't look at them." Inside the left tongue there is a printed tag. You read it twice: 9-1182 — EFFECTS — RETURN TO KIN.
boots.again: The boots, and the tag in the tongue.

tell.text: You tell her as gently as it can be told, which is not very. She doesn't sit down. She straightens the notice on the wall one more time, very carefully, and then she takes it down, and folds it, and puts it in her apron. "He hummed," she says. "Nobody up there will know what he hummed."
tell.again: Saba, with the notice folded in her apron.

exposed.text: Saba on the step of her shack with Dawit's name chalked on the door. "They shut it," she says. "Three hundred people. I didn't know there were three hundred people who would." She looks up the hill. "It won't bring him down."

text.text: The Weighhouse door, kicked in and nailed shut again from the outside with planks. WEIGHED written across the planks in somebody's blood or somebody's red paint, and under it a list of names that keeps getting longer.

A sign by the Weighhouse door in clinic-white enamel: WEIGHING — VOLUNTARY. SERVICE DISCHARGES ALL PAPER IN FULL (CLAUSE 31). SETTLEMENT TO KIN. And the iron deck of the old ore scale still set in the floor inside the door, so that everyone who comes in stands on it.

intro.text: A woman in clinic white at a table by the scale deck, with a board of names and a pen she uses like a scalpel. "Sit. Breathe." Then she sees you are not from the bench. "Fittings are by appointment. Weighing is for paper that has crossed the line. Which are you?"
intro.again: Dr Lisle, with her board of names.

text.text: Dr Lisle looks up and, for the first time, puts the pen down. "You've been reading," she says.
"Sit. Breathe," Dr Lisle says, to the bench, and then, to you: "Yes?"

again.again: Dr Lisle, with her pen.

mods.why: a pair of boots with a tag in the tongue

options.text: (Put Dawit Mekonnen's boots on her table.) 9-1182.
K, L, C, H. Kidney, liver, cornea, heart. You grade them.

what.text: "When a contract's paper crosses the line, the holder is weighed: what they can still carry, what the contract can still yield." She says it the way she would say a dose. "Most go home with a schedule. Some are offered service. Service discharges the whole of the paper under Clause 31 and the family is settled. It is the only door out of the Skirts that opens." She caps the pen. "Nobody is made to walk through it."
what.again: "The only door out of the Skirts that opens."

interject.text: "Yield," Nine says. "A term of assessment." Its lens holds on her board. "I would like to see the schedule it is assessed against." Dr Lisle does not answer it.

service.text: She looks at the bench, at the queue on it, and lowers her voice. "Service is on the Clinic floors. Floor nine. They go up on the freight car at two, asleep; it is kinder. I have never been up." She says the last part as if it were a defence. "I weigh. I don't ask what the scale is for. Someone has to stand between this bench and the Clean collecting the old way, and that someone is me."
service.again: "I weigh. I don't ask what the scale is for."

service_no.text: "Service is service." She uncaps the pen. "Next."

boots.text: She looks at the tag and her face does something small and quickly put away. "Effects return to kin," she says. "That is in the contract. It is a kindness. Most contracts don't send anything back."

nils.text: "Haber. Twenty-two, a miner's lungs, no cough yet, a father's paper by transfer." She reads it off the board without needing to. "Queued. He's a good weight." She hears herself say it. "The paper decides. Not me."

yield.text: She doesn't deny it. She closes the board. "Do you know what the Clean did before the Weighhouse?" Quietly. "They collected. Paper over the line, a family on the slope, and a cart in the morning. Now there is a bench, and a settlement, and the boots come home." She looks at you steadily. "Put it on the wall, if you like. They'll stop coming. The paper will still be over the line. And the cart will come back."

options.text: What's it worth to you that nobody reads it?
I'll keep it quiet. Take one name off your board: Nils Haber.
You pay for names, don't you?

pay.text: "A hundred and fifty." Out of a drawer, in clean Halcyon notes. "For the book, and for the Skirts not to read what it wouldn't understand."

decision.text: You took a hundred and fifty from Dr Lisle to keep the Weighhouse book off the wall.

favour.text: A long silence. Then she rubs one name off the board with her thumb. "Haber walks," she says. "He was never weighed." She looks at you. "And you owe the Weighhouse a silence, and I owe you a door, when you go up. The Clinic floors know my name."

decision.text: You kept the Weighhouse quiet for Dr Lisle, in exchange for Nils Haber's name off her board.

fee.text: "A finder's fee." She doesn't blush. "A hundred, for a name that comes to the bench of its own accord. People do find each other. The Skirts is full of paper over the line."

decision.text: You took the Weighhouse's finder's fee: a name for a hundred Tolls.

fee_done.text: She writes it on the board, and pays you, and turns back to the bench. "Sit," she says to the next one. "Breathe."
fee_done.again: A new name on the board.

interject.text: Wren is gone from the door before the notes are counted. You find her later on the platform, and she does not turn round.
Tamsin looks at you as if she has never seen you before. "Bits," she says. "You sold someone for bits."
Ash says nothing. It is the loudest thing he has ever said to you.
"I sold paper on people for thirty years," Odile says. "I never once sold the person to the doctor." She buttons her coat.

covered.text: "Thank you." She means it, which is the worst part. "Sit," she says to the bench. "Breathe."

read.text: NAME — DEBT — YIELD — SERVICE. Two hundred lines in a clean hand. The yield column is four letters with a grade under each, K L C H, 1 to 3, and a dash where there is nothing to grade. MEKONNEN, D. — 212 — K2 L2 C1 H1 — CLINIC 9, R30. Under the last ruled line, in pencil, the queue: HABER, N. — 90 (TRANSFER, §9) — K1 L1 C1 H1 — QUEUED. And four more, each with a father or a mother under Six East.
read.again: NAME — DEBT — YIELD — SERVICE. K L C H.

passives.text: K, L, C, H: kidney, liver, cornea, heart. Graded the way a surgeon grades an organ for a recipient. A dash under H means the heart is no good. This is not a ledger of debts. It is a donor list.
Four letters, four grades, a dash for the unusable: an inventory, not an assessment. Of four things a body has one or two of. Kidney, liver, cornea, heart.

interject.text: Kes reads over your shoulder and stops breathing for a second. "K L C H," she says. "I thought it was a pay grade." Her hand goes to the back of her neck. "My mother was on a board like this once. I thought it was a pay grade."

intro.text: A young man on a cot in the Weighhouse ward with his boots on, as if he might be leaving. "Haber," he says. "My father's under Six East. His paper came to me; that's the contract. Ninety over the line." He tries a smile. "They say service is up in the gardens. Orange trees."
intro.again: Nils, on the cot, with his boots on.

options.text: What do you think service is?

again.text: Nils sits up on the cot. "Still here."
again.again: Nils, sitting up.

options.text: What do you think service is?
I've read the book. Service isn't the gardens.
Walk out with me. Now, while the door's asleep.

mods.why: Kes blinds the ward's lens for a minute

decision.text: You walked Nils Haber out of the Weighhouse ward at night.

service.text: "Work. Up the hill. Clean work, gardens, orange trees." He looks at his boots. "Nobody writes back. They say that's because it's good up there and they forget us." He laughs. "I wouldn't forget."

truth.text: He listens, and when you have finished he takes his boots off, very slowly, and puts them side by side under the cot as if somebody would come to collect them. Then he puts them on again. "Get me out," he says. "Please."

walked.speaker: narrator
walked.text: Past the sleeping cots, past the scale deck, past the Clean at the door who is looking at Cascade, and out into the cold. He doesn't stop until he is on Nursery among the shacks, and then he sits down in the mud and shakes.

caught.text: "Back on your cot." The Clean at the door, without looking round. Nils lies down again with his boots on.
caught.again: Nils, lying down with his boots on.

free.text: Nils Haber on Nursery, splitting kindling for somebody else's stove. "Joran's boy," people call him. "My paper's nothing," he says. "First time in my life." He doesn't know what to do with his hands.

day.text: A gate in the fence at the top of the freight lane, and a board on it: FREIGHT — 02:00 — CONCERN CREW. The Concern runs its own freight on its own crew, strike or no strike. Crates on the dock behind the station, stencilled MEDICAL — COLD.

two.text: Two in the morning. The freight car comes down its track with no lamps lit and stops at the dock. Out of the Weighhouse's back door and up the lane come two of the Clean with a stretcher between them, and on it someone asleep under a white sheet with a tag on their wrist. Then another. They go into the freight car with the cold crates. A bag comes down off the car the other way and is put inside the Weighhouse's back door: a coat, a pair of boots.
two.again: The freight at two: stretchers up, a bag of effects down.

interject.text: "I have watched the Precinct's carts take people who would not be counted," Nine says, very low. "They did not send the boots back." It does not say which is worse.

intro.text: A shack with a surgeon's table in it, a good one, with a lamp on an arm and a tray of tools that are clean. The man at it is big and bearded and grey, and his hands are the steadiest thing on Nursery. "Lev. Dark work: no channel, no warranty, no Window." He looks at the back of your neck before he looks at your face. "What are you carrying?"
intro.again: Lev at his table.

again.text: "Sit still or I charge double," Lev says. "What?"
again.again: Lev waits.

options.text: What does "yield" mean, on the Weighhouse's board?
Can you take a Concern port out of somebody's neck without killing them?

who.text: "Nine years an orderly on the Clinic floors. Carrying holdfast, mopping, holding things still." He turns a clamp over. "I left the week I understood what I was holding still. Now I fit what people can bear and drink less than I did." He looks up. "Most weeks."

yield.text: He doesn't need to look at the book. "K, L, C, H. Kidney, liver, cornea, heart, graded one to three for match and wear." He sets the clamp down. "Nobody up there needs a whole Skirts body. They need it in pieces, and fresh, and the pieces go to the people who can pay to stay the age they are." He wipes his hands although they are clean. "I don't know whose. I carried holdfast. I didn't read the charts."
yield.again: "Nobody up there needs a whole Skirts body."

interject.text: Ash puts a hand flat on the shack wall as if the floor had moved. "They take the dead for the sky at Openfield," he says. "This is the other thing."

kes.text: Lev looks at Kes the way he looked at the back of your neck. "Lattice port. Window issue." He touches the cable at her nape with one finger and she doesn't flinch, which costs her. "It's in the top of the spine. Cut a live channel and it takes the person with it: that's the Scald's lesson, and the Pale's, and anyone who's held a hand while it went." He sets out the tray. "Somebody holds the channel quiet while I cut. If they hold it, she walks out blind on the grid and free. If they don't, she walks out and has fits. I don't lose people on this table."
kes.again: Lev, with the tray set out.

mods.why: Ash's word: burn the channel first, then cut
holdfast in the pack

decision.text: Lev Ostrander cut the Concern's port out of Kes's neck at his table, with you holding the channel. She walked out free.
Lev Ostrander cut the Concern's port out of Kes's neck. The channel slipped in your hands; she lives, and has fits now.

cut.text: An hour. Her hand on your wrist the whole time, hard enough to bruise. Then a small wet sound and Lev drops something the size of a coin into a dish, with a tail of fine wire. Kes sits up. She puts her hand to the back of her neck, where there is a dressing now and nothing else. "It's quiet," she says, astonished. "It's so quiet."
cut.again: The dish, and the coin in it with its wire tail.

fits.text: Halfway through, the channel jumps under your hands and her whole body goes rigid on the table, and Lev says something you don't catch and keeps cutting. The port comes out. Kes lives. That night at the fire she has her first fit, and you hold her head off the ground until it passes. "Worth it," she says after, with her teeth still chattering. "Obviously. Ask me again tomorrow."
fits.again: The dish, and her hand shaking.

intro.text: A woman on the platform beside the changer's booth with two children asleep on the bags and a tea tin held in both hands. "Two years," she says, not to you exactly. "A hundred scrip. The Line to Meridian is twenty-five a head, Tolls, and there are three of us." She opens the tin to show you: tens, tied with string. "He changes at six. That's sixteen." She closes it. "Meridian has schools. That's all I know about Meridian."
intro.again: Ama, the tin, the children asleep on the bags.

interject.text: "Six to one," Odile says, mostly to herself. She is looking at the booth's board the way she looks at a sheet. "My dear, I priced that spread on a slate at Ninebridge in the year the bridge had eight spans."

options.text: Let me see what the changer can do.

decision.text: You paid the difference on Ama Owusu's fares yourself. Her family went down the Line.

Through it they can see you, wherever you are. Numb you. Switch you off. Ask Baek about his arm." She touches the back of her neck. "I found it in mine when I was nineteen. And I turned it round. For an hour a night it looks the other way, and nobody on the hill can see me." She shrugs, too hard. "That's when the Shift meets. That's why the lenses go blind at the Lodge. That's me."

"There's nothing there now," she says, "and I still feel it twice. Once in the skin, once where their log was." She turns round. "I don't have to steal an hour any more. I'd still like to spend one with you. Say if you don't want to."

She pulls her collar down. The port at the top of her spine, a ring of dull metal with the cable seated in it, and the skin round it pale and too smooth. "Touch it," she says. "Go on." You do. She shivers. "I feel that twice. Once in the skin and once in their log. Somewhere up the hill it says where your hand is." She touches her own neck and the night goes a degree quieter. "There. Now it doesn't. That's my hour." She turns round. "I'd like to spend it with you. Say if you don't want to."

r2.again: Kes, with her collar down, waiting for an answer.

decision.text: You spent Kes's dark hour with her.

options.text: Not tonight. I'll sit the hour with you, though.

r2b.text: "Dark hour." She doesn't say anything else. She doesn't have to.

decision.text: You spent Kes's dark hour with her.

r2_fade.text: She kisses you like she does everything, fast and showing off, and then not fast at all and not showing off. For an hour nobody on the hill knows where she is, and for an hour she doesn't care where the hill is either. Afterwards she lies with her head on your chest and says, "Obviously that was better than I said it would be," and is asleep before you can answer.
r2_fade.again: Kes, asleep with her head on your chest.

r2_sit.text: "Fine." She leans on your shoulder for the hour instead, and tells you about the orange tree again, and when the hour is up she sits up and says, "Thanks," and means more than the word holds.
r2_sit.again: Kes, leaning on your shoulder for the hour.

r2_no.text: "Okay." She pulls her collar up. "Okay. Clear." She doesn't make it strange, which you can see costs her something.

r3.text: "I don't do slow." She is very serious for once, which looks wrong on her. "So: are we a thing? A real one, out loud, where I tell Rosa and she pours me a free one and pretends she isn't pleased." She waits. "You can say no. I'll still be insufferable."

decision.text: You told Kes you were a thing, out loud.

options.text: We're a thing. Wherever this road goes.

decision.text: You told Kes you were a thing, wherever the road goes.

options.text: I don't think I can be that.

r3_yes.text: "Good." She says it to the fire, then to you, then to the fire again, grinning. "Good. Obviously. I knew." She didn't, and you both know it.

r3_no.text: "Fair." She doesn't look away, which is brave of her. "Then it was good. It was really good." She moves her bedroll a little. Not far.

c_rom_end.text: "I'm sleeping over there." Her bedroll already is. "You know why. I watch everything, and lately I don't like what I'm watching." She doesn't raise her voice. "I'll walk with you. I won't lie down next to it."

decision.text: Kes ended it, at a fire. She watches everything.

x_nine.text: Kes has two fingers on the camp lantern's little lens, and the lens has gone politely blind. Nine's own lens has not left her. "I saw that," Nine says. "The record did not." A pause. "I find the difference restful." Kes looks at it. "Are you going to write me down?" "It is my function," Nine says. "It is also clause forty that I may not read a forecast. You are not in one. I looked."
x_nine.again: Nine, and Kes, and the lantern's blind lens.

options.text: Write it down, Nine. The record should know there's a door.
The record can't see her for a reason. Leave her out of it.

x_nine_report.text: "Noted," Nine says, and something behind its lens moves. Kes stands up. "That's once," she says, very quietly, to you. "Hand that door to anyone else and I'm gone." She goes to sit on the far side of the fire.
x_nine_report.again: Kes, on the far side of the fire.

x_nine_blind.text: Nine considers this for long enough that the fire needs feeding. "I will log it," it says, "as the Plan's largest error: a place it cannot see, and a person in it who walks out." Its lens dims, which is the nearest it comes to a smile. "Not her name." Kes grins at it. "Obviously," she says, and passes it the soup.
x_nine_blind.again: Nine and Kes, sharing the soup.

x_nine_leave.text: They leave it. Nine watches the lantern all night. Kes, for once, lets it.

x_odile.text: Odile reads with her glasses on their chain. Kes has been watching her for an hour. "You priced the spread," Kes says at last. "Six to one. Somebody had to." Odile takes the glasses off. "My dear," she says, "I priced the weather. Somebody else made it rain." "On the Skirts," says Kes. "On whoever stood under it," says Odile. "I never once went to see who that was."
x_odile.again: Odile with the glasses in her hand. Kes, watching.

options.text: She's right, Odile. You priced people.
She left the floor, Kes. She's unwinding it.
Odile. What would you price it at now?

x_odile_kes.text: "I did." Odile puts the glasses back on. "That is a cost." She does not read the page in front of her again tonight. Kes looks almost sorry, and is not.

x_odile_odile.text: "Unwinding." Kes tries the word like a cable she doesn't trust. "Unwind faster." She goes back to her box. Odile reads, and smiles very slightly.
x_odile_odile.again: Kes and her box. Odile, reading.

x_odile_both.text: Odile thinks about it properly, which Kes did not expect. "At par," she says, "and see who complains. Whoever complains is the one who was being paid." Kes stares at her. Then she laughs out loud. "Obviously," she says. "Obviously. Why didn't anyone—" "Because the ones who complain own the slate, my dear."
x_odile_both.again: Kes, still laughing at the slate.

x_ash.text: Ash is looking at the cable in her neck the way he looks at a wound. "I had one," he says. "A link. Under the jaw. Dog work, before the Choir." He touches the scar there. "I cut it out myself with a hot knife. You burn the channel first, with a cell across the pins, so it's dead when you cut it. Then it can't take you with it." Kes stares at him. "And you lived." "I lived," Ash says. "The man next to me didn't burn his first."
x_ash.again: Ash, with his hand on the scar under his jaw.

x_ash_kes.text: "A man who cut his link and thinks everyone can," Kes says, but there is no edge in it. "Burn it first." She looks at Ash. "Thanks." Ash nods, once, as if a debt had been paid somewhere.

t_gardens.text: "I saw them once. Sixteen, at my fitting." She doesn't need asking twice. "Glass over everything, and under it trees, real ones, in rows, with fruit on, and grass you could walk on in your boots. Rain came out of pipes in the ceiling at ten and at four, and it smelled of nothing. Nothing at all. And an orange tree, by itself, in a pot, with a bench, and an old man on the bench who didn't look old." She stops. "You let me go on."
t_gardens.again: "An orange tree, by itself, in a pot."

t_gardens2.text: She goes on for an hour: the paths, the glass, the man who swept the leaves before they fell. At the end she looks at you, startled. "Nobody ever lets me finish," she says. "Obviously I'm going to do that again now."
t_gardens2.again: Kes, startled that she was allowed to finish.

t_gardens3.text: "Obviously." She doesn't sound sure. She looks up the hill anyway.

t_mother.text: "My mother." The word costs her something. "She signed me to the Window at sixteen against the family's paper. It cleared my brothers. She died of the cough two years after." She winds the cable tight. "She did the sum. I'd have done the same sum." She stops winding. "Don't say anything. I mean it."
t_mother.again: Kes, with the cable wound tight round her hand.

t_chrome.text: "You're wearing theirs." She says it like a weather report. "Now they can see you too. Wherever you are." She looks at the back of your neck a moment longer. "Obviously it was your choice. I just wanted you to know I know."

t_fridge.text: "So it's a fridge," Kes says. "That says no." "Three times," says Tamsin. "To the city." "I love it," Kes says. "I want to meet it. I want to meet the Fridge." Tamsin is laughing too hard to answer. It is the most either of them has laughed since they met, and neither of them is sure why it's funny.
t_fridge.again: Kes and Tamsin, laughing about the Fridge.

t_wren.text: "Two people who got found by the wrong side." Kes says it quietly, because Wren is right there, and Wren hears it anyway and doesn't argue. "She got the Dogs. I got the Window." She looks at Wren's goggles. "She keeps hers on for the same reason I keep my cable in. So nobody reads the face."
t_wren.again: Kes and Wren, not quite looking at each other.

t_ilya.text: "Old." Kes grins. "Good eyes, though. He can see a lens at four hundred paces and tell you which way it's facing." She considers him across the fire. "He counts things under his breath. I count things in my neck. We'd get on, if he talked."

text.text: "Somebody told the Tonnage where the committee sat." Kes is already standing, already packed; she was always packed. "I keep the lenses on Cascade. I watched you walk down to the pit office." She doesn't raise her voice. "Maren took me in when I was eighteen. Don't come after me."
"You sold the Scales a name." Kes is already standing, already packed. "I keep her board. I watched it go up with your thumb on it." Her voice doesn't shake. "Don't come after me."

decision.text: Kes left you for what you sold in the Skirts.

c_sold.text: "You sold the door." Kes doesn't sit. Her hand is on the back of her neck. "The Letter's put a watch on every port in the Skirts since yesterday. Baek's arm went dead in the Pond. Mine goes dark and comes back with someone else's hand on it." She is very calm. "I told you it was a timetable. I'm gone."

decision.text: Kes left you for selling the door in the Concern's chrome to the Contract Office.

c_handed.text: "You told Rafe." Kes doesn't sit. "About the door. He came to me with your words in his mouth and asked me to switch off every piece on the slope." She is very calm. "Baek's arm. Mercy's eyes. Half the Shift's spines. I told you it was a timetable. I'm gone."

decision.text: Kes left you for handing the door in the Concern's chrome to Rafe Ansel.

c_floor.text: "I'm done." Kes has the box in her jacket and the cable coiled. "I watch everything. I've watched enough." She doesn't list it; she doesn't need to. "Don't come after me. I'll see you on every board on the slope before you see me."

decision.text: Kes left your fire. She watches everything, and she had watched enough.

text.text: Kes, with the cable in her neck and the box on her knee. She doesn't look up. "I said I'd see you first," she says. She did.
Kes, with a dressing on the back of her neck where the port was. Somebody cut it out of her in a hurry. She doesn't look up, and she doesn't speak.
Kes, with the box on her knee. She doesn't look up.

decision.text: You told Kes the truth, undressed, and she came back. Once, she said.

left_back.text: "That's the first true thing in a while." She stands, and puts the box in her jacket. "Once. I do this once. Obviously."

left_no.text: "No." She plugs the cable back in. "Go on."

gossip.text: "Nobody." She says it the way everyone on the Line says it. "Ask the factor, he's paying for an answer. Two hundred." She lowers her voice. "They never touch the coach. I've sold a ticket to every passenger on every train they stopped, and every one of them got off with their purse."

card.speaker: npc_rc_06
card.text: "So the card can't be sold on." She blows on your likeness to dry it. "And because the guild sends the faces south with the takings. Everyone's face goes somewhere." She does not say where, and you do not think she knows.

text.text: You wait on the platform for the seven o'clock. It comes in under its own smoke: Sixty, square-nosed and plated, pulling a pre-war coach with steel riveted over its windows to the height of a seated man, so that you look out over a rim of plate at the country going by. The guard punches your card and sits down opposite with a carbine across his knees. For the first hour you watch the land go past at the speed of a fast cart the way you would watch someone sleeping. At Kettle Cut the train slows for the curve, and in the ditch under the window two cars lie on their sides, opened like tins. The guard watches them go by and says nothing at all. Then, somewhere, you sleep too, and wake to Meridian Docks.

The seven o'clock, and at every halt the train stops for a pilot in faded orange who climbs into the cab with a red flag rolled under his arm, rides the section and gets down at the next, while the halt sells water on the platform and somebody sells bread through the coach's slots. At Kettle Cut the train slows for the curve, and in the ditch under the window two cars lie on their sides, opened like tins. The guard watches them go by and says nothing at all. Meridian Docks.

The seven o'clock: the coach, the plate at the windows, the guard and his carbine, the country going by at the speed of a cart. At Kettle Cut the train slows for the curve, and in the ditch under the window two cars lie on their sides, opened like tins. The guard watches them go by and says nothing at all. Meridian Docks.

interject.text: Tamsin has her face to the slot over the plate the whole way. "It's moving and nobody's pushing it," she says, three times, and then, without looking round: "Don't tell anyone I said that."
"Two cars, one key," Wren says, watching the ditch go by. "Somebody knew which ones. That's not robbing. That's shopping."
"The token for each section is drawn at its end and surrendered at the next," Nine says, watching the signals. "A system with no memory but the register. I admire it."

She looks at your face the way a clerk looks at a form, and draws it on a card in four quick lines: the guild puts a likeness on every card. "Seven o'clock both ways. Twenty-five a leg. The guild sets it, not me."
She looks at your pass, and at you, and punches nothing. "All sections. The seven o'clock, either way."
"Thirty a leg." She taps a new card pinned beside the grille: KETTLE LEVY — BY ORDER OF THE GUILD. "Don't look at me. Look at Kettle."

text.text: The main line bends out of the yard here, and anything on it slows for the bend whether it means to stop or not. The through comes round at two, walking pace, for half a minute. Ferris was right: you could step onto it.

look.again: The bend, and the flat stone.

night.text: Two in the morning, and down the line the through's lamp, coming slow round the bend: nineteen sealed cars with the closed eye on their doors, a ladder at every car's end, and the guard's lamp on the last.
night.again: The through, coming round the bend.

options.text: (Step off the stone onto a ladder as it passes.)

rods.speaker: narrator

interject.text: Wren lands on the roof beside you without a sound and lies there grinning at the stars. "Kessler would have charged for that," she says.

options.text: (Drop off at Kettle, where she slows for the curve.)
(Ride her all the way to the city.)

caught.speaker: narrator
caught.text: A lamp in your face and a carbine under it: the through's guard, hanging off the last car's step. "Twenty," he says, "or you walk from Kettle." The train does not slow down to discuss it.

options.text: (Let him put you off at Kettle.)

look.speaker: narrator
look.text: A handcar on the spur: a flat bed on four wheels, a see-saw pump handle, a lamp with a green hood, and WEST HALT — PERMANENT WAY stencilled on the side. The rails under it are bright.
look.again: The handcar, its green lamp.

passives.text: The flanges are bright with use and the axle greased this week. Somebody runs this a long way, often, at night.

options.text: (Ask Eamon to run you up the line.)

no.text: "Not for hire." Eamon does not look up from the axle. "Permanent way. It runs when the length needs it."

ride.text: "Where to?" Eamon has the lamp lit already. "Not Four Ways. Out of timetable's out of law on his track, and his watch shoots. Anywhere this side of it."

stop.text: Where the way runs down into a cutting beside the Line, a sleeper has been dragged across the rails and a lamp hooded green on the bank. A woman with a rifle steps out of the dark with her scarf down round her neck, as if she wants you to see her face. Behind her, three more in faded rail-crew orange; one is a boy who will not look at you. "Line's closed for an hour," she says. "Sit on the bank and keep your hands where I like them, and nobody gets hurt. We're not here for you."
stop.again: "Sit on the bank. Nobody gets hurt."

passives.text: Their boots are Line issue, hobnailed and resoled; their orange is a halt's work wear, not a raider's paint. And the ballast round your feet has been swept: they picked up their brass from last time.

interject.text: "Not raiders," Wren says under her breath, sitting down on the bank as if she does this every night. "Raiders don't sweep the brass."

decision.text: You opened fire on West Halt's watch on the road. Chela Ortega and Abe Mutasa did not go home. The guild owes you its bounty.

news.text: the band that stopped trains at Kettle was shot to pieces on the Line; it was West Halt's own watch

options.text: (Back away up the road and go round.)

who.text: "Nobody." She almost smiles. "The Line's weather. Tonight it's raining."

what.text: "Freight." She nods down the cut, where a lamp is coming. "Not yours. Never yours. The coach doesn't get touched and nobody's purse gets opened. That's the rule." The boy behind her says something you don't catch, and she says, without turning round, "That's the rule, Abe."

watch.speaker: narrator
watch.text: The freight comes up the grade at a walk: the lamp, the engine, a string of sealed cars with the closed eye on their doors. It stops at the sleeper with its brakes screaming. Nobody fires. The woman walks down the train with a key on a cord round her neck and opens one car, only one, and they carry crates out of it to a handcar on the other track in the time it takes to drink a cup of water. A guard sits on the last car's roof with his carbine across his knees and does not lift it. Then the sleeper is off the rails, the train goes on, and so do they, west, pumping, the green lamp going away into the dark.
watch.again: The green lamp going away west.

gang.text: Two people in faded orange with a rail on their shoulders and another in the grass, re-laying a length where the old one has cracked clean through. "Give us a shoulder," says the older one, "or give us the road."

lifted.text: It goes in on the third heave, and they key it while you hold it, and then the three of you sit in the grass and share their water. "Halt's length," the older one says. "Forty mile of it, and the guild pays us for a train that stops. Count the trains that stop."

dropped.text: You get your end to your knees and no further, and the rail goes back into the grass with a sound like a church bell. "Never mind," the younger one says. "It's been in the grass a month. It'll wait."
dropped.again: The rail, back in the grass.

pay.text: "Length money." The older one spits. "The guild pays a halt for keeping its length, per train that stops there. Then the guild and the Concern agree the freight runs through. Doesn't stop. Doesn't pay." He hefts the rail. "We keep it anyway. A length's not a thing you stop keeping."

again.text: The track gang again, further down the line, with the same rail on the same shoulders.
again.again: The track gang.

ankle.text: A young woman sitting in the grass beside the rails with one boot off and her ankle the wrong shape. "Fell off at the bend," she says. "Never fall off at the bend." She looks at your boots, then your pack. "Got anything straight?"
ankle.again: Dulcie, and the ankle the wrong shape.

splinted.text: She swears through it and then laughs. "Right. One for one." She draws in the dirt with a finger: a curve of track, a stone. "The through slows on the bend out of Yard Nine. Two in the morning, walking pace, half a minute. Ladder at every car's end. Step on, lie flat, get off where she slows again: Kettle, or the yard throat at the city." She looks up. "And don't fall off at the bend."
splinted.again: The curve drawn in the dirt.

botched.text: It goes back with a sound neither of you likes, and she passes out, and wakes, and says she has had worse. She hasn't. You leave her what you can and she waves you on, white to the lips.

water.text: "Ta." She drinks half and saves half. "Somebody'll be along. Somebody's always along, on the Line."

intro.text: A big grey man at a desk with a watch lying open on it beside the wire, who looks at the clock through his window before he looks at you. "Brodsky. Stationmaster." He makes a note. "You came in on foot, which is to say on no timetable at all. That is allowed. Walking is not a timetable offence."
intro.again: Brodsky, checking his watch against the clock.

text.text: "The instrument has failed." He says it with perfect gravity, and checks his watch. "Every section by pilot. The timetable has stopped them for me." He nearly smiles. "On time."
"The guild stops at the halts again, and pays." He checks his watch. "Kask bought me a drink at Batista's. I did not enjoy it. On time."
He looks at the clock, and at you, and says nothing about Kettle, which is what you were paid for. "On time."
He looks at the clock and not at you. "The guild has its riders on my Line. The halts have nothing." A note in the book. "On time, regardless."
"On time." He looks up. "What is it?"

again.again: Brodsky, checking his watch against the clock.

options.text: West Halt's watch rides your release to Kettle.

law.text: "Four rules." He counts them on a hand that has lost the top of one finger. "On the track out of timetable, the watch shoots. Theft from the Line, you are put off at the next halt in what you stand in. Murder, the rope. And the clock is right." He lets that sit. "Two hangings in nine years, and every halt from here to the sea eats. Find me a town with a better sum."

interject.text: "Four clauses and a clock," Nine says, after a moment. "The charter has eleven thousand. I am not certain it has a better sum." Brodsky looks at it for the first time with something like interest.

kettle.text: "Kettle is the guild's problem." He does not look up. "My timetable runs to Kettle and from Kettle. What happens between is weather."

passives.label: The cutting
passives.text: "Weather." The woman with the rifle in the cutting called herself that, in the same voice, as if it were a word they had agreed on.

halts.text: "Through-running." He says it the way other people say a disease. "The guild and the Concern agreed it. The Concern's freight runs on green, Two-Twelve to the city, stopping nowhere. The guild pays a halt length money for every train that stops. Do the sum." He goes back to the wire. "West Halt was forty families. It is nineteen."

confront.text: "Sit down." He closes the watch and puts it in his waistcoat, which is the first time you have seen him not looking at it. "Yes. West Halt's watch, on my release. I was born at West Halt. My mother kept its length forty years, and the guild paid her by the train." He nods at the wire. "Then Kask signed his sheet with the Concern: the through runs on green past every halt, and length money is paid per stop. No stop, no money. A halt that cannot keep its length loses the length, and a Line that loses its lengths stops being a Line. So on the nights a sealed car is worth it, I release the section to the permanent way, and what the permanent way does in the dark is the halts' business. The Concern's freight feeds the people the Concern's freight starves." A pause, exactly as long as he means it to be. "Nobody was hurt. That was the rule."
confront.again: "Nobody was hurt. That was the rule."

interject.text: "Per stop made," Odile says quietly. "I know that clause. I wrote the first one of those for a ferry company thirty years ago. It is the cheapest way there is to starve someone politely."
Wren has gone very still. "You rob the people who rob you, and give it to the people they rob," she says. "Kessler would have liked you. Then he'd have taken a cut."

gorse.text: "Yes. Hamish Gorse." He takes the watch out again and does not open it. "A guard on the last car, with a rifle and a family at Yard Nine. The car they stopped that night was not freight. The guild had put people in it: a stock car of debtors off the Ninebridge block, bound for the Concern. One of them was Chela Ortega's brother, sold for West Halt's water tower. Chela stopped the car for him. Gorse fired on them. Somebody fired back." He closes his hand on the watch. "On my release. My rule broken, in my section."

interject.text: Ash says nothing for a long time. Then: "Who fired back?" Brodsky looks at him and does not answer, which is an answer.

choose.text: "Now?" He looks at the clock. "Now you know, and the guild does not. That is a thing with a price, and I am a man who pays prices. Say what you want."

options.text: Stop the hold-ups. I'll get the guild to pay the halts again.
There's another way. Let the instrument fail.
The guild will hear this from me.

deal_open.text: "If you can get Severin Kask to pay a halt for a train that does not stop," he says, "I will stand the watch down myself and buy you a drink at Batista's, and you can ride my Line for nothing for the rest of your life. He will not." He goes back to the wire. "But try. I would like to see his face."
deal_open.again: "I would like to see his face."

pilot.text: For a moment he looks almost happy. "Rule one hundred and eighty-three." He says it like a prayer he had stopped saying. "If the instrument failed, every train would have to stop at every halt for a pilot, and the guild would have to pay him. And nobody could blame the halts, or me. Only the instrument." Then the look goes. "It has never failed. Halina would know if it had not failed by itself. Ask her, not me. I have not had this conversation."

price.text: "A hundred and twenty, and a pass on every section." He has it in the drawer; he has had it in the drawer for some time. "The guild will lose freight and put a levy on the fares to make it up, and the halts will eat. That is the sum."
price.again: "A hundred and twenty, and a pass."

decision.text: You took the stationmaster's hundred and twenty and a pass, and said nothing about Kettle. The hold-ups go on; the guild has put a levy on every fare.

news.text: the guild has put a Kettle levy on every fare on the Line; the hold-ups go on

paid.text: He counts it out in guild notes and writes the pass himself: your description, not your name, the way the guild does. "On time," he says, and that is the end of it.

tell.text: "Then tell him." He picks up the pen. "The guild will hang whoever fired, put the watch off the Line, and the halts will empty. The timetable will regret it. So will I." He writes the time in the book. "Close the door on your way out. It sticks."

text.text: There is a paper on his desk in his own hand, and he turns it round so that you can read it. ABE MUTASA, OF WEST HALT. HAMISH GORSE, GUARD, AT KETTLE. MURDER. "You were paid not to know about Kettle," he says. "You were not paid not to know about this. There is a dead man on my Line, and I have four rules, and one of them is the rope. My watch has fetched him from West Halt. Dawn, at the platform's end." He looks at the clock. "The timetable regrets it."

There is a paper on his desk in his own hand, and he turns it round so that you can read it. ABE MUTASA, OF WEST HALT. HAMISH GORSE, GUARD, AT KETTLE. MURDER. "The hold-ups are over," he says. "There is still a dead man on my Line, and I have four rules, and one of them is the rope. My watch has fetched him from West Halt. Dawn, at the platform's end." He looks at the clock. intro.text: A man in a guild coat that has been to a good tailor and come back, at a desk with nothing on it but a pen and a cup. "Kask. Factor for the Line." He gives you his whole attention, which is a thing guild men are taught to do. "You have the look of somebody who has come about the reward. Most people in Four Ways have the look of somebody who has not."
intro.again: Kask, his whole attention on you.

options.text: The reward. Tell me about Kettle.

text.text: "The guild pays its debts." He nods to you as to a colleague. "Anything else?"
"I am paying halts for trains." He says it without inflection, as if it were weather. "I am told it is the price of having a Line. Anything else?"
"The instrument at Four Ways has failed," he says, "the week after you arrived. The guild is paying pilots." He looks at you for a long moment. "I do not suppose you know anything about instruments."
"Factor for the Line." Kask waits.

again.again: Kask, waiting.

options.text: The reward. Tell me about Kettle.
The band at Kettle is West Halt's own watch, on the stationmaster's release.
Pay the halts for the trains that don't stop, and Kettle goes quiet.
Kettle is done. West Halt's watch is broken.
The one who shot Gorse is in Four Ways' watch house: Abe Mutasa, of West Halt.

decision.text: You gave Abe Mutasa to the guild for a hundred Tolls. The guild hanged him at Kettle for Hamish Gorse.

reward.text: "A band has been stopping freight at Kettle Cut since the spring. Five times. They lay a sleeper on the rails, open one sealed car, take what is in it, and leave." He turns the pen over. "They have never touched the coach. They have never opened the wrong car. Every car they took was the Concern's, and the Concern's manifests come up from Two-Twelve by wire to the box at the end of this platform and go nowhere else." He lets you do that sum. "Then a fortnight ago they shot Hamish Gorse off the last car. Two hundred, and a pass on every section, for the band."

through.text: "Progress." He means it. "The Concern's freight runs on green from Two-Twelve to the city, stopping nowhere, with first call on every path. It arrives a day sooner, the Concern pays the guild for the day, and the Line has a customer who pays on time." He folds his hands. "The halts complain. Halts always complain."

interject.text: "Severin," Odile says, in the voice of an old friend at a funeral, "you were my clerk once. You priced fish." Kask looks at her for a long moment and says, "Madame Marchetti. You taught me to."

bounty.text: "Good." He writes your description in a book, not your name. "They ride when there is a car worth riding for. The through on its next night carries a car of Concern controllers, and someone on the Line knows it, because someone on the Line knows everything. Kettle, between midnight and four." He closes the book. "Bring me the band, or proof of it. The guild does not mind which."

proof.text: "Proof?" He does not sound surprised, which is the most surprising thing he has said.

"Lawful," Nine says on the platform, and then, after a long time: "I have filed a great many lawful things."

deal_ok.text: He is quiet for a long time. Then he takes a sheet of guild paper and writes on it, and signs it, and blots it. "Length money per train passing, not per stop. Request stops at both halts, and the through to stop when flagged." He hands it to you to carry down the platform. "The Concern will be displeased. The Concern is displeased by most things it does not own." Brodsky reads it in his office, twice, and checks his watch, and goes out to the platform without his coat. That night West Halt's handcar does not go out, and in the morning there is a pass on your seat at Batista's in the stationmaster's hand.

interject.text: "Per train passing," Odile says, reading it over your shoulder. "My dear. You have just rewritten a guild contract with a speech and a cup of tea. I never managed it in thirty years with a pen."

deal_no.text: "No." He says it pleasantly. "The guild does not pay for nothing; that is the whole of the guild." He looks at you a little longer than before. "And I think somebody on this platform has been telling you things."

claimed.text: He counts out two hundred and writes a pass without looking up. "The guild pays its debts." A pause. "West Halt's keeper came to ask where her niece was. I told her Kettle. It seemed the least I could do."

abe.text: A hundred, counted, and two riders sent across the platform before you have put it away. "The guild thanks you," Kask says. By the evening the boy has been taken to Kettle on the guild's handcar, and by the morning there is a rope on the signal post there.

intro.text: A small woman with white hair tied back hard, writing in a ledger by a lamp among brass instruments and levers worn bright, who finishes her line before she looks up. "Wrona. Signals." She puts the pen down exactly parallel to the page. "If you have come to move a lever, don't."
intro.again: Halina Wrona, finishing her line.

text.text: A red card hangs on the instrument: SECTION WORKED BY PILOT — RULE 183. Halina is writing. "Pilot for the down seven o'clock, West Halt, Eamon Fahy," she reads aloud as she writes it. "Paid."
Halina writes the time, and looks up.

work.text: "Each section of the Line is single track between two ends, and only one train may be on it. To enter, a driver must hold the section's token." She lifts a brass disc on a hoop from a slot. "The instruments at both ends are wired here. I release a token; it comes out at the end; the train carries it through and surrenders it at the far end; nothing else may enter until it is back. Token out. Token in." She puts it back. "And everything that is released, I write in the register. The register does not lie, so I do not write lies in it."

interject.text: "Absolute block," Nine says, with something close to reverence. "A system that does not trust anyone, and is therefore safe for everyone." Halina looks at it over her glasses. "Yes," she says. "Exactly that."

read.text: "The register is the Line's." She turns it round on the desk to face you. "Anyone may read it who can read."
read.again: "Anyone may read it."

fails.text: She takes a tin down from the shelf over the instruments and opens it: pages cut from a rule book older than the guild. "Rule one hundred and eighty-three. When an instrument fails, the section is worked by pilot. No train enters without a pilotman aboard, found at the section's end and paid by the operator for each passage." She closes the tin. "Every train would stop at every halt to take one up. In forty years my instruments have never failed."

copy.text: She writes it out at once, without being asked twice, in a square hand: every line for the West Halt section on five nights, and the release beside each. She blots it and gives it to you. "I write what happens," she says. "What people do with it is theirs."

agrees.text: She looks at the register a long time, and at the instruments, and then at you. "If it fails," she says, "it fails. I will write that it failed, and it will be true." She takes her coat from its peg. "After eleven. Come up the stair. Don't touch anything I haven't told you to touch."

refuses.text: "No." Not angrily. "Forty years. They have never failed. I will not be the one who makes them liars." She picks up the pen. "Find a reason that is true, and come back."

spare.text: She is quiet. Then she goes to the cupboard under the instruments and comes back with something wrapped in oilcloth: a board, green, older than the Burn, with no mark on it but the maker's. "My last spare," she says. "If one of mine goes now, it stays gone." She puts it in your hands. "An engine should be its own. Go on."

spare_no.text: "That is the last one." She shakes her head. "If an instrument goes and I have no spare, the Line stops. I am sorry for the engine."

page.text: The Line's register, a column for every section, every token out and in, every train, every release, in one square hand. On the nights the guild's poster names, and on one more, the same line in the West Halt section: SECTION RELEASED. OCCUPATION — PERMANENT WAY. 01:40. C.B. Then: TOKEN IN, 05:10. Then the through, at two, as on every other night, with nothing written beside it at all.

The station clock: a white face the size of a cartwheel, black hands, and under the twelve a little window with a number in it: 30. Nobody in Four Ways can tell you what it counts. It goes up by one every spring, by itself, on a day nobody here has ever chosen. Everyone sets their watch by it.

The reward is gone. Its four corners are still under the tacks.

THE LINE — REWARD — TWO HUNDRED TOLLS AND A PASS ON ALL SECTIONS — FOR THE BAND THAT STOPS FREIGHT AT KETTLE CUT. HAMISH GORSE, GUARD OF THE GUILD, KILLED THERE IN THE DISCHARGE OF HIS DUTY. APPLY TO THE FACTOR.

text.text: THE TIMETABLE IS THE LAW OF FOUR WAYS. 1. On the track out of timetable: the watch shoots. 2. Theft from the Line: put off at the next halt. 3. Murder: the rope. 4. The clock is right. And under the third rule, newer, in the stationmaster's hand: UNLESS FIRED UPON FIRST — PUT OFF.

text.text: The guard nods to you, which guild guards do not do. "Gorse was a friend," he says. "Thanks."
"Ticket's at the window." The guard looks past you down the line, toward Kettle. "Stand back from the edge."

decision.text: You took Abe Mutasa out of Four Ways' cell in the night. He went south toward Openfield, and Brodsky has not forgotten whose hand it was.

told.text: "He fired at the car. The stock car, with Chela's brother in it, with all of them in it. Five times, from the roof." He says it to his knees. "I had the pistol for the lamp. intro.text: The old refreshment room: tiles, a long counter, a mirror with the station's name in gilt half rubbed off it, and a broad man with a moustache drying cups. "Batista's. intro.again: Nuno Batista, drying a cup.

again.again: Nuno, holding a cup to the light.

ahead.again: A length ahead, the points coming.

off.again: Into the grass at the points.

stocks.text: Chela Ortega in the stocks at the platform's end, where the four rules are, with her braid cut off and her boots taken. She looks at you and keeps looking. "They hanged Abe at Kettle at dawn," she says. "On the signal post. Kask watched. I'm to go west on the next seven o'clock in what I stand in, which isn't much." She looks at your boots. "You came in on your own feet. Remember that."
stocks.again: Chela, in the stocks, looking at you.

intro.text: A woman in faded rail-crew orange with a rifle across her back and a work braid down it, cleaning a lamp at the watch house door with a rag. Her hood is green. "West Halt's watch." intro.again: Chela, cleaning the lamp.

passives.label: The cutting
passives.text: You know her. She knows you: her rag stops on the lamp, once, and goes on. The woman in the cutting with her scarf down, as if she wanted you to see her face.

text.text: Chela is on the platform with the pilot's flag rolled under her arm, waiting for the seven o'clock to stop, which it will. "You," she says, and almost smiles. "Pilot's pay goes in the tin for the tower. Nobody hurt."
"You took his money." She does not look up from the lamp. "Fine. We'll keep riding. Somebody has to."
Chela looks up from the lamp. "What?"

again.again: Chela, and the lamp.
