watch.text: "The length. Forty miles of it, every bolt. The tower. The flag." She puts the lamp down. "And the halt, from anybody who thinks a halt nobody stops at is a halt nobody will miss."

kettle.text: She finishes the lamp. She takes her time about it. "Then you know we never took a purse and never touched the coach. You know what Kask's sheet says about length money." She sets the lamp on its hook. "We take the Concern's sealed cars, the ones Casimir ticks, and the halts eat. That was the rule: nobody hurt." She looks down the line, east, toward Kettle. "Then the guild put my brother in a car."

interject.text: "Your brother," Wren says. It is the first thing she has said all day. "Sold for what?" "For the tower," Chela says. "For the water." Wren nods slowly, as if she had expected nothing else.

brother.text: "Joaquin. Seventeen." She says it to the lamp. "The guild fixed our tank last year and sent the bill, and we had no money, because nobody stops here to buy water. So the guild took a person instead. Joaquin said he'd go; he's the one who could." Her jaw works. "He went on the block at Ninebridge and came back up the Line in a stock car with eleven others, sealed, bound for the Concern. So I stopped it." She looks at you. "They're in the tower. Don't make me sorry I said so."

abe.text: "Abe." She does not hesitate. "The guard was on the stock car's roof, Gorse, and when we opened it he fired down into it, five times, at people in a box. Abe had the pistol for the lamp. He fired once." She breathes out. "If it comes to the rope, and it will, because Casimir has four rules and one of them is a rope, you speak for him. You owe me nothing. I'm asking."

plead.text: Chela is at the watch house door with the lamp unlit in her hand, and she does not pretend to be doing anything with it. "Casimir's watch took Abe to Four Ways last night. Dawn, he says, at the platform's end." She looks at you. "Speak for him. The guard fired first. Ferris on the rods saw it; ask him. I'm asking you."

sold.text: Chela Ortega is standing on the platform with her rifle in her hands, not across her back, and she does not lift it, which costs her something you can see. "They came for the tower at dawn," she says. "The Concern's men, with a paper, and a list with your description on it where the name should be." She turns her back on you. "Get on your train."

hi.text: A boy of nineteen sitting on an upturned crate by the fire barrel in his watch orange, a pistol in his belt he keeps touching as if to check it is still there. "I'm all right," he says, before you have asked him anything. "It's fine."
hi.again: Abe, by the fire barrel, touching the pistol.

kettle.text: He goes grey. "He fired at the car. At the stock car, with Joaquin in it, with all of them in it, five times, from the roof." He swallows. "I had the pistol for the lamp. I fired once." He looks at the fire. "I'd do it again. And I can't sleep. Both."

interject.text: Ash sits down on the next crate and holds his hands to the fire barrel as if he were cold. "Both is right," he says. "Both is what you carry. Don't let anybody take one of them off you to make the other one lighter."

intro.text: A woman at a table in the keeper's house with a ledger, a jar of bolts and a loaf, which she covers with a cloth as you come in. "West Halt. I keep it." She does not get up. "Water's a Toll a cup, when the tank is working. It's not working."
intro.again: Socorro, with the cloth over the loaf.

Socorro looks up from the ledger. "Yes?"

the trains stop here again

tank.text: "It leaks." Flat. "It's shut." She looks at the cloth over the bread, and then she looks at you looking at it, and does not explain.

length.text: "Badly." She taps the ledger. "The guild pays length money for every train that stops. Since the through, nothing stops. We keep forty miles of track for a guild that pays us for none of it, and we owe the guild for mending the tower." She lifts the cloth and puts it down again. "And the stalls sell tins, two Tolls, very good tins. Don't ask me where from."

key.text: She looks at you a long time. Then she takes a key off a nail behind the stove. "If you're lying," she says, "I'll know by morning, and so will everyone on this Line. Go up."

nokey.text: "The tower leaks." She covers the bread again. "Go and catch your train."

casimir.text: "Casimir Brodsky." She almost smiles. "His mother kept this length when we were children. He went to the Junction and became a clock." She looks out at the platform. "He still knows every bolt between here and Kettle. He sends us his weather, when he can."

intro.text: A red-haired man under the handcar with his sleeves rolled, who comes out on his back on a board when your boots stop by his head. "Eamon. Length." He sits up. "Every bolt on forty miles of track, I know by its first name."
intro.again: Eamon, on his back under the handcar.

Eamon wipes his hands. "What?"

bread.text: Eamon at the foot of the water tower in the dark with a sack of bread over his shoulder and the ladder's rope in his hand. He goes very still when he sees you. "It leaks," he says. "The tower."

"Yaw Boateng," he says. "We were bought at the Ninebridge block, all of us, and put in a car to go up the Line, and a woman in orange opened the car at a cutting and said run. So we ran here." He holds out a sheaf of paper. "This is what we are. Read it, if you can read."

Wren is down on her heels by the nearest blanket before anyone can stop her, looking at faces, one after another, and then she stands up. "No," she says, to nobody, and her voice is quite ordinary. "Not here."

"No. Nobody on the block knows." He folds the papers. "Everybody on the block knows nobody comes back."

Yaw Boateng on the platform with the paper in his hand that says he owes nobody anything, reading it again. "I keep thinking it will say something else," he says.

West Halt's watch board: brass tags on pegs, WH 1 to WH 9, one for each of the watch, so the halt knows who is out on the length. The peg for WH 4 is empty, and there is a pale ring on the wood where the tag usually hangs.

Inside, scratched into the boards at the height of a sitting person, names, a dozen of them, and under the bench a child's shoe.

A second bright line along the inside of each rail, narrower than an engine's wheels: something small, run often, from the west. And boot prints in the ballast, hobnailed.

A guild stake over a mound of red clay, stencilled: HAMISH GORSE — GUARD — IN THE DISCHARGE OF HIS DUTY. Somebody has left a cup on it, upside down, the way you leave a cup for a man who won't be back to drink from it.

She looks up. "Two lives. The Sow, for one: the court takes her boat. Her salvage off every barge she brought down, for the other, to the drowned men's kin wherever the guild keeps them." Yewande closes her eyes. "And you'll teach off Ade Bankole's boat," Oona says, "because the Stilts can't spare your lungs, and nobody else on this shore can count."

decision.text: The Stilt Court judged Yewande Coker for the false light: it took her boat and her salvage for the two drowned bargemen, and kept her on the stage.

news.text: the Stilt Court at Gull Stilts judged its own dive master for wrecking guild barges, and denied the guild its hanging

light_off.text: "Page four." Oona writes without looking up. "The court doesn't hang; the Stilts never had the rope for it. Yewande Coker is put off the stilts, and her boat with her." Yewande nods once. That night the Sow goes out past the Jesty with two people in her, a woman at the oars and a girl in the bow with an unlit lamp in her lap, and the stage off the south walk belongs to Ade Bankole, who is nineteen.

decision.text: The Stilt Court put Yewande Coker off the stilts for the false light; Ade Bankole keeps the dive stage now.

news.text: the Stilt Court at Gull Stilts put its dive master off the stilts for wrecking guild barges

ebb.text: She does not look up from the net. Up close you can see it is a child, eleven or so, small for it, and that somebody has washed the black off his face and could not get it out of his hair. "Kai," she says, as if you had asked. "He went under the Gut for my net. I told him a net's a net." The tide goes out over his feet. "The Rig did this. The Rig and its oil. I've called the court. Page nine." She looks at you, then: a stranger, off the road, with nothing to do with any of it. "The Stilts won't stand up. They need Hum's tar and they're scared of the guild's scale. Will you?"
ebb.again: Lua keeps her hands flat on the net.

interject.text: Ash kneels on the step below her without being asked, so his head is lower than hers. "Water's a grave that doesn't hold still," he says. "I'm a digger. I'd dig him one if you'd let me." "No," she says. "He's a Stilts boy. He goes out." Ash nods as if he had been told something holy.
Tamsin stands a step back with her arms wrapped round herself. She does not say anything at all, which for Tamsin is a lot.

options.text: I'll find out what happened. Then I'll stand up.
Sometimes the sea just takes people.

text.text: Lua's loft, empty. Somebody has taken the nets down.
Lua at her loft door with a lamp, mending nothing. "Well?"
Lua at the table in her loft with a net across her knees she is not mending. "Well?"

again.again: Lua waits.

options.text: It wasn't the Rig. The guild opened Hum's line to its own tank.
When I'm ready, Oona will call the court.

yes.text: She nods, once. "Then find his net. He was under the Gut, third pile from the Greta, where the old pipe goes. Everybody says don't swim there. Everybody swims there." She goes back to his face.
yes.again: "Third pile from the Greta. Find his net."

where.text: "Under the Gut. Third pile from the Greta, where the old pipe runs along the bottom to Blackcap. It snagged on something and he went down for it, because he's eleven and it was his first net that was a net." She is quiet. "The water there's been black since the thaw. You can't see your hand. He couldn't see his."
where.again: "Third pile from the Greta. Black since the thaw."

sea.text: "Don't." Not loud. "Don't say the sea to me. The sea's been taking people off this shore for sixty years and it never once came back black."

net.text: She takes it and holds it and does not cry, which you would have preferred. Her thumb finds the brass collar knotted in the mesh. "Joint fourteen," she reads. "That's the old line." She gives it back. "Keep it. The court will want to hold it. I already have."
net.again: "Keep it. The court will want it."

guild.text: She takes it in slowly. "The guild." She looks out at the tide post at the Greta's stern, where Thorne is weighing fish. "Then it's the guild's boat I want." A pause. "Or it's the guild's boat I'll burn. I haven't decided which."
guild.again: "The guild's boat. One way or another."

court.text: "Then be ready." She goes back to the net on her knees.

text.text: Lua at her loft door with a net across her knees. "Oona wrote the guild's barge down as his boat," she says. "The one that burned at Blackcap." She looks at you a long moment. "I saw the smoke from here. I thought it was the tank." She does not ask. She goes back to the net.

Lua at her loft door. She has started a new net, small, green, the kind a child is given to learn on, and is not hiding it. "Kai's boat went out a long way," she says. "Longer than any of ours would."
Lua at her loft door with a net across her knees, mending it. "They paid," she says. "Oona wrote that they paid. Not what." She bites the twine. "That's right. It's right."

after_how.text: "Breathing." She holds the net up to the light. "My mother said when the water takes one of yours you make something with your hands for a month or you go in after them." She almost smiles. "Twenty-nine days."

after_rig.text: Lua at her loft door. "The Stilts' boats went out to Hum," she says. "Kai's Rig." She looks at you as if you had given her something. "Thank you." You have never been thanked for anything worse.

intro.text: A woman on the stage with one hand on the air hose and her lips moving. "Thirty-eight. Thirty-nine. Forty." She tugs the line twice, and a long way down something tugs back, and she lets her breath out as if it were hers. "Yewande. Coker's stage." She looks you over: lungs, shoulders, hands. "You dive? I take people down to Ellery at slack water. Six for the roofs, eight for the high street, and you keep what you bring up, and I keep you alive. That's the whole bargain."
intro.again: Yewande counts under her breath, one eye on the line.

interject.text: "Can't read water," Wren says, looking down at the green. "Doesn't keep tracks." Yewande does not look up. "It keeps every track, girl. It just keeps them at the bottom."

text.text: Yewande is not here.
Yewande on Ade's boat, teaching him to read a line by its shiver. She nods at you, and it costs her something, and she pays it.
Yewande on the stage at night, with the hose coiled and her eyes on the fog coming in over the Jesty.
Yewande on the stage, one hand on the hose. "Slack at the turn. You going down?"

again.again: Yewande counts under her breath.

options.text: Let me see what you've got.
You put out Lean's light, and hung your own on the Jesty.
Stop it. Nobody needs to know.

mods.why: the fish are coming back
Amara's fingers
Tamsin asks her for the girl

decision.text: Yewande Coker put the false light away for good, and nobody but you knows she ever hung it.

ellery.text: "The town. Port Ellery, before." She points down with her chin. "That's the Strand under the Gut, that's the high street under Low Row, that's the Majestic, the Jesty, where you see the roof. Shops, flats, a clinic, a bank with its door open and nothing in it. Ninety years in the dark and she still gives, if you ask her nicely and come up when I pull." She tugs the line again. "Most people don't come up when I pull."
ellery.again: "Ellery. She gives, if you come up when I pull."

kai.text: The counting stops. "I didn't take him down. I don't take children down. I never have." She looks at the water. "He went on his own, under the Gut, in black water, for a net. I was on this stage. I heard them shouting." The hose shivers in her hand and she starts counting again, from one.

bag.text: "One. A bag: a rebreather off a dead man at the bank's door, glued more times than it's been filled. A hundred and twenty, and you don't pay me for the hose again." She shrugs. "It makes you cleverer than you are down there, which kills more people than it saves. Your choice."

light.text: She does not stop counting, which is how you know. She gets to forty and pulls the line twice and the diver comes up, and she helps him onto the stage and sends him to the smokehouse with a word. Then: "Since the thaw." Very quiet. "The fish went black, and the guild's salt went up, and the twine, and a child in Low Row died of the cough because the post's medicine was eleven Tolls a bottle. So in the fog I put Lean's light out, and I hang ours on the Jesty, and the guild's barges steer for it like they're coming home." She looks at the broken barge on the roof. "Five. Five barges of salt and twine and medicine, and Gull Stilts has eaten this season. And this time two men drowned." She says the number like a diver. "Two."

interject.text: Ash is quiet for a long time. "You fed them," he says. "And two men are in the water for it, with families somewhere upriver that don't know yet." "I know," she says. "I can count."
"Right," Ilya says. Just that, as if he were agreeing with the fog.

light_amara.text: "She rows. I hang it." Too fast. Then slower, because she is an honest woman who has decided to lie and cannot keep it up: "She rows it out. I can't row and count the fog at once." She looks at you properly. "If the guild comes for it, it comes for me. Whatever you do with it, it comes for me."

stopped.text: She looks at the water for a long time. "All right." She unhooks a lamp from under the stage, an old ship's lamp with its glass blacked on one side, and drops it off the edge. It goes down slowly, turning, until the green takes it. "All right," she says again, to Ellery.
stopped.again: Yewande watches the place where the lamp went down.

not_stopping.text: "Not while the water's black." She does not raise her voice. "You want it to stop, shut the line that's killing the fish. Then come and ask me again."
not_stopping.again: "Shut the line. Then ask me again."

framed.text: Yewande on the stage. She does not look at you. She has not looked at you since the morning Ewan Tulloch hung from the tide post, and she is not going to start. When you speak, she counts over you, out loud, until you stop.

intro.text: A man in the shore's one good coat, writing in a day-book behind a counter in a steel container, with a scale beside him whose brass has been polished so long it has gone soft at the edges. "Cyprian Thorne. The tide post." He finishes his line before he looks up, and when he does he is pleasant. "Fish bought by the weight, salt sold by the measure, medicine at the guild's price, which is the only price on the shore. The scale is honest. Check it, if you like. Everyone does once."
intro.again: Thorne finishes his line before he looks up.

interject.text: "Cyprian." Odile says it the way you say the name of a dish you once sent back. He sets his pen down. "Marchetti. The floor misses you." "The floor misses my commission," she says. They smile at each other like two knives in a drawer.

options.text: What do you make of the oil on the water?

text.text: Thorne behind the counter, writing, his scale polished. He looks up and is pleasant, and it costs him more than it used to. "The guild bears no grudge. The guild keeps a book."
Thorne behind the counter, writing. "A sad business," he says, without looking up. "The sea is a hard neighbour."
Thorne finishes his line. "Yes?"

again.again: Thorne waits, pen raised.

options.text: What do you make of the oil on the water?
I know what's in your barge at Blackcap, and whose oil it is.
You sold Mateo Ibarra to the press, on Rui Sousa's word.
Your wrecker is Yewande Coker, the dive master.
Your wrecker is Ewan Tulloch. Lean's lamp-keeper. His light was dark that night.

sheen.text: "The Rigs." He says it with real regret, like a doctor. "Hum is ninety years old, and so are its pipes. The guild has said to Mr Farouk, more than once, that a line kept open past its life is a liability. He keeps it open; the guild buys what he sells." He makes a small note. "It would be a mercy, frankly, if somebody shut it. Mr Farouk will not."

anchorage.text: "For the mooring, yes. A courtesy." He turns the day-book so you can see the figure, because he is a man who wants you to know he has nothing to hide, and the figure is large. "The court's widows eat on it. The guild is glad to be a neighbour." He turns the book back. "Nobody has to be unreasonable."
anchorage.again: "A courtesy. The widows eat on it."

text.text: He caps his pen. For the first time he looks at you as if you were a column rather than a customer. "The guild holds the Line from Meridian to the Skirts now, end to end, and the Line runs on Hum's oil. You will understand that this is not a small matter." He lets that sit. "You also know that the guild's post is the only buyer of fish on this shore, and the only seller of salt and twine and medicine, and half the widows' bread. If the court hangs a barge on the guild, the guild will not be unreasonable. It will simply go." He takes a purse out of a drawer and sets it on the scale, where the needle moves. "A hundred and fifty. For a widow's grief to find the sea, which is where grief on this shore usually goes."

He caps his pen. For the first time he looks at you as if you were a column rather than a customer. "Then you also know," he says pleasantly, "that the guild's post is the only buyer of fish on this shore, and the only seller of salt and twine and medicine, and half the widows' bread. If the court hangs a barge on the guild, the guild will not be unreasonable. It will simply go." He takes a purse out of a drawer and sets it on the scale, where the needle moves. "A hundred and fifty. For a widow's grief to find the sea, which is where grief on this shore usually goes. Nobody has to decide anything at once."

offer.again: The purse sits on the scale. The needle has not moved back.

interject.text: Wren looks at the purse and then at him. "Man's weighing a boy," she says. "On a scale. In front of me." She does not say anything else, and does not need to.

decision.text: You took Factor Thorne's hundred and fifty to let Kai Tanoa's death find the sea.

options.text: Keep it. The court will hear what the water knows.

taken.text: He makes a note. "The guild remembers its friends," he says, and means it as a kindness, which is the worst of it.

refused.text: He puts the purse back in the drawer without any change in his face. "Then the court will hear it," he says, "and the guild will listen. I hope the widows like fish."

press.text: "The guild bought a debt." Not offended; correcting. "Three hundred Tolls of salt and twine on credit, and a debtor who would not pay and could not. The guild does not sell people, whatever they say in the Sink. It collects them." He writes a line. "Mr Sousa was helpful. The guild pays for help. A boat is a fair fee for a boat's worth of help."
press.again: "The guild collects. It does not sell."

interject.text: Wren's burned hand closes. "Collects," she says. "That's the word they use at the block too."

bounty.text: "A false light on the Jesty in the fog, where no lamp should be, and Lean's light out the same night. The guild's salt barge steered for it and broke her back. Two of the guild's men drowned." He does not look at the barge on the roof; he has looked at it enough. "The Stilts call what the water wrecks salvage. The guild calls it theft, and the men murder. A hundred for a name the guild can hang."
bounty.again: "A hundred for a name the guild can hang."

name_yewande.text: He writes the name down. "The dive master." He is not surprised; he is never surprised. "Thank you. The guild will want her at the post at dawn." A purse, on the scale: a hundred. "If there is a girl," he says, as if mentioning the weather, "the guild is not interested in girls. Mrs Coker will see to that herself, I expect."

decision.text: You gave Yewande Coker to the guild for the false light.

news.text: a stranger gave Gull Stilts' dive master to the guild for wrecking its barges

name_ewan.text: He writes it down. "The lamp-keeper." He considers the name the way he considers fish. "A drunk, whose light was dark the night the barge struck. That will satisfy the guild's men." He looks up. "Whether it satisfies anyone else is not the guild's concern." A purse, on the scale: a hundred.

decision.text: You gave the guild Ewan Tulloch, Lean's lamp-keeper, for the false light he did not hang.

news.text: the guild took the Rigs' old lamp-keeper for the wrecks on the Jesty

taken_ewan.text: "Dawn," he says, and blots the line.

intro.text: A man sitting on a crate at the Landing with his back to the village, too thin for his frame, with a beard he has not had long enough to know what to do with. "You're not from the Stilts." He seems glad of it. "Nobody from the Stilts will look at me. I'm in the Book." He laughs, once, at nothing. "Mateo Ibarra. Taken by the water, two years back. Ask the old woman; she wrote it. My boat's the Curlew. My wife's Paz." He looks along the Gut toward the Netlofts. "I hear the Curlew's Rui Sousa's now. I hear Paz is too."
intro.again: Mateo looks along the Gut toward the Netlofts.

passives.text: Under his cuff, on the inside of the left wrist: a brand, healed two years, the colour of a burn. Letters and a number.

interject.text: Ilya looks at the man's hands, which are a labourer's hands now and were a fisherman's once. "Two years," he says. "On a winch. Right." Mateo looks at him. "How'd you know?" "Counted," Ilya says.

text.text: Mateo on his crate at the Landing in the dark, not sleeping.
Mateo on his crate. "Well?"

again.again: Mateo waits.

options.text: That's a Ninebridge block brand on your wrist.
Stand up on the Greta and ask the court. I'll stand up with you.
Take a boat and go up the delta. Leave her be. Mele's old skiff, eighty Tolls; I'll pay.

decision.text: You paid for Mateo Ibarra to row up the delta and leave Paz be. She never knew what Rui did.

news.text: the man the Stilts' Book had drowned rowed up the delta again in a bought skiff

where.text: "On the water." He means to leave it there, and does not. "On the guild's barges, upriver. Two years on a winch at Low Landing for three hundred Tolls I owed the post for salt and twine, the winter the mackerel didn't come. They took me off the Gut at night, two of them, with a sack, and they knew where I slept." He turns his left wrist up and pushes the cuff back. N-B 4471. "Lot four thousand four hundred and seventy-one at the Ninebridge block. Bought by the guild's own barges, from the guild's own block, for the guild's own debt." He pulls the cuff down. "I walked off at Low Landing when the paper ran out. Nobody told me I'd drowned."

interject.text: Wren has gone still in the particular way she goes still. "Lot four thousand," she says. "They had the girl at four hundred and something." She does not say whose girl.

options.text: Who told them where you slept?

who.text: "I don't know." He has thought about nothing else for two years, and it shows. "Somebody on the Stilts. Everybody on the Stilts knew where I slept. I slept on the Curlew." He looks at the Netlofts again.

brand.text: He pushes the cuff back and shows you properly. "N-B 4471. You know the block." He covers it. "Don't tell the Stilts. No. Tell them. Tell them all."

want.text: "My boat." No pause. Then a long one. "And my wife. If she wants me. I don't know which of those I can ask the court for. The Book says a drowned man's got no claim to either." He picks at a splinter on the crate. "I didn't drown. I keep saying it. It doesn't get any truer."
want.again: "My boat. My wife, if she wants me."

court.text: "On the Greta." He breathes out. "In front of all of them. In front of her." He stands up, and is taller than you thought. "All right. Tell the old woman. I'll be here."
court.again: "Tell the old woman. I'll be here."

quiet.text: He looks at the purse for a long time. "She'd never know," he says. "Would she." It is not a question. In the morning Mele's old skiff is gone from the Landing, and so is Mateo Ibarra, up the delta on the flood, and the Book still says what it said.

rig.text: Mateo on Hum's deck in a crew jersey, carrying a drum of tar he does not need both arms for. "They take anyone who can carry," he says. "I can carry." He looks east, where the Stilts are a line of posts on the water. "You can see the Curlew from the flare stack. If you know where to look."

text.text: Mateo in the Curlew at the finger jetty, mending a net with his back to the Netlofts. "She's got a child," he says, before you can say anything. "Two years is a long time to be drowned." He bites the twine. "The Curlew still pulls left. Rui never fixed it."

Mateo in the Curlew under Paz's loft, mending a net. He does not look up at the loft. He has not looked up at it all day, which means he has looked at nothing else. "She says good morning," he says. "Yesterday she didn't."

A woman at a loft door with a baby on her hip, who knows exactly who you have been talking to. "You were at the Landing." Low, so the baby does not wake. "He's thin." It is the first thing she says about him and you can see she hates herself for it. "Paz. I said the words for him at the Ebb Steps over his coat. I meant them. I didn't have anything else to say them over."
A woman at a loft door with a baby on her hip, mending a net one-handed. "Paz. Talk quiet or go; she's only just down."

intro.again: Paz shifts the baby to her other hip.

text.text: Paz at the loft door with the baby. Below her, in the Curlew, a man mending a net looks up and then down. "Morning," she says to him. Then, to you: "Well?"
Paz at the loft door with the baby. "Well?"

again.again: Paz waits.

options.text: Rui told the guild's press where Mateo slept. The Curlew was his fee.

rui.text: "At dawn, off the Jesty, a week after. Adrift, with his coat in the bow." She says it like a thing she has said many times to herself. "Page twelve: a boat found on the water is the finder's. Rui brought me the coat. He brought me fish all that winter. He didn't ask for anything. Then he asked." She looks at the baby. "I said yes. I'd say it again. I think."
rui.again: "He brought me the coat. He brought me fish."

want.text: She laughs, very quietly, so as not to wake the baby. "Nobody's asked me that. Oona asked who found the boat. The guild asked who'd pay the debt. Rui asked if I'd have him." She looks down the Gut toward the Landing. "I want it to have been the sea," she says. "That's what I want. I can live with the sea."
want.again: "I want it to have been the sea."

interject.text: Tamsin is looking at the baby. "Nobody asked her," she says to you, afterwards, on the Gut. "Everybody's going to decide what she is, and nobody asked her."

told.text: She does not say anything for a long time. The baby wakes and she rocks it without looking at it. "Get off my loft," she says at last, and it is not to you; she is looking past you, at the net store, where Rui keeps his gear. Then it is to you. "Get off my loft." She goes in and shuts the door, and you hear her not crying through it.

intro.text: A broad man in the Curlew, or by her, coiling a line with hands that know it. "Rui." He does not offer anything else. "If it's about the Landing, I found her adrift. Found is found. Page twelve." He goes on coiling. "Good boat, the Curlew. Pulls left."
intro.again: Rui coils the line.

again.text: Rui coils a line that is already coiled. "What."
again.again: Rui waits, the coil in his fist.

options.text: You told the guild's press where Mateo slept.

mods.why: his name is in the guild's own tally
the oars were shipped and lashed
Wren knows the block

found.text: "Off the Jesty. Dawn. A week after he went." He stops coiling. "His coat in her bow. Oars in." He starts again. "Mele found her first. I got a line on her first. That's finding."

deny.text: "Get off my boat." He does not get up. "Mateo owed. Everybody knew he owed. The guild collects. I found a boat." His hands have stopped. "Get off my boat."

confess.text: The coil goes down in the bottom of the boat. He looks at it, not at you. "He owed three hundred. The factor said the guild would have it out of him or out of her. Out of her." His jaw works. "He said if I said where Mateo slept they'd take him and not her, and the debt would go in the water with him, page whatever, and the guild would write me a boat for my trouble." He looks up at the Netlofts. "I'd have married her anyway. I'd have—" He stops. "I wanted the boat too. I always wanted his boat."
confess.again: Rui looks at the coil in the bottom of the boat.

options.text: Then she never needs to know.

court.text: "On the Greta." He laughs, and it is not a laugh. "Page whatever: put off the stilts." He picks up the coil again. "If the old woman asks me straight, I won't lie to her. I never lied to Oona in my life. I'd rather the sea."
court.again: "If she asks me straight, I won't lie."

quiet.text: He nods, slowly, and you can see him decide to believe that you mean it. "She never needs to know," he repeats, as if that were a thing a person could keep in a boat.

intro.text: A woman at the tiller of a flat delta boat with an outboard that runs on Hum's rig diesel and a mast for when it does not. She looks at the water before she looks at you, the way some people look at a sky. "Mele. The tide boat. Up the delta to the city at six every morning and back on the evening flood; out to the Rigs when there's a fare; Blackcap if you've a reason, and I'll not ask it." She spits over the side, downwind. "Water keeps every track. You have to know how it writes."
intro.again: Mele watches the water.

interject.text: "Every track?" Wren says, interested despite herself. Mele points at a line of foam going out across the bay at an angle to the wind. "That's the old line under the bottom. Warm. Oil's warm." Wren looks at it for a long time.

options.text: Up the delta to the city at six: Carrick's water stairs. (6 Tolls)

text.text: Mele's boat tied up for the night, and Mele asleep in the bottom of it under a tarp. She opens one eye. "Morning," she says, and shuts it.
Mele at the tiller. "Where to?"

again.again: Mele waits at the tiller.

options.text: Up the delta to the city at six: Carrick's water stairs. (6 Tolls)
You found the Curlew adrift, two years back.

night.text: "Nobody with an honest face." She considers. "The guild's barge, three nights in four, out to Blackcap with no lamps and back before light, low in the water. Coker's girl rows when there's fog." She looks at you. "You didn't hear the second thing from me."
night.again: "The guild's barge. No lamps. You didn't hear the rest."

curlew.text: "Off the Jesty at dawn, a week after he went." She does not have to think about it. "Oars shipped and lashed, neat as you like, his coat folded in the bow. A drowning man doesn't ship his oars. A drowning man doesn't fold his coat." She looks along the Gut at the Netlofts. "I said so to the Book. Oona wrote it. Then Rui put a line on her and towed her in, and the Book said what it says."
curlew.again: "Oars shipped. Coat folded. I said so to the Book."

night.text: The tide boat, tied up at the jetty for the night, with someone asleep in the bottom of it under a tarp. Not tonight.

boat.text: The tide boat at the jetty: flat-bottomed, tarred, an outboard on the transom and a mast laid along the thwarts. Mele is at the tiller. "Where to?"

options.text: Up the delta to the city at six: Carrick's water stairs. (6 Tolls)

text.text: A big grey-bearded man in a smokehouse that smells of driftwood and fish and, faintly, less of anything else than it did. "Hassan. Smoked fish, water, twine, and a cabin under the old hull over the net store if you want a roof." He holds up a mackerel to the light like a jeweller. "Look at that. Clean. The water's thinning out east."

A big grey-bearded man in a smokehouse that smells of driftwood and fish and something under both that belongs in an engine. "Hassan. Smoked fish, water, twine, and a cabin under the old hull over the net store if you want a roof." He holds up a mackerel and sniffs it and puts it down. "Tastes of the Rig. Eat it anyway. Everybody does."

intro.again: Hassan turns a rack of fish in the smoke.

again.text: Hassan in the smoke. "What'll it be?"
again.again: Hassan turns the racks.

work.text: "At dawn. Out with the nets in my boat, three hours, and you get a fish and a wage when there's a catch to pay it from. The board's by the door." He shrugs. "Lately there's no catch to speak of. The ones we bring up taste of Hum."
work.again: "At dawn. The board's by the door."

text.text: "Salt comes up the delta on Mele's boat now, at the city's price, which is the guild's price plus Mele." He laughs into his beard. "And I sell my fish in the city myself, at the city's price, which is twice the guild's. Swings and roundabouts. My father used to say that. I never knew what a roundabout was."

"The guild buys my fish at the guild's weight and sells me the salt to cure it at the guild's measure. The salt's dearer every season and the fish are worse." He shrugs. "Salt's up again. Twine too. A child in Low Row died of the cough in the winter because the post's medicine was eleven a bottle. Nobody's going to hang Thorne for a price."

board.text: A board by the smokehouse door in chalk: HANDS AT DAWN — THE NETS — A FISH AND A SHARE. Below it, smaller: NO CHILDREN.

dawn.text: Hassan's boat at the smokehouse steps in the grey before dawn, nets heaped in the bow, two of his hands already at the oars. "Coming?"

thin.text: Three hours on the grey water, hauling, and the nets come up with a skin of oil on every float and a few mackerel that smell of Hum. Hassan gives you one and nothing else, apologetically. "When there's a catch," he says.

full.text: Three hours on the grey water, and the nets come up heavy and silver and clean, and Hassan laughs out loud at the first haul and does not stop for an hour. Three fish and six Tolls, and he would give you more if he had it.

full_poor.text: Three hours on the grey water. You foul a net and lose half a haul over the side, and Hassan says nothing about it, which is worse. Two fish.

intro.text: A girl of fourteen sitting on the edge of the stage with her feet in the water, sculling an oar for no reason. "Mam says don't talk to the guild." She looks you over. "You're not the guild. Guild wear coats." She sculls. "I row. I don't dive. Mam won't let me dive since Kai."
intro.again: Amara sculls the oar.

passives.text: The tips of her right fingers are shiny and pink: small burns, a few days healed, the kind you get holding hot glass.

again.text: Amara on the stage's edge, sculling. "What."
again.again: Amara sculls.

row.text: "Places." She sculls harder. "The Sow, for Mam. Out to the wreck and back." She looks at the fog bank lying out past the Jesty. "You can smell the fog before it comes. Mam can't. I can."

hands.text: She puts the hand in her armpit. "The stove." She is a bad liar, like her mother, and knows it, and stops trying. "Don't tell Mam you saw."
hands.again: "The stove." She doesn't look at you.

after.text: Amara on the stage's edge with her feet in the water. She does not scull the oar. She does not look at you. Ade Bankole stands behind her at the pump with his hand on her shoulder and looks at you instead.

pump.text: A young man at the air pump's crank, turning it in a rhythm he does not have to think about. "Forty a minute," he says, without missing one. "Ade. I'm hers. Talk to her about diving; I just keep you breathing."

options.text: How long have you worked for her?

how.text: "Since I was nine. She pulled me off the bottom of the high street when I went down after a tin." He grins. "I owe her forty strokes a minute for the rest of my life. That's the rate."

runs.text: Ade on the stage alone, with the pump and the hose and the ladder, looking younger than nineteen. "It's mine now," he says. "I charge more. I'm not her. I pay the pumpers more because I'm not her." He looks at the water. "Slack at the turn, if you're going down."

hi.text: The boy off the dike, at the Netlofts with a net in his lap and a mending needle he is holding wrong. "It's you." He holds up the net. "Paz is teaching me. I'm bad at it." He does not stop. "My mam doesn't know where I am. I'll write. Somebody here can write."

ok.text: "They feed you if you mend. Nobody's got a sack." He says it as if that were the whole of what a place could offer, and for him it is.

tide.text: The ladder going down into the green, and the water moving past it hard, carrying weed. Not on this tide. The city's table on the Landing says when the water is slack: before dawn and late in the afternoon.

text.text: Ade Bankole's boat at the stage, and Yewande in it, teaching. "Slack water," she says. "Where?"
Yewande at the pump with the hose coiled ready. "Slack water," she says. "Where?"

text.text: Down the hose into green light, along roofs of slate and tar paper with weed growing on them like hair, past a chimney with a gull's skull in it. A gutter full of iron; a tin with its label long gone, sealed. Forty strokes a minute, and then two tugs, and up.

Down among the roofs again. A skylight, its glass still in, and under it a room nobody has been in for ninety years: a bed, a chair, a coat on a hook moving in the water like someone just turned round. You take the curtains and two bottles off the sill and you do not look at the bed.

Down to a roof you have not tried, and in its gutter, wedged, a leather purse gone hard as wood. Inside, pre-Burn coins nobody spends any more and somebody always buys: copper and nickel and one in silver with a woman's face on it. You come up grinning. Yewande does not.
Down among the roofs. Ellery gives less every time; the easy gutters are picked clean. A strip of lead, a rag of something. Up.

roofs_up.again: You sit on the stage, dripping, and count your breath.

text.text: Down past the roofs to the street, eight fathoms, where the light goes brown. A pharmacy's window with its shutters rusted half up. You go in on your belly. A drawer of boiled bandages in a sealed tin, and a till with a board in it that the water never reached.

Down to the high street again, to a hardware shop with its door open and its stock still on the walls in the dark, furred with growth. A repair kit in a box that had its lid on, and copper wire on a drum that will not stop coming. You come up with your lungs on fire and the wire round your arm.

Down to the street's far end, to the clinic with the red cross gone brown over its door. Behind the counter a steel fridge, sealed, its door gasket still holding after ninety years under the sea. Two boxes of holdfast inside, dry, and a cash tin. Yewande looks at the holdfast for a long time when you surface. "That's a winter," she says.
Down to the high street. The shops are open and empty; somebody has been everywhere you go, and so have you. A board out of a dead till, a twist of wire. Up.

street_up.again: You sit on the stage, dripping, and count your breath.

down_fail.text: Down into the green, and at three fathoms your ears go, and at four the cold gets into your chest and squeezes, and you are already climbing the hose hand over hand when the two tugs come. You surface with nothing and your heart going like a fist on a door. "Next slack," she says. "Breathe slow. Nobody does."

net_up.text: Under the Gut the water is black, not green: you cannot see your hand, so you go down the third pile by feel, and at the bottom the old line runs along the mud as thick as a man, warm through your gloves. At a joint where its collar has split, the black comes out of it in slow breaths, and in the black, caught on the collar's lip, a small net. You work it free by touch. The brass collar comes with it, still knotted in the mesh. You think about an eleven-year-old doing this in the dark, and then you stop thinking and climb.

net_fail.text: Under the Gut the water is black and you cannot see your hand. You go down the pile by feel until something warm moves against your face, and then you are going up, fast, faster than you meant to, with your lungs screaming and the taste of the rig in your mouth. "Not like that," she says, holding your head while you cough. "Again at the next slack, or not at all."

table.text: A printed sheet under glass in a frame at the head of the Landing, salt-bleached to the colour of tea: TIDE TABLE — LOWER DELTA — RESTORATION YEAR 30 — ISSUED BY THE PRECINCT. Two low waters a day, every day of the season, to the minute: before dawn, and late in the afternoon. Somebody has written under it in pencil, in a careful hand: NEVER WRONG YET.
table.again: The city's tide table: slack before dawn and late in the afternoon.

interject.text: "The lower delta table," Nine says, with something in its voice that in a person would be fondness. "Hydrography was the Ledger's third department. It has never been wrong because water is the one thing in the basin that does what the record says." It considers the pencilled line. "They are grateful. That is rare."
Tamsin reads it twice. "So the city knows when the sea's going to do it," she says. "And nobody minds." She sounds as if she would like to mind and cannot find the way in.

book.text: The Book of Water on the Greta's chart table: a ferry's logbook swollen to the size of a brick with sixty years of pages sewn in, in three hands, the first two dead. A pen on a string. Nobody stops you reading it; on the Stilts, everybody reads the Book.
book.again: The Book lies open where Oona left it.

wrecks.text: WRECKED ON THE JESTY, and under it, in Oona's hand, this season: a guild salt barge in the fog of the first thaw; a guild twine barge; another; a medicine barge; the salt barge on the roof now, TWO DROWNED. And before them, going back eleven years, nothing. Not one wreck on the Jesty in eleven years, while Lean's light burned. Five since the fish went black.
wrecks.again: Five guild barges on the Jesty since the thaw. None in eleven years before.

anchorage.text: ANCHORAGE — THE GUILD — FOR THE TIDE POST'S MOORING, a figure every month in Oona's hand, and beside each one, WIDOWS. The widows' column is twice as long as the anchorage column. Half of everything in it is guild money.
anchorage.again: The anchorage: half the widows' fund.

text.text: TAKEN BY THE WATER, the long list, sixty years of it. Near the end: IBARRA, MATEO — THE CURLEW, and through it a single line, and in the margin, in fresh blue ink: CAME BACK. SEE PAGE TWELVE, THE SECOND HALF. And at the very end: TANOA, KAI — ELEVEN — UNDER THE GUT.

TAKEN BY THE WATER, the long list, sixty years of it in three hands. Near the end: IBARRA, MATEO — THE CURLEW — FOUND ADRIFT OFF THE JESTY — OARS SHIPPED (M. TUI SAYS SO). And at the very end, the ink still wet: TANOA, KAI — ELEVEN — UNDER THE GUT.

drowned.again: The long list of the drowned.

text.text: The tide post's notice board: prices, the scale's last inspection, and a paper that has been taken down, leaving four clean corners in the salt.

A paper on the tide post's board, in a clerk's hand: A FALSE LIGHT WAS HUNG ON THE JESTY IN THE FOG OF THE NINTH, WHERE NO LAMP IS, AND LEAN'S LIGHT PUT OUT. THE GUILD'S BARGE SALT 3 WRECKED. TWO MEN DROWNED. ONE HUNDRED TOLLS FOR THE NAME OF THE WRECKERS. — C. THORNE, FACTOR. Somebody has scratched under it with a nail: WHAT THE WATER WRECKS, THE WATER GIVES.

cot.text: A small cot made up neatly with a blanket somebody has knitted out of net-twine, and on it a boy's things laid out in a row: a knife with a cork handle, a gull's feather, a pre-Burn coin with a hole in it on a string, a hand line wound on a stick. Nothing has been moved in a long time, and it has only been since this morning.

boat.text: The Curlew at the finger jetty: a clinker-built boat, old and much loved, tarred black, with a name painted on the transom in a hand that has gone over it every spring. On the starboard bow, a hand under the gunwale, a patch: birch over tarred canvas, eleven copper tacks, one of them bent.
boat.again: The Curlew, with her bent tack.

passives.text: Somebody very particular put that patch on, and has not been back to it: the tar round it is older than the tar round everything else. Whoever fishes her now has never touched it.

let.text: A trawler's hull turned keel-up on the stilts over Hassan's net store, with a door cut in her side and a ladder to it: a cabin under her ribs, a bed of nets and blankets, a locker, a porthole over the water. A card on the ladder: TO LET — ASK HASSAN — 20. Somebody has written under it: BRING YOUR OWN SMELL.

decision.text: You rented the cabin under the upturned hull over Hassan's net store at Gull Stilts.

mine.text: Your cabin under the upturned hull: the bed of nets, the locker, the porthole over the water, the Stilts' lamps coming on one by one along the Gut, and Lean's light out west on the horizon.
mine.again: Your cabin under the hull at Gull Stilts.

text.text: The Ebb Steps at low water, and at their foot, black in the green, the ribs of a burned barge settled on the bottom, with weed beginning on them. Somebody has tied a strip of green twine to the highest rib that shows.

The Ebb Steps, going down into the water: some drowned hall's steps, broad and shallow, worn into dips by sixty years of people carrying their dead down them. A strip of green twine on the bottom step, where a net was.
The Ebb Steps, going down into the water, and half the village on them.

p.text: The Jesty's parapet on its seaward corner, the highest point of the drowned hotel's roof, where you would hang a lamp if you wanted a ship coming in from the west to think it was the Stilts.
p.again: The seaward corner of the parapet.

passives.text: An iron hook driven into the parapet, new, with soot above it in a fan on the old concrete, the kind a lamp leaves.

found.text: Under a loose slab, an iron hook driven into the parapet, new, and above it a fan of soot on the old concrete, the kind a lamp leaves hanging in the wet for hours. Nobody lights a lamp on the Jesty. There is nothing on the Jesty to light.

nothing.text: Salt, gull droppings, a broken bottle. Nothing you can read.

w.text: The guild's salt barge, SALT 3 on her bow in the guild's stencil, broken across the Jesty's parapet with her stern in the water and her hold open to the sky. The Stilts' divers have had most of what was in her; the hold smells of brine and tar and, faintly, of the men who were in it. A clerk's chalk on a bulkhead, from the guild's salvage: TWO LOST. Coker's divers have chalked under it: WHAT THE WATER WRECKS.

passives.text: She struck steering south-east, hard over, as if she had seen the Stilts' lights dead ahead where only the Jesty is. A ship making for Lean's light from the west would never come in on this heading.

high.text: The old sea wall, going east out of the village into open water. A yard of it shows; then the tide covers it. At low water, they say, you can walk it all the way to Blackcap.

low.text: Low water, and the old sea wall stands clear of the bay all the way east, a grey road of slabs with weed on it and the sea on both sides, to a black shape on the water that must be Blackcap.
low.again: The wall stands clear at low water.

book.text: Factor Thorne's day-book from the tide post, in a neat hand that never hurries: fish bought, salt sold, anchorage paid to the court. The back pages are ruled differently.

fuel.text: BLACKCAP — LINE ACCOUNT. A load a fortnight off the tank at Blackcap since the thaw, entered to the Line's fuel book at the Ninebridge floor at market. Beside it: HUM — PAID — ONE TANKER A MONTH, AT CONTRACT. And a third column, small, totalled at the foot of each page with a little flourish: SHRINKAGE.
fuel.again: Two loads a month off Blackcap, one paid to Hum. SHRINKAGE.

interject.text: "Shrinkage," Odile reads over your shoulder. "The guild's word for what falls off a cart between the field and the floor. On a crude line it means a leak. Cyprian costed the leak." She sounds almost admiring, and then she does not. "He priced it, and booked it, and a boy swam into it."

press.text: COLLECTIONS: names, debts, dates, a column headed GIVEN BY. Most of the shore is in it somewhere. Two winters back: IBARRA, M. — 300 — TAKEN AT THE GUT, NIGHT — GIVEN BY J. SOUSA — FINDER'S FEE: HIS BOAT (THE CURLEW) — LOT 4471, NINEBRIDGE. And under it, in the same unhurried hand: VESSEL SET ADRIFT OFF THE JESTY, COAT ABOARD. DEBT WRITTEN OFF TO THE WATER, PER LOCAL CUSTOM.
press.again: IBARRA, M. — GIVEN BY J. SOUSA — FINDER'S FEE: HIS BOAT.

interject.text: Wren reads it and does not say anything for a long time. "They wrote the debt off to the water," she says. "So the widow wouldn't owe it. Kind of them." Her burned hand is shaking and she puts it in her pocket.

text.text: "It's you." A nod from somebody mending a float. "Mind the boards by the Greta. Rotten since the spring."
They look at you, and then at the water, and go on with what they were doing.
"Mackerel came in clean this morning." Said as if it were the weather, which on the Stilts it is.
"Off the road?" Not unfriendly. "Mind your feet. The Gut's slippy when the tide's been over it."

a0.text: "Hassan's got a cabin under the old hull over the net store, twenty. Or the Greta's deck, if Oona doesn't catch you."
a0.again: "Hassan's got a cabin under the old hull over the net store, twenty. Or the Greta's deck, if Oona doesn't catch you."

a1.text: "The Rig." They spit. "Or it isn't, and everybody says it is because it's easier. Ask Oona; she's the one who writes it down."
a1.again: "The Rig." They spit. "Or it isn't, and everybody says it is because it's easier. Ask Oona; she's the one who writes it down."

a2.text: "Nobody. The Book. Oona, when the Book needs a mouth." A shrug. "And the guild, when it's buying."
a2.again: "Nobody. The Book. Oona, when the Book needs a mouth." A shrug. "And the guild, when it's buying."

intro.text: A grey man in the control room with his hand flat on a steel desk, feeling it the way a doctor feels a wrist. The whole room trembles faintly; he trembles with it and does not notice. "Hamid Farouk. I keep Hum." He looks you over for oil on your boots and finds it. "Nobody comes out to Hum to visit. You want lamp oil, tar, or work? Leila sells; I don't."
intro.again: Hamid keeps his hand on the desk.

interject.text: Kes has gone straight past him to the board, which is a wall of dials and switches older than anyone's grandmother. "Oh, you beauty," she says to it. "Pre-war production controller. Not networked. Dumb as a brick and twice as stubborn." Hamid looks at her with the first warmth you have seen in him. "She is," he says.
"A private platform," Nine says. "Never municipal. The record has nothing on it at all after R minus forty." Hamid: "Good."

options.text: A boy drowned at Gull Stilts in your oil. His mother has called the court on the Rigs.

text.text: Hamid at the board. The pressure needle stands where it stood in his father's day. "She's not tired," he says. "She never was."
Hamid in the mess with a mug of something, listening to the hull. "She sounds better at night," he says. "Everything does."
Hamid at the board, hand flat on the desk. "Yes?"

again.again: Hamid keeps his hand on the desk.

options.text: A boy drowned at Gull Stilts in your oil.
Your board reads the export line to Blackcap open.
There's a guild seal on your export valve, under the sea. TOLLMEN — LINE ACCOUNT.

mods.why: the crew speak well of you

options.text: Blackcap's line is sleeved. The tank could be half Hum's, half the Stilts', and the guild buys from your deck at the old price.

kai.text: Something goes over his face and is put away. "Not my oil." Flat. "My oil goes in my tanks, on my deck, and into the guild's tanker once a month. Hum's line to the shore was cut at the riser before I was born; my father cut it." He taps the desk. "The Stilts say the Rig because they've said the Rig for thirty years. When a gull dies, it's the Rig."
kai.again: "Not my oil. The line was cut before I was born."

hum.text: "Saltire Bravo, on the plates. Hum, since my grandfather climbed her leg with a knife in his teeth." He looks up at the ceiling as if he could see through it. "She burns the gas she lifts to lift the oil, and she has done it for ninety years, and if she ever stops she will not start again; there's no black-start left in her. So we don't let her stop. Forty people, lamp oil, rig diesel, tar, a tanker a month for the guild's Line." He shrugs. "Nothing grows out here. Everything we eat, we buy with her."
hum.again: "Don't let her stop. That's the whole of it."

line.text: "It reads open." He does not look at the dial. "It has read open since the thaw. The board's ninety years old; it reads what it likes." Then he does look. "Pressure's falling. Eleven points. She's tired, that's all. Things get tired." He says it like a man who has been saying it to himself every night.

seal.text: He goes still, in the way the platform never does. If you have the seal, you put it on his desk, and he picks it up and reads it and puts it down very carefully, as if it might go off. "Thorne asked for two tankers in the winter," he says. "I said she can't give two. He said nobody has to be unreasonable." The trembling desk; his hand flat on it. "So he went down my leg in the night and took the second one himself. Through the old line. Under the Stilts." He does the sum in his head and you watch it arrive. "Under the Stilts."

options.text: Stand up for Lua at the Stilt Court. With me.

seal_court.text: "On the Greta." He laughs, without any pleasure in it. "In front of the Stilts. They'll spit." He takes his hand off the desk for the first time since you came in. "I'll come on the launch. Tell the old woman to save me a bench at the back, by the guild."
seal_court.again: "Save me a bench. By the guild."

seal_shut.text: "The wheel's down the north-east leg, under the water, where the guild's diver turned it. Sun-hee can go down. You can go down; you've been." He looks at the pressure dial. "Shut it, and she gets her breath back, and the guild gets one tanker and screams. Leila's got some idea about a sleeve. Ask her. She's cleverer than me; she's told me so."

dive_yes.text: "Stump's hatch. Sun-hee runs it; she'll take your fare and your life in her hands, and she's better with the second." He goes back to the board.

dive_no.text: "Stump's for crew." Not unkind. "Strangers drown down there and we have to fish them out, and then the Stilts say the Rig."

terms.text: "Half a tank." He tries the idea on like a coat. "The Stilts holding half of Hum's oil. The Stilts, who spit when our launch comes in." He looks at the dial, steady now. "And the guild buying from my deck at the old price, one tanker, and not a drop more, and whatever's in Blackcap ours and theirs to sell in the city." A long breath. "Leila would stay. For that, Leila would stay."

options.text: Then shake on it, before the guild finds a way back in.

mods.why: he knows what the guild did
the sleeve is not fitted yet

decision.text: Blackcap's tank is Gull Stilts' and Hum's, half each, with its line sleeved and clean.

news.text: Gull Stilts and the Rigs' crew struck terms over the old tank at Blackcap: half each, and the guild buys at the old price

options.text: Then shake on it, before the guild finds a way back in.

mods.why: he knows what the guild did

terms_yes.text: He puts his hand out, and it is shaking a little, and that is the platform. "Half," he says. "Tell the old woman Hum's word is on her book. She knows what that's worth."

terms_no.text: "No." He turns back to the board. "The Stilts would sell their half to the guild by the spring, and then I'd have Thorne's seal on my own tank." He is probably wrong about the Stilts. He is not wrong about Thorne.

taking.text: Hamid at the board with every man and woman of his crew behind him in the control room and out on the deck, and through the window, coming across the bay from the Stilts, a line of boats. "The court says she's theirs," he says. "For the boy." He does not take his hand off the desk. "She's never floated in her life. Page three. Anything that floats and works." He laughs. "Forty people, and a turbine that'll never start again if it stops, and the Stilts can't keep a pump going on a fishing boat."
taking.again: The boats come on across the bay.

interject.text: Kes looks at the board, and then at you, and does not say what she is thinking, loudly.

options.text: Take your crew and go before they get here. The Line runs east from the city; there's work at the Skirts.

mods.why: the crew speak well of you
Leila has wanted to go for years
he knows it was the guild, and you let the court say Hum

decision.text: Hamid Farouk took Hum's crew off the platform before the Stilts' boats came; Hum is Gull Stilts' now.

news.text: the Rigs' crew left Hum to Gull Stilts without a fight and went up the delta for the Line

stays.text: "No." He says it to the board. "My father kept her forty years. I've kept her twenty-two. The Stilts can come and take her off me." Behind him somebody racks a shotgun. The boats are close enough now to hear the oars.
stays.again: The boats are close enough to hear the oars.

options.text: (Then the Stilts will take her. Stand with them.)

decision.text: You went onto Hum with the Stilts' boats when Hamid Farouk would not give her up.

gone.text: He looks at the board for a long time. Then he takes his hand off the desk. "Leila," he says, not loudly, and she is already there. He goes out to the launch with forty people behind him and a bag each, and he does not look back at Hum, and Hum hums. The Stilts' boats come alongside an hour later and their men climb up her legs, and somebody finds the chalk on the turbine and reads it out loud: DON'T LET HER STOP. Nobody laughs.

intro.text: A young woman in the turbine hall with ear defenders round her neck and a wrench in her back pocket, reading a gauge with her nose almost on the glass. She shouts over the noise without turning: "Leila Farouk. Engineer. If you want to buy, I sell; if you want to talk, outside." Outside, on the deck, she pulls the defenders off and her ears ring in the quiet. "Pressure's down eleven since the thaw," she says, as if you had asked. "Hum isn't tired. My father says she's tired. Something's drinking."
intro.again: Leila wipes the gauge glass with her thumb.

options.text: What do you want, out here?

again.text: Leila on the deck with the defenders round her neck. "What?"
again.again: Leila waits.

options.text: What do you want, out here?
If the old line to Blackcap stays open, could it be made not to leak?

drinking.text: "The export line reads open. Father says the board lies." She shrugs. "The board doesn't lie, it's too stupid to lie. If the line's open, Hum's oil is going down it under the Stilts to that tank at Blackcap, and the line was laid ninety years ago and every joint on it's rotten." She looks east. "So some of it's getting to Blackcap. And some of it isn't."
drinking.again: "Some of it's getting to Blackcap. Some of it isn't."

you.text: "A city." She says it without any shame. "Streets you can walk on that don't move. A room that isn't a container. I hear the Precinct has a library you can sit in all day." She looks at the turbine house. "I'd stay if Hum had a future that wasn't one tanker a month for the guild until she stops. She hasn't."
you.again: "A city. Or a future for Hum. One or the other."

sleeve.text: She grins for the first time. "I've had it made since the thaw. Nobody asked." She goes into a container and comes out with a split steel sleeve, its bolts in a bag, gaskets cut from a tyre and a tin of Hum's own pitch. "At the valve, round the riser where the old joint's weakest. Takes the strain off the line so it runs clean all the way. Then Blackcap's a real tank, for whoever holds it." She hands it over. "It's a two-hand job under water. Somebody with good hands."

interject.text: "Obviously that works," Kes says, turning the sleeve over. "Obviously nobody's done it. That's the whole history of the world, that sentence."

intro.text: An old man in the lamp room on Lean's derrick with a bottle he hides badly behind a coil of hose. The lamp burns behind him, a great lens with a gas flame in it, and the whole listing room is gold. "Tulloch. Ewan. The light." He gestures at it as if introducing a wife. "Lit every night for thirty-one years. Mostly." He looks at you sideways. "You're not the guild, are you? You don't smell like the guild."
intro.again: Ewan keeps the bottle behind the hose.

again.text: Ewan in the gold of the lamp room. "Back. Have you a drop? No? No."
again.again: Ewan waits.

light.text: "Brings the Stilts' boats home in fog. They steer on her from the west and she puts them in the channel past the Jesty, safe." He pats the lens's brass. "If she's dark, you steer on the Stilts' own lamps, and the Stilts' lamps are behind the Jesty from the west. Then you're on the roof." He shakes his head. "Then you're on the roof."
light.again: "If she's dark, you're on the roof."

mostly.text: "Five nights since the thaw she's been dark. Foggy nights, every one. Gas line cut." He holds up the end of a hose. The cut is clean and square. "Cut. I know perished, and that isn't perished. Somebody comes up Lean's leg in the fog with a knife and cuts my line, and in the morning I splice it, and nobody believes me because I'm Ewan." He drinks, not hiding it now. "The guild's factor came out and asked me about it. Asked me very nicely. I didn't like how nicely."

interject.text: Ilya takes the cut end from him and turns it to the lamp. "Knife. Right-handed. Sharp." He gives it back. "He's not lying."

intro.text: A small woman in a cut-down survival suit on Stump's grate, wringing out a hood. "Sun-hee. I dive for Hum." She looks at your chest, judging your lungs, and does not say what she thinks. "Stump goes down sixty feet and then it goes down some more. If Hamid says you can, I'll take you. Ten Tolls and you do exactly what I say."
intro.again: Sun-hee wrings out her hood.

options.text: Have you seen anyone at Hum's legs who shouldn't be?

again.again: Sun-hee waits.

options.text: Have you seen anyone at Hum's legs who shouldn't be?

night.text: She stops wringing. "Ninety-odd nights back. A boat at the north-east leg with no lamps, low in the water, and bubbles in the moonpool that weren't ours. Two hours, then gone." She looks across at the control room. "I told Hamid. Hamid didn't want told. The guild's tanker is how we eat."
night.again: "No lamps. Bubbles that weren't ours. Hamid didn't want told."

options.text: Will you say that at the Stilt Court?

mods.why: Hamid knows now

court_yes.text: "On the Greta." She considers the Stilts on the horizon. "They'll hate it. Good." She goes back to the hood.

court_no.text: "And have Hamid lose the tanker?" She shakes her head. "Not on your word. Show me something."

board.text: Hum's board: a wall of dials and switches behind glass gone yellow, a mimic panel of the platform in enamel with little lamps where the wells and pumps are. Most of the lamps are dark. A row near the bottom still lights: TURBINE B — RUN. LIFT PUMPS 1, 2 — RUN. And on the line that leaves the platform's outline and runs off the panel's edge toward the shore: EXPORT — OPEN, with a pressure dial beside it whose needle has a pencil mark under it from some better year.
board.again: EXPORT — OPEN, and the needle under the pencil mark.

interject.text: Kes has the panel's side cover off before anyone can stop her and is reading a strip of paper that comes out of it on a spool, inch by inch. "Event log. It prints." She taps a line. "EXPORT VALVE — MANUAL — OPEN. Ninety-four days. Not the controller. Somebody's hands, down there." She looks at you. "This thing's too stupid to lie."

options.text: (Read the pressure log in the drawer.)

log.text: A ledger in two hands, father and daughter, a line a day: EXPORT PRESS. — and a number. Steady for years. Then from the thaw, falling every week, a point here, a point there, eleven in all. Beside the latest entry, in the father's hand: TIRED. Beside it, in the daughter's: DRINKING.
log.again: The log: eleven points since the thaw.

printer.text: Behind a side cover, a printer older than anyone's grandmother still feeding a strip of paper an inch at a time. You run it back. EXPORT VALVE — MANUAL — OPEN. Ninety-four days ago, at night. Not the controller: somebody's hands, down there, on the wheel.

printer_fail.text: There must be a log somewhere; boards like this kept one. You do not find it.
printer_fail.again: Somewhere in the board, a log you cannot find.

hatch.text: A hatch in the grate over the north-east leg, a yard across, with a ladder going down into a steel well and the sound of the sea breathing at the bottom of it. Cold comes up out of it like a hand. A board on the hatch rim, in old stencil: MOONPOOL — DIVERS ONLY — LINE AND LAMP.

options.text: (Go down on a line and a held breath.)

mods.why: your lungs

down.text: Down the ladder into the cold.

cold.text: Ten rungs down the cold takes the breath out of you like a fist, and you are back on the grate before you decide to be, gasping. Sun-hee, passing, says without stopping: "Bag. Or better lungs."

text.text: The Stilts' boat at Hum's landing stage now, with a Stilts boy at the tiller who looks as if he cannot believe where he is.
Hum's launch at the landing stage: a steel lifeboat from before the Burn with its canopy cut off, running on Hum's own diesel. A crewman at the tiller.

options.text: (Wait for the tide boat to the city: by the Stilts to Carrick's water stairs. 12 Tolls)

lamp.text: Lean's lamp: a lighthouse lens the size of a man, salvaged from somewhere and hauled up the dead derrick, with a gas flame in it fed by a hose of Hum's gas that comes across the catwalk in a sling. A spliced joint in the hose, fresh tape over old.
lamp.again: The lamp and its spliced hose.

passives.text: The hose has been spliced in five places in the last few months, each one at the same reach from the deck, each one a clean square cut. Not perished. Cut.

crew.text: Stump's deep hatch: a square of black water inside the leg-tops, with a winch over it and a stencil: CREW ONLY. Sun-hee looks up from her hood. "Hamid says who goes down Stump. Ask him."

tide.text: Stump's hatch, and the water in it moving, sucking at the leg-tops. "Not on this tide," Sun-hee says. "Slack, or never."

gone.text: Stump's hatch, with nobody at the winch. Whoever dives Hum's legs now, it is not anyone who knows them.

hatch.text: Sun-hee at the winch over Stump's black square, with a lamp on a line. "Down the leg-tops to the old pump deck at thirty feet, then the control room at sixty. Boards, cells, and if you're lucky a controller nobody's pulled. Ten Tolls. You come up when I pull."
