text.text: Down through black water lit by Sun-hee's lamp, past ninety years of mussels on the legs, to a pump deck where the sea has kept everything exactly as the last crew left it. A rack of boards in a sealed cabinet, and a cell still in its wrapper. You come up shaking with cold and with something else.

Down to sixty feet, to the control room the platform's builders put underwater on purpose, and in its sealed rack, one controller still in its potting, pins bright. Sun-hee looks at it in your hand on the grate and says nothing for a long time. "That's a rifle," she says. "That's two rifles. Don't tell the guild you have it."

Down to the control room again, into a cabinet you had not tried, and in it a cash box some pre-war engineer kept his card money in, and two cells, and two boards. Sun-hee pulls before you are ready and you come up whether you like it or not.
Down Stump's legs. Hum's crew have been diving these for thirty years; you find what they left, which is not much. A board.

legs_up.again: You sit on Stump's grate, shaking.

legs_fail.text: At forty feet the black closes in and the pressure is a hand on your head, and you lose the line, and then Sun-hee is hauling and you are coming up whether you want to or not. On the grate she holds your head and says, very calmly, "Next slack. Or never. Your choice."

l.text: The moonpool ladder going up into the hum and the light.

text.text: The gauges in the pump room's air pocket, dripping. EXPORT FLOW — nothing. The needle lies against its pin.
The gauges in the pump room's air pocket, dripping. EXPORT FLOW, and a needle trembling well off its pin: Hum's oil going out along the sea bed toward the shore, steady, the way a vein goes.

The export valve, and its wheel turned open again, all the way, its spindle bright. Through the rim a second twist of wire, newer than the first you cut: TOLLMEN — LINE ACCOUNT. The guild's diver came back.

The export valve: a manifold rising out of the floor of the leg in the waist-deep black water, and a wheel on it as wide as your arms, its spindle bright where it has been turned. Round the wheel's rim, through a hole drilled for it, a twist of wire and a lead seal, new and dull: TOLLMEN — LINE ACCOUNT. The guild seals what it means to bill.

valve.again: The wheel, and the guild's seal on it.

interject.text: Odile reads the seal by your lamp and laughs, short and not happy. "LINE ACCOUNT. That's the Line's fuel book on the Ninebridge floor. My dear, they've billed the railway for this man's oil." She touches the lead. "Cyprian always did like a spread."
"A municipal valve would have a register number," Nine says, its lens close to the seal. "This has an account." It sounds as if that were the worse of the two.

Wren, waist-deep and miserable in the black water, looks at the seal and then at the wheel's bright spindle. "Turned at night. From a boat. Somebody who knew where." She does not like the sea, but she can read a track in it.

options.text: (Cut the seal off and keep it.)

mods.why: your back

decision.text: You shut Hum's export valve under the sea. Nothing goes down the old line to Blackcap now.

news.text: somebody went down Hum's leg and shut the old export line to Blackcap

options.text: (Fit Leila's sleeve round the riser, and leave the line open to run clean.)

mods.why: Kes holds the bolts
your own air

decision.text: You fitted Leila Farouk's sleeve on Hum's export riser: the old line runs clean to Blackcap now, and the tank fills without a leak.

news.text: Hum's old line to Blackcap was sleeved under the sea and runs clean

sealed.text: Your knife through the wire, and the seal comes away in your glove: a disc of lead the size of a coin, the guild's neat letters pressed into it. You put it somewhere dry.
sealed.again: The seal is in your pack.

shut.text: You get your shoulder under the rim and turn it. It fights you for the first quarter, and then the gear catches, and you turn it until you cannot turn it any more. Somewhere in the steel round you something changes note. The needle on the pump room's gauge lies down against its pin. Out under the Stilts, a long way off, the old line stops breathing.

stuck.text: You get your shoulder under the rim and heave, and the wheel does not move, and your feet go out from under you in the black water. You come up spitting oil. The wheel has not moved a hair.

sleeved.text: It takes an hour in the black water by lamp, bolt by bolt, gasket by gasket, the pitch tin warm in your hand from the leg's own heat. When the last bolt is home, the riser stops weeping. The needle on the pump room's gauge comes up, a little, and stays up. The line runs clean to Blackcap now: whoever holds that tank holds Hum's oil, without a drop under the Stilts.

sleeve_fail.text: Under the black water the sleeve's halves will not meet, and a bolt goes out of your fingers into the dark and is gone. You come up for air and look at what is left. Not this time.
sleeve_fail.again: The sleeve's halves, and a bolt short.

text.text: The export wheel, turned shut, the water round it going slowly clear.
The export riser with Leila's sleeve bolted round it, tight and dry, and the line beyond it running clean.

h.text: A pump on the tank's north rim, new as nothing on the shore is new: steel hose with brass couplings, clamps that still shine, a guild padlock on the drive, and the guild's mark stencilled on the housing over a number. The hose goes over the rim and down into the black.
h.again: The guild's pump on the rim.

passives.text: On the water on the tank's west side, a line of bubbles comes up every few seconds, out of the bottom, going west toward the Stilts and the Rigs. Something under the bay is carrying something into this tank and breathing out as it goes.

text.text: The tank's roof hatch. The oil inside stands a long way down now, and falling: the guild's pump drawing, and nothing coming in.
The tank's roof hatch, a square of steel on a hinge. Lift it and the smell comes up like a blow: the oil inside stands a hand under the roof, full to the brim, warm.

day.text: The guild's barge at Blackcap's jetty: a steel tank barge, low and broad, with the guild's colours under the rust and a hose coiled on deck. One man on watch with a revolver, bored. At night, they say on the Stilts, she loads.

night.text: The barge at night with no lamps, low in the water and getting lower, the guild's pump on the tank's rim chugging softly and the hose across the jetty to her deck. Three men on her. A big man with a shotgun on the deck-house roof watches you come along the jetty and does not move.
night.again: The barge loads in the dark.

interject.text: Ilya, very low: "Three. Shotgun on the roof, revolver by the hose, the third's got a knife and no stomach for it." He counts again. "Right."

decision.text: You came at the guild's night barge at Blackcap.

after.text: The barge at Blackcap's jetty with nobody alive on her deck, the hose still running, the tank's oil going into her belly in the dark. She is low enough now that a match would do.

decision.text: You burned the guild's night barge at Blackcap with her load in her.

news.text: the guild's night barge at Blackcap burned to the waterline with a load of crude in her

burning.text: She goes up slowly and then all at once, a column of black smoke with fire at its root that the Stilts will see from every boardwalk and Hum from its flare stack. The jetty's boards catch at the end and you get off them. By dawn there is a black hull on the bottom by the tank with the sea in it, and an oil fire on the water that burns itself out on its own.

burned.text: At the jetty's end, a black hull settled on the bottom with the sea in her, and a ring of scorched boards.

gone.text: An empty mooring at Blackcap's jetty where the guild's barge used to load.

off.text: The big man on the deck-house roof, with a shotgun across his knees and his face shaved to the skull. "Silas Venn. Bargemaster. Guild's business." He does not get up. "No lamps on the water. You didn't see a barge. Off my jetty."

options.text: Twenty Tolls to look at your manifest.

load.text: "The guild's." He says it without interest. "Two loads a fortnight off this tank, entered at Ninebridge. Who's counting?" He settles the shotgun. "Not you."

bribed.text: He considers the money and the dark and the long way to the next man who might care. Then he takes the twenty and tosses you a sheaf of paper from inside the deck-house without getting up. "Copy. Keep it dry. You never saw it."

no.text: "Off my jetty," he says again, exactly as before, and keeps your twenty.

intro.text: A diver in a guild jersey with salt in his stubble and a bottle he is not drinking from. "Zielinski. Marek." He does not look at you; he looks at the water. "I dive for whoever pays. That's diving." Then, before you ask: "Don't talk to me about the boy."
intro.again: Marek looks at the water.

again.text: Marek with his bottle, looking at the water.
again.again: Marek turns the bottle in his hands.

options.text: You went down Hum's leg at night and turned the export wheel open. And sealed it.

mods.why: the seal he pressed, in your hand
a child's net with the joint in it
Wren reads him like a road

boy.text: "I said don't." He drinks, finally. "I knew about the joints. Everybody who's been down that line knows about the joints. I didn't know a boy would be stupid enough to go under the Gut in black water for a net." He stops. "That's not what I meant. That's what I said, but it's not what I meant."

confess.text: He looks at the thing in your hand, or at nothing, for a long time. "On the factor's word. At night, off the barge, down the moonpool on a line. I turned it a long way." He puts the bottle down. "If the old woman calls me, I'll stand up. Not for the guild. Not for you." He does not say who for.
confess.again: "If she calls me, I'll stand up."

shut.text: "I dive for whoever pays," he says again, and turns his back.

said.text: Marek, sober, looking at the water. "I said I'd stand up. I will."

n.text: "Guild barge. Keep off." He has the look of a man who has been told to say exactly that and nothing else, and is relieved to have been told.

high.text: The old sea wall going west into the water toward the Stilts. The tide is over it; only the posts show. The skiff at the jetty, if you can row.

low.text: Low water, and the sea wall stands clear going west, a grey road of slabs to the Stilts' posts on the horizon.

options.text: (Walk the wall back to Gull Stilts.)

s.text: A skiff tied at the jetty with a pair of oars in her and a painted board nailed to her thwart: BORROW HER, BRING HER BACK — M. TUI.

text.text: "You again." A crewman with tar to the elbows nods at you as if you were nearly crew. "Don't let her stop."
A crewman looks at you and then at the Stilts on the horizon, and spits in the sea.
"Off the boat?" A crewman with tar to the elbows. "Mind the steam line. Mind the gas line. Mind everything; it all bites."

options.text: What do you do out here?
What do you think of the Stilts?

a0.text: "Cook her oil. Lamp oil off the top of the still, rig diesel off the middle, tar off the bottom for the Stilts' hulls." A shrug. "Keep the turbine fed. Don't let her stop. That's the job."
a0.again: "Don't let her stop. That's the job."

a1.text: "They buy our tar and spit when the launch comes in. We buy their fish and complain it tastes of us." A grin with gaps in it. "My mother was a Stilts girl. Don't tell anyone."

hi.text: An old woman on the dike's edge in waders to her chest, hauling a wicker trap up out of the reeds hand over hand, with a fire going on the dike behind her and a pot on it. Eels in the trap, knotting. "Winona Crabbe. Eels." She looks you over. "You've walked from the city. You've the look. Sit, if you want; the pot's for anybody who doesn't steal the trap."

options.text: What's the news on the water?

news.text: "The eels taste of the Rig up as far as the third channel now. Never used to past the Stilts." She guts one with her thumb. "And a guild barge goes down past here three nights in four with no lamps, low in the water, toward the city's far bank. Doesn't wave." She flings the gut to a gull. "I wave at everybody."

sit.text: You sit on the dike by her fire with the reeds hissing on both sides and the sea a grey line to the west, and she gives you an eel off the pot and tells you, unasked, about every person she has ever buried, by the place on the dike where she buried them. It is a long dike.

stop.text: Two men in the guild's colours on the dike road with a boy of fifteen between them on a rope, his wrists tied in front and a sack over one of the men's shoulders that you understand, after a moment, is meant for his head. The older one holds up a paper without letting go of it. "Guild paper. A debt collected, for the barges. Stand aside, friend, and nobody has to be unreasonable."

interject.text: Wren has stopped walking. Her burned hand has gone to the knife at her back and she has taken it away again, deliberately. "Look at me," she says to you, quietly, "and tell me we're walking past."

options.text: What's the paper for? I'll buy it. (40 Tolls)

decision.text: You bought a Sink boy's paper off the guild's press on the dike road and sent him to Gull Stilts.

options.text: That paper's in his mother's name. It doesn't bind him. Show me his mark on it.

mods.why: Odile reads the paper over your shoulder
Wren knows the block's paper

decision.text: You talked the guild's press off a Sink boy on the dike road: the paper was his mother's.
You cut a Sink boy loose from the guild's press on the dike road.

boy.text: The boy looks at you as if you might be another one of them. "My mam's," he says. "Not mine. She owes the post at the Sink for medicine. They came for her and she was sick, so." He shrugs, and the rope pulls. "Ishmael," he says, though you did not ask, as if somebody ought to know.

bought.text: The older man counts it twice and hands you the paper and cuts the rope himself, with a care that is almost courtesy. "The guild's obliged." To the boy: "You're lucky." The boy does not look lucky; he looks at you. "Gull Stilts," you tell him. "Down the dike. Ask for Paz at the Netlofts." He goes, running, then walking, then running.

talked.text: The younger one looks at the paper again, properly this time, and then at the older one, and the older one swears softly and folds it away. "Mother's name," he says. "Should've been the mother." He cuts the rope. The boy stands there rubbing his wrists until you tell him: Gull Stilts, down the dike, ask for Paz at the Netlofts. He goes.

no.text: "His mark's his mother's mark. That's debt." The older man puts the paper away. "Stand aside."

decision.text: You bought a Sink boy's paper off the guild's press on the dike road and sent him to Gull Stilts.
You cut a Sink boy loose from the guild's press on the dike road.

walked.text: You stand aside. They go past you along the dike toward the city, the boy between them, and at the bend the older one puts the sack over his head, gently, like a man putting a hood on a falcon.

read.text: Chalk on the Wall's foot where the rubble road turns south along it: an arrow, and DOCKS — CARRICK — NO BRIDGE — THIS WAY ROUND. Under it somebody has drawn a crane, carefully, the way a child draws a horse, and a box hanging from it.
read.again: DOCKS — CARRICK — THIS WAY ROUND, and the careful crane.

read.text: Chalk on a bollard where the river road comes down off the Wall's shoulder: GATE ↑ 1 HR — PAPERS. Under it: CLOVER BY THE QUAY TRAM. And under that, small, in a child's hand: KOBBY'S ROPE AT NIGHT.
read.again: GATE ↑ 1 HR — PAPERS. CLOVER BY THE QUAY TRAM. KOBBY'S ROPE AT NIGHT.

through.speaker: npc_dk_12
through.text: "The through doesn't sell tickets." Femi nods down the shed, where a second road runs straight past the platform and out through the far end into a fenced cut toward the Bond. "Comes in at the throat at two in the morning, nineteen cars sealed, goes into the Bond without stopping, comes out empty or not and goes back east at four. Nobody gets a look." He shrugs. "Nobody weighs it, either. That's not my department. That's Hruska's, and it isn't his."
through.again: "Nobody gets a look. Nobody weighs it."

text.text: You wait on the platform for the seven o'clock. It comes in under its own smoke: Sixty, square-nosed and plated, pulling a pre-war coach with steel riveted over its windows to the height of a seated man, so that you look out over a rim of plate at the country going by. The guard punches your card and sits down opposite with a carbine across his knees. For the first hour you watch the land go past at the speed of a fast cart the way you would watch someone sleeping. Then, somewhere, you sleep too, and wake to West Halt.

The seven o'clock, and at every halt the train stops for a pilot in faded orange who climbs into the cab with a red flag rolled under his arm, rides the section and gets down at the next, while the halt sells water on the platform and somebody sells bread through the coach's slots. West Halt.
The seven o'clock: the coach, the plate at the windows, the guard and his carbine, the country going by at the speed of a cart. West Halt.

interject.text: Tamsin has her face to the slot over the plate the whole way. "It's moving and nobody's pushing it," she says, three times, and then, without looking round: "Don't tell anyone I said that."
"Two cars, one key," Wren says, watching the ditch go by. "Somebody knew which ones. That's not robbing. That's shopping."
"The token for each section is drawn at its end and surrendered at the next," Nine says, watching the signals. "A system with no memory but the register. I admire it."

At Kettle Cut the train slows for the curve, and in the ditch under the window two cars lie on their sides, opened like tins. The guard watches them go by and says nothing at all. Four Ways.

The seven o'clock: the coach, the plate at the windows, the guard and his carbine, the country going by at the speed of a cart. At Kettle Cut the train slows for the curve, and in the ditch under the window two cars lie on their sides, opened like tins. The guard watches them go by and says nothing at all. Four Ways.

interject.text: Tamsin has her face to the slot over the plate the whole way. "It's moving and nobody's pushing it," she says, three times, and then, without looking round: "Don't tell anyone I said that."
"Two cars, one key," Wren says, watching the ditch go by. "Somebody knew which ones. That's not robbing. That's shopping."
"The token for each section is drawn at its end and surrendered at the next," Nine says, watching the signals. "A system with no memory but the register. I admire it."

text.text: You wait on the platform for the seven o'clock. It comes in under its own smoke: Sixty, square-nosed and plated, pulling a pre-war coach with steel riveted over its windows to the height of a seated man, so that you look out over a rim of plate at the country going by. The guard punches your card and sits down opposite with a carbine across his knees. For the first hour you watch the land go past at the speed of a fast cart the way you would watch someone sleeping. text.text: The window cut into the shed's brick at the Line's end. Femi Adebayo looks at your pass, and at you, and punches nothing. "All sections. Seven o'clock, east."
The window in the shed's brick. "Thirty a leg." Femi taps a card pinned to the grille: KETTLE LEVY — BY ORDER OF THE GUILD. "Don't look at me. I've never seen Kettle."

The window in the shed's brick, and two of the guild's riders on the platform behind you with carbines, watching who buys. "Seven o'clock, east," Femi says. "Twenty-five a leg. They're on every train now. Smile for the card."

A ticket window cut into the brick of the freight shed at the very end of the Line, with a grille and a young man behind it with a card punch and a pencil, who draws your face on a toll card in four quick lines before you have said where you are going. "The Line, east. Seven o'clock. Twenty-five a leg; the guild sets it, not me."
The window in the shed's brick. "Seven o'clock, east," Femi says. "Twenty-five a leg."

board.again: Femi Adebayo, behind the grille, with the punch.

options.text: (West Halt, one leg. 30 Tolls, with the Kettle levy.)
(Yard Nine, 2 legs. 60 Tolls, with the Kettle levy.)
(Four Ways, 3 legs. 90 Tolls, with the Kettle levy.)
(East Halt, 4 legs. 120 Tolls, with the Kettle levy.)
(Two-Twelve, 5 legs. 150 Tolls, with the Kettle levy.)
(Look at the map of the Line.)

text.text: The tide boat at the water stairs, flat and tarred, with salt sacks and a crate of smoked fish coming off it hand to hand, and Mele Tui at the tiller watching the water before she watches you. "Down the delta on the ebb at five," she says. "Stilts, six. Rigs, twelve. Mind your hands on the gunwale."

The water stairs: worn granite down into the Basin, green to the third step, iron rings in the wall for boats. A slate on the ring post, chalked: TIDE BOAT — IN ON THE FLOOD — DOWN THE DELTA AT 5 — STILTS 6 — RIGS 12 — M.T.

stairs.again: The water stairs, and the slate on the ring post: DOWN THE DELTA AT 5.

interject.text: Tamsin sits on the top step and watches a crate of fish go up the stairs and a sack of salt come down. "Everything in the Reach ends up here," she says. "Fish, oil, copper, people. It's a drain with cranes."

options.text: (Down the delta to Gull Stilts. 6 Tolls)
(Down the delta and out to the Rigs. 12 Tolls)

stop.text: THE QUAY — CARRICK. A single tram car off the Loop's old Docks line, its trolley pole bent up to a wire that still carries something, and a board with one name on it: CLOVER 2. The far bank's half of the Loop, running north round the ring road and over the old ring bridge to the Loop's last halt, outside the Wall.

interject.text: "The Loop's Docks branch," Nine says. "Its far half. The drawings show a single line from Clover over the ring bridge to this terminus; the bridge at Bridgeward carried the other half, with a tram on it, the day it fell." The lens clicks. "The timetable for that tram is still in the record. It is very punctual."

day.text: Crane One, dead on the bank above the river wall, its jib out over the dry bed like an arm held out for balance. From the jib's end a cable runs out into the air over the Hulls, sagging, to the torn end of Bridgeward's bridge on the far bank. At the crane's foot a winch with a drum of cable as thick as a wrist, and a steel basket chained to the bank. By day it does not move.
day.again: Crane One's jib, the cable to Bridgeward's drop, the basket chained.

night.text: Night, and the cradle working: the winch's brake squealing, a lamp on the basket going away over the bed toward Bridgeward with two people crouched in it, and Kobby Ofori at the drum with his sleeves rolled. "Over?" he says. "Five. Sit in the middle and don't look down; there's nothing to see but the bed."
night.again: The winch, the lamp going out over the bed, Kobby at the brake. "Over?"

interject.text: Ilya climbs into the basket last and holds the rim with both hands. "I've been shot at from further than this," he says. "I've never hung."

options.text: (Ride the basket over the dry river to Bridgeward's drop. 5 Tolls)

cut.text: Crane One, dead on the bank, its jib bare. The cradle's cable has been cut at the drum and lies in coils on the bed below, already half buried in silt, and the winch is padlocked under the guild's seal.
cut.again: The bare jib, the cut cable in the silt.

text.text: Sixty under the shed, drinking from the water column, and the through's road beside her empty: no through has come in since the wreck east of East Halt, and the Bond's yard is half dark. The dockers on the platform are playing cards on a crate.

Sixty under the shed, drinking from the water column, and on her footplate a pilot in faded orange with a red flag rolled under his arm, drinking tea out of the driver's can: the halts' men ride every section now, even the last.

Sixty under the shed, drinking from the water column, with two of the guild's riders on her step and a third walking the platform, looking at faces. The guild holds the Line end to end, and it wants you to see it holding.

Sixty under the shed: square-nosed, plated, steaming gently at the buffer stop with the water column swung over her tank and a fireman on her roof with a hose. The Line's last ten feet of rail, and a lamp on the buffer that is lit day and night.

read.again: Sixty at the buffer, drinking.

text.text: GUILD FLOOR — CARRICK — FREIGHT BY THE TON — DUES BY THE BERTH. The Concern's notice is gone; four drawing pins hold a square of cleaner paint where it was.

Notices on the guild floor's door: GUILD FLOOR — CARRICK — FREIGHT BY THE TON — DUES BY THE BERTH — THEFT FROM THE QUAY: THE HOOK. And pinned over the guild's, in the Concern's clean type on clean card: RETURNABLE LOST FROM BOND — ONE — REWARD 60 — APPLY THE BOND OFFICER. Somebody has written under it in chalk, small: IT WASHES POTS.

read.again: FREIGHT BY THE TON. RETURNABLE LOST FROM BOND — ONE — REWARD 60.

read.text: THE BOND — CONCERN — UNDER SEAL. Below it, in smaller letters cut into a steel plate as if somebody expected to be argued with: BONDED PREMISES UNDER THE HARBOUR ACT, s. 19. THE HARBOUR MASTER'S AUTHORITY DOES NOT EXTEND WITHIN. The lights on the fence posts are on at noon.
read.again: THE BOND — UNDER SEAL — s. 19. The lights on at noon.

read.text: HARBOUR NOTICE — THE RIVER BERTHS — LEASED TO HOUSE VANE FOR WORKS UNDER THE ACT, s. 41 — OCCUPIERS TO QUIT ON COMMENCEMENT — H. DAHL, HARBOUR MASTER. Somebody has chalked under it, in capitals that go downhill: WE ARE NOT OCCUPIERS WE ARE CREW.
read.again: LEASED TO HOUSE VANE. WE ARE NOT OCCUPIERS WE ARE CREW.

text.text: Crane Two, Constance's, with a strip of red cloth tied to the cab's rail that nobody has taken down since the morning on the Stand.

Crane Two: the other crane on the quay that still works, older than Six and slower, its cab windows patched with tin. CONNIE painted on the counterweight in letters a yard high, and under it, smaller, older: NO BOX DOWN — 22 YEARS.

read.again: Crane Two, and NO BOX DOWN on the counterweight.

text.text: The barge goes at six, flat-bottomed and black with tar, a deckhouse aft and the cargo under tarps, and you sit on a coil of rope and go up the river behind the guild's tug, an old diesel launch that burns the Rigs' oil and coughs it out black, towing three barges on a cable like a string of beads. Everything is wet. Nothing is in a hurry. Herons stand in the shallows and watch you go by as if they had seen barges before and expected better. At Ashby the barges go one at a time into the lock's grey chamber, and the gates close behind, and the water lifts you up between the walls until the Water lies level and grey ahead, while a young woman with red hair walks along the top with a key on a cord and calls the marks. Sawtown.

The barge at six, full-loaded and low in the water, up the river behind the guild's tug, an old diesel launch that burns the Rigs' oil and coughs it out black, towing three barges on a cable like a string of beads, on a river that runs high and steady between its banks. "It's all going somewhere," she says at last. "All of it. On its own. Nobody pumping." She rolls over. "Rust it, I want one."
"A road that moves," Wren says, watching the bank. "Leaves no tracks either." She almost smiles. "I could get used to it."
Ilya counts the bends aloud, under his breath, and then the herons, and then stops counting anything and sleeps sitting up with his rifle across his knees.

sweeps.speaker: narrator
sweeps.text: The bargemaster looks at your arms. "Sweeps take two and the river takes everybody. A turn on the oars and you ride free, if you can keep a stroke."

sweeps_ok.speaker: narrator
sweeps_ok.text: "Good enough." He spits over the side. "Next six o'clock, either way. You're on the bow sweep."

sweeps_no.speaker: narrator
sweeps_no.text: You catch a crab on the first stroke and go over backwards into the cargo. "Pay the fare," he says, not unkindly. "The river's safer with you sitting down."

text.text: The barge quay: timber staging along the Basin's edge where the Wet's barges tie up, black with tar and white with gull. A long flat barge lies against it with timber stacked on her deck and a family living under a tarp at her stern. A slate on a post: THE BARGES — LOW LANDING — ASHBY — SAWTOWN — UP AT SIX — 10 A REACH — ASK ABOARD.

board.again: The barge quay. UP AT SIX — 10 A REACH.

options.text: (Low Landing, one reach up. No fare.)
(Look at the map of the river.)

read.text: GRIGOR'S STEPS — MULLET — LINES AT DAWN 2 — BRING THEM BACK. A painted fish beside it, smiling, which nobody who has eaten a Basin mullet would do.
read.again: GRIGOR'S STEPS — LINES AT DAWN 2.

text.text: The fuel berth: a tank on the quay stencilled LINE ACCOUNT in the guild's neat letters, and a gauge on its side reading a quarter. The night barge from the delta that used to fill it does not come any more. The guild's men have started buying Hum's diesel off the tide boat, a drum at a time, at Hum's price.
The fuel berth: a tank on the quay stencilled LINE ACCOUNT, and alongside it the Rigs' own launch, low in the water, pumping across a hose with HUM painted on it, at a price somebody on Hum set.

The fuel berth: a tank on the quay stencilled LINE ACCOUNT in the guild's neat letters, a hose coiled on the staging, and a slick on the water round it, purple and gold. The night barge from the delta ties up here with no lamps, every few nights, and nobody on the quay is awake to see it.

read.again: The tank, LINE ACCOUNT.

read.text: THE HARBOUR ACT, framed under glass on the long room's wall, its pages pinned open side by side and gone the colour of tea. Section 19: BONDED PREMISES — the Harbour Master's authority does not extend within. Section 41: IDLE BERTHS — may be leased by the concession for works. Schedule 2, GOODS: cargo, livestock, mails, ship's stores, ballast. Schedule 3, VESSELS IN PORT: a vessel in port shall not be moved, broken or removed while she has a crew aboard, save by her master's leave or the court's order on proof of abandonment.
read.again: The Act under glass: s. 19, s. 41, Schedules 2 and 3.

interject.text: "Schedule 2 has no persons in it," Nine says, reading with its lens almost on the glass. "Schedule 3 has no definition of a vessel's being afloat." It reads both again. "The drafters were thorough about everything except the future. That is the usual way."

text.text: The box Six dropped, empty now: the copper went over the weighbridge in barrows, bar by bar, with the whole quay watching the needle. The dockers have started using it as a windbreak.
The box Six dropped, emptied by the Bond's men in the night and left where it fell. The stain where the tarp was is being worn out of the concrete by boots.

A forty-foot box on its side, the closed eye on its doors and the Concern's seal whole on its wire. Stencilled on the end: MACHINE PARTS — 14.0 T — 7-2390. One end has gone into the concrete and burst along the seam, and through the seam, stacked as neat as loaves on a baker's board, red-brown bars as long as a forearm, each one stamped with the closed eye. Beside it, the tarp, and the boots.

look.again: The box on its side, the copper in the split.

passives.text: Cast copper. A bar that size is thirty kilos if it is a gram, and a box like this holds a thousand of them packed like that. Thirty tonnes, on a bill of fourteen; under a crane whose plate says twenty-five.
The spreader's twistlocks are still in the box's corner castings, sheared clean through. They did not come unlatched. They broke.

interject.text: Kes crouches at the split and turns a bar over with her boot. "Copper," she says. "Halcyon pulls it out of the Teeth by the trainload; the whole arcology's wired with it. They're selling it west." She reads the stencil. "And lying about it, obviously."
"A man under a load," Ilya says quietly. "You don't unlatch wrong after eleven years. You get tired. Or somebody tells you to hurry."

ladder.text: Crane Six's ladder goes up inside a cage on the crane's leg, forty feet to the cab: a steel box with its glass gone dark. A chain across the ladder's foot with a padlock, and a guild guard on the quay who looks at the chain every time he turns.
ladder.again: The ladder in its cage, the chain, the guard turning.

options.text: (Unhook the chain and climb, as Connie's relief.)
(Climb the outside of the cage while the guard's back is turned.)

mods.why: you know when a man is not looking

night.text: At night the cab is dark, the guard is up at the Customs House steps, and the chain is still on the ladder with its padlock.
night.again: The dark cab, the chain, the padlock.

caught.text: "Off the leg." The guard has not raised his voice or his shotgun; he has only turned round at the wrong moment. "Ten Tolls for the climb, or the Harbour Master hears about it."

locked.text: The padlock is older than it looks and better. It does not give, and something in it bends that should not. Better come back by day with somebody's leave.
locked.again: The padlock that would not give.

cab.text: The cab: a seat with the stuffing out, two levers worn bright as cutlery, a pre-war panel with a dial for the load and, under a glass lid, a recorder with a strip of waxed paper hanging out of it like a tongue. Beside the dial, a key switch: OVERRIDE. The quay below is a map of hats.
cab.again: The cab: the dial, the recorder's tongue of paper, the key switch.

interject.text: "Pre-war and unnetworked, no Concern board anywhere in it," Kes says, rapping the panel with a knuckle. "Dumb as a fencepost and about as honest. It said no." She looks at the key switch. "Somebody made it shut up."

mods.why: the printer's codes are an old standard
Kes reads it over your shoulder

tape.text: You tear the strip off and read it against the light. 02:06 LIFT 31.2 T — OVERLOAD — CUTOUT. 02:07 KEY 6/N — OVERRIDE. 02:08 LIFT. 02:10 SPREADER — LOCK FAULT. Then nothing at all: the box was on the quay, and the recorder had nothing more to say.

tape_no.text: Codes in faded purple on waxed paper, times and numbers and abbreviations in a pre-war standard you cannot read. The strip tears off in your hand anyway. Somebody who weighs things for a living would know what it says.
tape_no.again: Codes you cannot read on a strip of wax.

keyswitch.text: The override is a key switch beside the load dial, its brass collar polished by thumbs. Round the slot the brass is scratched bright in a ring: a key that did not quite fit, turned hard, many times over many nights. A factory key does not do that.
keyswitch.again: The scratched ring round the key switch.

done.text: Crane Six's cab, where you tore the tape off the recorder. Somebody has fitted a new roll.
done.again: Six's cab, a new roll in the recorder.

text.text: The tally board on its post: every gang ON, Gang Nine among them, all eight names. Chalked across the top, in letters a hand high, by somebody who has never written so big: WE STOOD.
The tally board: GANG NINE — OFF — BY ORDER. Somebody chalked BLACK across the board once; it has been washed off, and the wash left a grey cloud the shape of the word.
The tally board: every gang on it chalked BLACK — BOND, and under the board, on the concrete, a ring of boots where people have been standing all night so that nobody can say the Stand was empty.

The tally board: GANG NINE — ON. Under it, in the Harbour Master's clerk's hand: ALL THROUGH BOXES TO THE PLATE — BY ORDER OF THE COURT. And under that, in chalk: LYSENKO SOLD THE CUTOUT, which somebody else has half rubbed out.
The tally board: GANG NINE — ON — NEGLIGENCE STRUCK BY THE COURT — SIX AT COMPLEMENT. Somebody has drawn a small crane beside Dmytro's name, very carefully.

The tally board on its post, the gangs in columns of names. GANG NINE — STOOD DOWN — DOCKER'S NEGLIGENCE (LYSENKO, D., HOOKER-ON) — NO FUNERAL TALLY — BY ORDER. The other seven of Nine's names have a chalk line through them.

board.again: The tally board, and Gang Nine's names.

text.text: Dawn, and nobody on the Stand is being called: the whole quay is on the line with its arms folded, facing the Bond.

Dawn on the Stand: a hundred people on a white line with their breath smoking, and the gang-masters walking down it with clipboards, choosing with a tap on the shoulder. Gang Nine stands at the back of the line, and nobody taps them.
Dawn on the Stand: a hundred people on a white line with their breath smoking, and the gang-masters walking down it with clipboards, choosing with a tap on the shoulder.

callon.again: The line at dawn, the clipboards coming down it.

options.text: (Stand on the line for the call-on.)

mods.why: Connie nods at you, and the gang-master sees it

text.text: A tap on the shoulder. Eight hours on Two's gang, slinging timber off a barge, with a full gang and a break at the fourth hour that nobody has to ask for. Twelve Tolls in tallies at the floor at the end of it, and Constance on Two's lever calling the lifts as if she had all the time in the world.

A tap on the shoulder. Eight hours on a gang, slinging timber off a barge and hooking on boxes for a crane that lifts what it is given, until your hands are somebody else's. Eight Tolls in tallies at the floor at the end of it, which the floor pays out at par, minus one for the floor.

picked.again: Eight hours on a gang, and tallies at the floor.

passed_over.text: The gang-master walks past you without slowing, taps the man beside you, and the line closes up behind him. By the time the clipboards are at the end of it the sun is up and the Stand is half empty, and the half that is left goes home.

line.speaker: narrator
line.text: Dawn, and the Stand is full: every docker on the quay on the white line with their arms folded, Constance in the middle of them, Oksana at the end with her fish knife in her apron. Facing them, between the line and the Bond's gate, three men from the Ring: one with a sledge on his shoulder, one with a pipe, one with a zip gun stuck in his belt. Behind them, at a careful distance, Platt with his clipboard, not calling anybody. The one with the sledge says, to the line in general: "Day's pay to work a crane. Nobody has to get hurt. Off the line."
line.again: The Ring's men, the line, and nobody moving.

talked.text: The one with the sledge looks at you, and at the line, and at Platt behind him, who is looking at the sky. Then he puts the sledge back on his shoulder. "Day's pay's a day's pay," he says. "Night's pay's more than they offered." They go off up the river road the way they came. By noon the Bond's clerk comes down to the Stand with an envelope for Oksana Lysenko, through the guild, with nothing written on it; by night the first Concern box sits on Hruska's plate under its seal while the needle swings, and the whole quay watches it settle.
talked.again: The Ring's men gone up the river road, and a box on the plate.

paid.speaker: narrator
paid.text: You count sixty into the sledge man's hand. He weighs it, looks at the line, and shrugs. "Same pay for less work," he says. "The Ring always takes that." They go off up the river road. By noon the Bond's clerk comes down to the Stand with an envelope for Oksana Lysenko, through the guild, with nothing written on it; by night the first Concern box sits on Hruska's plate under its seal, and the whole quay watches the needle settle.

aside.speaker: narrator
aside.text: You step off the line. Nobody says anything. Then the man next to where you were steps off it too, and the woman next to him, and the line comes apart from the end like a rope unlaying, and the Ring's men walk through the gap to Crane Six. Constance is the last on the white paint, alone, and then she walks to Crane Two and climbs into the cab and sits there with the door shut.
aside.again: The line come apart, and Connie alone on the paint.

intro.text: "You walked round the tarp instead of over it. Most strangers don't." A woman on the Stand with a crane driver's gloves through her belt and grey in the roots of her cornrows, watching the tally board. "Constance. Connie, on the line. That's Dmytro Lysenko under there: hooker-on, night gang, Gang Nine, eleven years on Six and never a box down. The guild's board says he unlatched the spreader wrong. Gang Nine's stood down until the Harbour Master hears it, no tally, and his widow gets no funeral. Eight families." She looks at you. "You look like somebody who asks questions. Ask them. We can't; we'd lose our place on the line."
intro.again: Connie on the line, watching Gang Nine's names with the chalk through them.

interject.text: Wren looks along the white line, at the gang-masters, at the Bond's lights. "Same as the halts," she says to you. "The ones who carry it don't get paid when it doesn't arrive."

options.text: What does the Harbour Master need to hear?
Can I get up into Six's cab?

text.text: "Look at it." Connie nods down the line: full, every gang, Nine among them. "Twenty-two years on Two and I didn't know we could. Now we do. So does the guild. So does the Bond."

"Dmytro sold the cutout." She says it flatly. "If you'd told me that the day he died I'd have put you in the Basin. Gang Nine's on the line. That's what I asked you for." She looks at the tarp's stain. "It isn't what I wanted."
"The guild paid for his funeral. The quay thinks the guild killed him." She looks at you, longer than she needs to. "Is that what happened?" She does not wait for an answer.
Connie does not look round. "Gang Nine's still off the line," she says to the tally board. "Whatever you found."
"Dawn," Connie says. "On the line. They'll send to the Ring for men; they always do. We'll be here."
Connie on the line, watching Gang Nine's names with the chalk through them.

The Stand could black the Bond. Every Concern box, until it pays.

hear.text: "Something she can hold." Connie holds up a hand, empty. "Dahl keeps the port by the Act, and the Act's a book. Bring her a thing that's written or a thing she can put on the table, and she rules on what's in front of her, at the change of shift, on the steps. She's hanged guild men on the facts. She's hanged dockers on the facts. She has never once ruled on what anybody felt."

think.text: "I think Six lifted a box Six shouldn't lift." She looks up at the crane. "Six has a cutout: pre-war, dumb, honest. Over twenty-five tonnes and she won't lift; the arm just sits there humming. That box —" She does not finish. "Ask the box. Ask the cab. And ask Platt, the night gang-master, why Nine was five hands on Six the night it happened, when Six wants eight."
think.again: "Ask the box. Ask the cab. Ask Platt."

cab.text: "Six is the guild's. I drive Two." She thinks about it. "The cab's not locked by day; the ladder's chained and the guard on the quay watches the chain. I'll tell him you're my relief. He won't believe it, and he won't say so." She puts two fingers in her mouth and whistles at the guard, and points at you, and the guard looks at you and away.
cab.again: "You're my relief. He won't say so."

callon.text: "Dawn, on the line." She toes the white paint. "The gang-masters walk down it and tap who they want. You stand, you look like you can lift, you get tapped or you don't. A day on a gang is eight in tallies at the floor, which pays you seven, because it's the floor." She shrugs. "It was ten, when I started. Nobody voted on that either."
callon.again: "Dawn, on the line. Eight in tallies; the floor pays seven."

bond.text: "The Concern's yard." She does not look at it. "Everything off the through goes in there sealed and comes out sealed. Their fence, their lights, their man in his clean office. The Act says the Harbour Master's word stops at the fence. We work the boxes in and out of the gate and we don't go past the line." She spits, neatly, on the guild's side of it. "The lights never go off. I've always wondered what they need to see."

girl.text: Connie looks at you for a long moment. "Espe's got a lot of nieces," she says. "Every one of them's from the Hulls." Then, lower: "If you're going to ask her, ask her straight, and don't ask her near the fence. Tell her I said you could be told."
girl.again: "Tell Espe I said you could be told."

text.text: Her face does nothing at all. "Show me." You show her the tin. She takes the key out and turns it over and holds it up to the light, the hand-cut teeth, the 6/N stamped a little crooked. "He cut it himself. I taught him to cut keys." She puts it back. She looks at the blue caps for a long time. "His girl," she says. "Those blue things. That's what she breathes through." She closes the tin and gives it back. "So what do I tell the line? That Dmytro was a thief? That the guild was right?"

Her face does nothing at all. "Prove it." You tell her what you know: the tape, the key, the blue caps. She listens to the end without moving. "His girl," she says. "Those blue things. That's what she breathes through." She looks at the tarp. "So what do I tell the line? That Dmytro was a thief? That the guild was right?"

truth.again: "So what do I tell the line?"

interject.text: "He sold it for his girl's breath," Ash says. "That's not a thief. That's a father with a bad choice and a good reason." He looks at Connie. "Bury him as one."

options.text: Tell them the Bond paid him to do it, so its boxes would never be weighed.

black_offer.text: "The Bond pays a docker to switch off the thing that keeps dockers alive, so it can cheat the guild on the ton. And the guild never weighs the through, because its contract with the Concern says the through doesn't stop." She looks down the line, the length of it. "If the Stand stopped working Concern boxes. All of us. Every gang. Until the Concern pays Oksana and every box goes over the plate." She looks back at you. "They'd send to the Ring for men who'll work a crane for a day's pay. They always do. Will you stand on the line with us at dawn?"
black_offer.again: "Will you stand on the line with us at dawn?"

black_yes.text: "Dawn, then. On the line." She walks off down the quay without another word, and you watch her stop at every box in the Boxes, one by one, and at the barge, and at the fish steps, and at the Hulls' stairs. By dark there is chalk on every gang's column on the tally board: BLACK — BOND.

black_no.text: "Not on what you've got." She shakes her head. "The line won't stop for a story. Two hundred families lose a day's tallies for every day it stands. It'll stop for a paper it can read, that says the Bond did this on purpose." She looks at the fence. "Bring me that."
black_no.again: "Bring me a paper the line can read."

intro.text: A big man with a clipboard and a whistle on a cord, who calls the night gangs' names off the board without looking at the board. "Platt. Night gang-master. If you're on the line, stand on it. If you're asking about Nine, the board says what happened."
intro.again: Platt, with the clipboard.

options.text: How many were on Six that night?

Platt, with the clipboard. "The board says what happened."

short.text: "Five." He does not need the clipboard for it. "Six wants eight: the driver, the hooker-on, two on the tag lines, four on the deck. Nine was five. By order." He taps the clipboard with the whistle. "The through turns in four hours or the guild pays the Concern for every hour it stands at the throat. The Harbour Master's clerk writes the order. I call who I'm told I can call."
short.again: "Five, by order. I call who I'm told I can call."

interject.text: "Demurrage," Odile says, very quietly. "A clause that charges you for the hours a train stands is a clause that has bought your clock." She looks at the clipboard. "I wrote the first sheet of that contract, at Ninebridge, a long time ago. The demurrage was mine. I meant it for the Concern's trains." A pause. "That is a cost."

key.text: "Mine." He pulls it out on its chain from under his shirt: a factory key, heavy brass, 6/N stamped deep and square. "On my belt every night of my life. It was on my belt at two. I was at the yard throat with the through's guard, counting seals." He puts it away. "Ask the guard. Ask the seals."

dmytro.text: "Eleven years on Six. Best hooker-on I had. Didn't drink." He looks at the tarp, and away. "His girl coughs. He asked me for day shifts so he could be home with her at night. I couldn't give him them; the night gang's short as it is." He says it as if somebody had asked him to justify it, and nobody had.

order.text: He unclips a sheet from the bottom of the stack and hands it to you without looking at it. NIGHT — GANG NINE — FIVE HANDS — BY ORDER. "Take it. I wrote the eight in, in pencil, when it came down. Then I crossed it out, because the clerk said."
order.again: "I wrote the eight in. Then I crossed it out."

order_no.text: "The order's guild paper." He clips the board shut. "You want guild paper, climb the Customs House steps and ask the Harbour Master for it."

intro.text: A woman on the fish steps with a short knife and a basket of mullet, gutting without looking at her hands. She does not stop when you speak to her. "If you're from the guild, say so. If you're from the Bond, go away."
intro.again: Oksana on the fish steps, gutting.

interject.text: Tamsin sits down on the step below her without asking, takes a mullet out of the basket and starts gutting it, badly. Oksana watches her ruin it, and something in her face lets go a little. "Not like that," she says. "Like this."

options.text: What did he do on the night gang?

text.text: "The Concern paid." Oksana does not look up from the knife. "Through the guild, in an envelope, with nothing written on it. Nobody said sorry. I didn't want them to." She guts a fish. "He's under the Star. Zoya chose the place."

"They said his name on the steps." She guts a fish. "The man who sold the cutout." Another. "Zoya breathes over a kettle now, with a towel on her head. The Bond doesn't pay the dead." She does not say it to you as an accusation. She says it to the fish.
"The guild paid for the funeral. He's under the Star." She looks at you once, sideways. "They think the guild killed him." She goes back to the fish. "Let them."
"We've moved down to the Hulls," Oksana says. "Kobby had a cabin on the Star." She guts a fish. "The box is cheaper than the Boxes."
Oksana on the fish steps, gutting.
